name: MNG: Earthquake - 04-2026 - MNG: Earthquake-04-2026
summary:
At 12:23 on 26 April 2026 (Ulaanbaatar time), a 5.5 magnitude earthquake struck Zereg soum in Khovd province. The epicentre was located at latitude 46.90 and longitude 93.01. The earthquake was followed by a 4.2 magnitude aftershock at 12:27 PM, shortly after the initial event.

This marks the third seismic event recorded in the same area within four days. On 22 April 2026, two earthquakes measuring 4.2 and 3.9 magnitudes were recorded in the region. 

The epicentre was located approximately:

  • 26 km southeast of Zereg soum centre, Khovd province;
  • 28 km northeast of Must soum centre, Khovd province;
  • 166 km south of Jargalant soum, Khovd province;
  • 40km northwest of Tsetseg soum centre, Kobd province.

According to official sources, no damage has been reported at this time. Information collected from heads of primary-level Red Cross branches in the affected soums also indicates that there are currently no reported casualties, damage, or other impacts.

countries.name: Paraguay
dtype.name: Epidemic
name: PRY: Epidemic - 04-2026 - Epidemic / Outbreak of respiratory diseases (Influenza / ETI)
summary:
There is a sustained increase in consultations for Influenza-like Illness (INFLU-like Illness) in Paraguay, with an increase of 22% in epidemiological week 14. The event is mainly associated with the early circulation of the Influenza A H3N2 virus, at the beginning of the seasonal period. There is a risk of an increase in hospitalizations due to severe acute respiratory infections (SARI), especially in vulnerable populations, which could put pressure on health services. 

The sustained increase in cases of Influenza-like Illness (INFLU-like Illness) is generating a greater demand for outpatient consultations in health services, constituting the main primary effect of the event. This situation increases the risk of progressive saturation of the health system, especially in emergency and primary care services. 

Among the side effects, there is the potential increase in hospitalizations for severe acute respiratory infections (SARI), particularly in vulnerable groups such as children, the elderly, pregnant women, and people with chronic diseases. This could lead to a greater occupancy of hospital beds and intensive care units, as well as the need to reinforce medical supplies, medicines, and human resources. 

In addition, the high transmissibility of respiratory viruses favors community spread, which impacts the population through increased absenteeism from work and school, as well as pressure on public health services. 

Together, these effects show a risk of overloading the health system in the coming weeks, requiring the strengthening of surveillance, prevention, and response capacities.

name: COD: Population displacement - 04-2026 - Population movement in Pangi territory, Maniema Province in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
summary:
It is since April 01, 2026 that tension has been observed in the Pangi Territory, precisely in the cities of Kampene and Kayuyu and the surrounding villages. The populations of this part woke up under a strong psychosis, at the base, the presence of elements of the Wazalendo group of the Self-proclaimed General KIWIS, who came to impose their law in contradiction to the Rega custom  originating in the area. The natives, not wanting to bend to this constraint,  triggered a confrontation, going as far as the loss of human lives, including a major of the Wazalendo group shining brightly. Part of the population of Kampene center, Kayuyu and the surrounding villages who could not bear this confrontation, decided to withdraw and move towards the bush in search of a safer place.  

The clashes resurfaced on Monday 20/04/2026; where some houses have been shining, on the other hand acts suffered by the victims of other times. On their return, the Rega customary guardians resolved to confront the opposing party, made up of members of the Zimba tribe, with whom they have shared the borders since their existence, between the Territory of Kasongo and Pangi. This climate of despair characterized the entire day of Monday, April 20, 2026, disturbing the tranquility of the population in the city of Kapane. In view of this atmosphere, the members of the Zimba community, the population were forced to move to shelters considered safer.

This displacement has pushed more than 562 households , or 3372 people  , out of their homes, most of whom are exposed to bad weather, including children, pregnant women and3rd age people, to the fear of insecurity in the environment.

There is a risk that the movement of the population will continue with the arrival of the FARDC in the city of Kindu  where their movement is observed at the beach/right bank of the Congo River, towards the road to the city of Kampene.

countries.name: Malaysia
dtype.name: Fire
name: MYS: Fire - 04-2026 - Sandakan Fire
summary:
A major fire incident occurred in the early hours at Kampung Bahagia, Batu Sapi, Sandakan, resulting in extensive destruction and significant impact on the local community. The incident, which took place at approximately 1:30 a.m., was reported to the authorities and subsequently led to the area being declared a disaster zone at 4:00 a.m. by the relevant authorities.

Kampung Bahagia, a densely populated water settlement consisting of approximately 1,200 houses, was severely affected by the fire. Initial assessments indicate that nearly 1,000 houses were destroyed, affecting an estimated 9,007 individuals. The scale of the incident places it among the most significant fire events recorded in the area, with widespread displacement and loss of shelter among affected households.

Preliminary information further indicates that approximately 70 percent of the affected population are non-citizens, while the remaining 30 percent are Malaysian citizens. The area has previously been associated with displaced communities, including individuals formerly under UNHCR arrangements, and has been identified by the state government for potential development into a formal settlement.

name: PRY: Civil Unrest - 04-2026 - Incident at Mass Sporting Event – Superclásico (Asunción, Paraguay)
summary:
In the context of the Paraguayan soccer superclassic, incidents were recorded in the vicinity of the Defensores del Chaco Stadium, involving attendees of the event and security forces. These events led to disturbances and damage in areas near the stadium.

As a result, at least 56 people were injured, including civilians and police officers, who required attention in health centers, mainly at the Barrio Obrero Hospital.

The event had an immediate impact on the health of those affected, with injuries such as trauma and contusions, as well as a one-off demand on emergency services and health care.

Additionally, damage to homes and affecting the resident population in the vicinity of the stadium is reported, reaching more than 300 families. This has generated impacts on the living conditions of the local community.

The incidents were not limited to the immediate surroundings of the event, but also affected nearby neighborhoods, evidencing risks associated with the management of large concentrations of people in urban contexts.

The situation was contained after a few hours after the intervention of the competent authorities; however, impacts on the affected population persist and there is a risk that similar situations may be repeated in future events.

dtype.name: Population Movement
name: COD: Population displacement - 04-2026 - Population movement in Oicha capital of Beni Territory, North Kivu Province in the Democratic Republic of Congo
summary:
Since October 2025, the population of the Mambanika, Tenambo, Mabasele and  Kekelibo neighborhoods have moved  to Oicha, the capital of Beni territory, following the resurgence of attacks by the ADF (Allied Democratic Forces) against the civilian population in Mambasa territory in Ituri province. These attacks were far from being brought under control after the carnage in Mutchatcha, but they  hit several villages before hitting the center of Mambasa and advancing northwards on the Mambasa-Komanda axis. Apart from these villages, it should be noted  that several villages on the Eringeti-Komanda axis had also been  affected by the same rebels before coming to resettle in the Bambuba-Kisiki grouping in a mining area in Kamanyola 800km from the national road after attacking the village of Kamungu on the Eringeti-Kainama axis in North Kivu. Apart from the axes cited, it must also be said  that the territory of Lubero is not to be outdone, similar attacks have been reported in the Bapakombe groupings in the Bapere and Mwenye sectors since January 2026 until the present day.

The toll is more or less 250 deaths recorded since January 2026 to date. In addition to this toll, several families report the disappearance of some of their loved ones, more or less 103 injured have been recorded, more than 100 residential houses have been burned, several livelihoods  burned and/or looted by the attackers.

The incursion of Wednesday, April 15, 2026, in the evening, in the village of Kamungu, 15 km from Eringeti, Kainama axis where the provisional toll was several civilians reported missing  according to civil society,  it should be mentioned that in Mambasa territory, a series of attacks on mining quarries as well as several villages were recorded between March 31 and April 15, 2026 resulting in more than 35 recorded deaths, several missing, houses burned and the displacement of populations to the supposedly secure entities. The villages attacked are Muchacha, Badengaido, Bafwakoa, Mambasa center and others. These figures come from  local whistleblowers  as the search continues and as a result, the death toll could rise at  any moment to our attention.

Overall, since January 2026 to  the present day, 40434 households, or 240056 people , have moved  to the city and territory of Beni with about 8247 households spread over rural communes, including 4400 in Oicha ; 1950 in Mangina and 3550 in Mabalako. There are 4 sites of displaced people in Oicha namely Oicha  1 site,  Oicha  2 site,  Mulohu  site and Mabasele site.

name: IDN: Earthquake - 04-2026 - Disaster Assessment Report: East Flores Earthquake
summary:
1. Event Overview

An earthquake struck East Flores Regency, East Nusa Tenggara Province, on Thursday, 9 April at 04:53 WIB. The earthquake had a magnitude of 3.7 and occurred at a depth of 10 km. The epicenter was located on land, approximately 24 km southeast of Larantuka, at coordinates 8.42°S and 123.17°E.

2. Seismic Activity

Following the initial earthquake, several aftershocks were recorded:

  • At 04:59 WIB, magnitude 4.0 at a depth of 3 km
  • At 05:42 WIB, at a depth of 5 km

According to the Meteorological, Climatological, and Geophysical Agency (BMKG), the earthquake was felt at intensity levels II–III on the Modified Mercalli Intensity (MMI) scale in East Flores. The event has no tsunami potential.

As of Thursday afternoon (9 April), approximately 60 aftershocks have been recorded, indicating ongoing seismic activity with the possibility of further tremors.

3. Impact Summary

The earthquake has resulted in the following impacts:

  • 35 households (140 individuals) affected
  • 35 houses severely damaged
  • 2 people lightly injured
  • 1 prayer facility (musala) affected

4. Current Situation

Assessment activities are still ongoing to determine the full extent of the damage.
As of now, there are no reports of displacement.

BMKG continues to advise the public to remain vigilant due to the potential for additional aftershocks.

summary:
1. SEISMIC EVENT DATA
A powerful earthquake has been recorded with the following parameters:

2. TSUNAMI OBSERVATIONS & THREAT ASSESSMENT
Following the earthquake, a Tsunami Early Warning (Level 3) was issued. The following observations and predicted arrival times have been recorded:
A. Verified Tsunami Observations (Actual Readings)
 1) West Halmahera    0.3 Meters    06:08 WIB    23:08 UTC (April 1)
 2) Bitung    0.2 Meters    06:15 WIB    23:15 UTC (April 1)

1) North Minahasa    0.75 Meters    06:18 WIB    23:18 UTC (April 1)

5) Bitung    0.20 Meters    06:15 WIB    23:15 UTC (April 1)

3. CURRENT FIELD SITUATION
As of the current reporting cycle, the following conditions are confirmed:
1) Casualties: One (1) reported fatality. Investigations are ongoing to determine if the cause of death was trauma from the earthquake or other medical complications.
2) Aftershocks: Seven (7) significant aftershocks have been detected following the main 7.6 M quake.

3) WASPADA (Advisory): Instructing the community to stay away from beaches and riverbanks.

5. EMERGENCY CONTACTS & ACTIONS
1) Residents are urged to stay away from the coastline until the tsunami warning is officially lifted.
2) Monitor official channels: BMKG (InaTEWS) and BNPB.
3) Verify all information before sharing to prevent the spread of misinformation/hoaxes.

countries.name: Pakistan
dtype.name: Pluvial/Flash Flood
name: PAK: Pluvial/Flash Flood - 04-2026 - PAK: Pluvial/Flash Flood - 04-2026 - PAK
summary:
As of 4 April 2026, Pakistan is experiencing a high-alert weather situation due to an active westerly system expected to persist until 8–9 April, bringing widespread heavy rain, thunderstorms, strong winds, and snowfall in high-altitude areas. The system has already caused serious impacts, including at least 25 fatalities and dozens of injuries in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP), along with the damage or destruction of over 70 houses, road disruptions, and localized flooding. Additional casualties and property damage have been reported in other provinces. Ongoing rainfall continues to heighten the risks of urban flooding, flash floods, landslides, and glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs), particularly in northern regions such as KP and Gilgit‑Baltistan.

Authorities have issued warnings for continued rain, windstorms, and thunderstorms, especially in Balochistan from 5–9 April, and have urged residents to avoid unnecessary travel, exercise caution, and follow local preparedness measures. The Pakistan Red Crescent Society is on standby with its response teams and has activated its Emergency Operations Centre (EOC) to coordinate preparedness and response efforts. The situation remains highly dynamic, with further heavy precipitation expected to exacerbate existing hazards and disrupt infrastructure, services, and livelihoods.

Tuberculosis is an airborne infectious disease, whose spread is favored in closed environments, with overcrowding and limited ventilation, conditions present in the affected establishment. The event has led to the declaration of a health alert and the implementation of exceptional control measures.

countries.name: Congo

name: COG: Epidemic - 03-2026 - Response to the Mpox and Cholera Epidemics in Congo Brazzaville
summary:
The Africa Centres for Disease Prevention and Control have long announced that Mpox is a public health event of continental concern, while the World Health Organization (WHO) held a meeting to determine whether the current Mpox situation in Africa constitutes a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC). 
The Republic of Congo has been facing cholera and mpox epidemics since July 2025, which required the activation of national public health emergency management mechanisms.
As of July 26, 2025, a total of 181 suspected cases and 12 deaths have been recorded in the two localities. The epidemic mainly affects men (62%). The age groups over 50 years old, followed by those aged 15 to 29, are the most affected.

They represent 42 per cent of those of concern to UNHCR, of whom 37 per cent are refugees and 5 per cent are asylum-seekers, mainly from Nigeria (59 per cent), Mali (29 per cent) and Burkina Faso (11 per cent). countries.name: Afghanistan
dtype.name: Flood
name: Afghanistan: Flash Floods, 2026
summary:
Following heavy and sustained rainfall, flash floods occurred in March 2026 across the country, affecting communities in Helmand, Herat, Badghis, Uruzgan, Samangan, Laghman and Parwan provinces. Low-lying areas and settlements located along riverbeds were particularly impacted. The floods resulted in loss of life, injuries, and widespread damage to shelters, livelihoods and agricultural land, reflecting the broader pattern of seasonal flooding currently affecting several parts of the country.

According to preliminary information compiled by the Afghan Red Crescent Society (ARCS), more than 280 families were affected. The floods caused 9 deaths and 14 injuries, with no cases of missing persons reported. Shelter damage was significant, with 287 houses completely and partially damaged, particularly in several provinces of Helmand, Herat, Badghis, Uruzgan, Samangan, Laghman and Parwan. In addition, the floods had a severe impact on livelihoods, resulting in the loss of 1,124 livestock and damage to approximately 2,213 jeribs of agricultural land, further increasing vulnerabilities among farming and pastoral households.

ARCS, through its provincial branches and volunteers, is monitoring the evolving situation and conducting initial assessments in coordination with local authorities and Movement partners. Priority humanitarian needs identified include emergency shelter and essential household items for families whose homes were destroyed or damaged, food assistance and multipurpose cash support, as well as livelihood and agricultural recovery assistance, including livestock support. With possibility of further rainfall, affected communities remain at risk of additional flooding, underscoring the need for timely humanitarian support.

countries.name: Russian Federation
dtype.name: Flood
name: RUS: Flood - 03-2026 - Emergency in Dagestan Region (Russian Federation)
summary:
1. General Overview of the Situation
Since 28 March 2026, a complex flood situation has persisted in the Republic of Dagestan, caused by heavy rainfall and strong gusty winds. The most affected areas include Makhachkala, the Khasavyurt district, Derbent, and a number of municipalities across the republic.
As of 30 March, the situation has begun to stabilize; however, recovery and emergency response operations continue in certain areas.

2. Scale of the Emergency
A state of emergency has been declared in Makhachkala, Buynaksk, and the Khasavyurt district. Previously, a high-alert regime had been in place across the republic, while the consequences of the severe weather affected dozens of settlements and hundreds of households.
At the peak of the disruptions, more than 500,000 residents were left without electricity. By 29–30 March, power supply had been restored for the majority of consumers.

3. Affected Population
According to the Ministry of Emergency Situations of Russia, 3,338 people, including 1,033 children, were evacuated from flooded areas. Temporary accommodation centers hosted 58 individuals, including 32 children.
In the Khasavyurt district, hundreds of households in four villages were flooded; 43 patients were evacuated from a hospital in the village of Botayurt. In Makhachkala and other cities, residents experienced flooding of homes and yards, as well as disruptions in water and electricity supply.

4. Damage
As of 29 March, 760 residential houses and 950 household plots remained flooded, alongside reported damage to road and utility infrastructure. By 30 March, the number of affected objects had decreased: 235 residential houses, 550 household plots, and 10 road sections remained flooded.
The disaster also damaged energy infrastructure: at the peak, hundreds of power lines were simultaneously out of service, while pumping operations and equipment restoration continued at several substations. Damage and erosion of bridges were also recorded, including railway infrastructure.

5. Affected Settlements
The most significantly affected areas include Makhachkala, Khasavyurt, Derbent, Dagestanskiye Ogni, Izberbash, Kaspiysk, as well as villages in the Khasavyurt district, including Adilotar, Kadyrotar, Tutlar, and Novy Tsilitl. Flooding was also reported in the Kaitag district and in several mountainous and foothill areas.
As of 30 March, hundreds of households in the Khasavyurt district remained flooded, while restoration work continued at the “Makhachkala-110,” “Vostochnaya,” and “Primorskaya” substations in Makhachkala.

6. Distance from Makhachkala
Makhachkala is the center of the events; Kaspiysk is approximately 15 km away; Izberbash is about 65 km to the south; Derbent approximately 120 km to the south; Dagestanskiye Ogni about 130 km to the south; Khasavyurt approximately 160 km to the north; and villages in the Khasavyurt district are located roughly within 150–170 km from Makhachkala, depending on the specific locality.
The Kaitag district is located approximately 110 km south of Makhachkala, while certain mountainous settlements identified as most affected by precipitation are situated even further, at distances of approximately 200 km or more.

7. Response Measures
Temporary accommodation centers were established for evacuees, drinking water supply was organized, and round-the-clock operations were carried out to pump out water, restore electricity, and clear affected areas. Emergency response teams, rescue personnel, and assessment commissions were deployed on site.
According to official reports, as of 30 March, priority efforts are focused on restoring substations, eliminating localized flooding, and assessing damage in order to provide subsequent assistance to affected families.

Heavy and persistent rainfall in Rungwe District has triggered a deadly landslide affecting several wards, including Nkunga, Lupepo, Kawetele, and Ikuti. According to an official statement issued by the Regional Police Commander of Mbeya Region, the incident has resulted in 18 fatalities, including 14 children, with additional reports of injuries and missing persons.

Effects of the hazard

The landslide has caused widespread destruction of homes and infrastructure, burying houses and personal belongings under mud and debris. Key impacts include:

  • Loss of life and multiple injuries
  • Destruction of houses, leaving families homeless
  • Damage to roads and access routes, limiting rescue and relief operations
  • Disruption of livelihoods, particularly for households dependent on agriculture

Search and rescue operations are ongoing, with communities and responders working under challenging conditions due to unstable ground and continued rainfall.

Current context

The situation remains critical as rains continue, increasing the risk of secondary landslides. Access to some affected areas is still constrained, slowing emergency response efforts. Local authorities, in collaboration with humanitarian actors including the Tanzania Red Cross Society, are actively engaged in search, rescue, and initial relief operations.

Emergency needs are rapidly evolving, with priority on:

  • Search and rescue
  • Emergency shelter
  • Food assistance
  • Health services and psychosocial support
  • WASH (water, sanitation, and hygiene) interventions

Affected population and impact

The disaster has significantly affected vulnerable populations, particularly children, women, and elderly individuals. Many households have lost:

  • Shelter and essential household items
  • Food stocks and sources of income
  • Access to clean water and sanitation facilities

Displaced families are currently seeking refuge in temporary shelters and with host communities, facing heightened risks of disease outbreaks and protection concerns.

Search and rescue operations are ongoing, led by government fire and rescue teams in collaboration with the Tanzania Red Cross Society. Efforts are focused on locating individuals feared to be trapped under debris following the landslide. Red Cross volunteers are providing First Aid (FA) on-site and facilitating referral services for injured individuals to nearby health facilities. In addition, Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) is being delivered to affected families, particularly those who have lost relatives or remain missing, to help address trauma and emotional distress caused by the incident.

summary:
On March 2, 2026, Guinean soldiers seized equipment owned by BK Enterprise, a Liberian company mining sand on the Makona River, claiming mineral extraction and ownership of the river. Despite intervention by Liberia’s Minister of Internal Affairs, tensions escalated when Guinean soldiers hoisted Guinean national flag on Liberian soil on March 10, later removed by local youths. A MRU Heads of State meeting on March 16 produced a communiqué committing to peace, security, and respect for territorial integrity, yet Guinean soldiers remain armed on Liberian soil. Their presence has displaced families from Sorlumba and 25 other surrounding villages, disrupted schooling, and restricted access to farmland, raising urgent humanitarian concerns, including possible food insecurity (depending on duration of conflict) and protection risks.

·       Guinean soldiers remain entrenched on Liberian territory at Sorlumba.

·       Citizens from Sorlumba and 25 surrounding villages have been displaced, particularly along the riverbank.

·       High-level Liberian security and government officials have visited the area. Reports indicate displaced families lack food because of their inability to access their farmland, raising concerns of a possible food insecurity.

·       Liberia has deployed armed police and border patrol immigration officers to stabilize the area. Citizens have been advised to remain calm as the government pursues diplomatic channels.

  • March 2, 2026: Guinean soldiers seized equipment belonging to BK Enterprise, a Liberian construction company conducting sand mining on the Makona River. Soldiers alleged the company was extracting minerals (gold/diamonds) and claimed the river belongs to Guinea.
  • March 4, 2026: Following intervention by Liberia’s Minister of Internal Affairs, Guinean soldiers stated that equipment would only be returned if Liberia’s Ministry of Mines and Geology confirmed it was solely for sand mining.
  • March 10, 2026: Guinean soldiers hoisted their flag on Liberian soil, causing panic. Local youths removed the flag and replaced it with Liberia’s flag. Soldiers withdrew.
  • On March 16, 2026, an emergency Mano River Union (MRU) Heads of State meeting was convened in Conakry, facilitated by the Foreign Minister of Côte d’Ivoire. The meeting brought together the Presidents of Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone.
  • On March 20, Guinean soldiers again entered another border community in Liberia (Konadu), where they hoisted their flag on Liberian soil. 

    The situation at the Liberia–Guinea border in Sorlumba presents significant risks of escalation at both security and humanitarian levels. The continued presence of heavily armed Guinean soldiers on Liberian soil undermines territorial integrity and raises the potential for violent confrontation, particularly given the mobilization of local youths. Diplomatic efforts, including the MRU communiqué, have so far failed to deter renewed incursions, creating uncertainty about regional stability. Humanitarian risks are already evident, with the displacement of families from 25 villages, restricted access to farmland, and disruption of schools, which could quickly evolve into food insecurity, protection concerns, and loss of livelihoods if the situation remains protracted. Without urgent resolution, the crisis risks deepening community trauma, straining cross-border relations, and destabilizing the wider Mano River Union region.

    Humanitarian needs in Sorlumba and the surrounding villages are significant, though not fully verified due to limited access. Displaced families are reported to require food assistance, temporary shelter, and basic non-food items, as access to farmland and livelihoods remains disrupted. Gaps in health services and water and sanitation support may increase the risk of disease outbreaks, while school closures have left children without access to education. Protection concerns persist, with communities experiencing fear and trauma linked to the presence of armed forces. Ongoing monitoring continues; however, limited humanitarian access makes it difficult to confirm the full scale of needs, which may worsen into food insecurity, livelihood loss, and prolonged vulnerability if the situation persists.

summary:
Between March 19–24, 2026, violent windstorms struck communities across Nimba and Lofa Counties in Liberia, severely damaging fragile housing structures and displacing families. A total of 213 households occupied by approximately 3,704 people were directly affected. The storms affected six communities in Nimba and five in Lofa, leaving families exposed to harsh weather conditions and without basic household items. Vulnerable groups, including women, children, the elderly, pregnant women, and persons with disabilities, were disproportionately impacted, heightening protection concerns and increasing the urgency for humanitarian support.

The scale of displacement has placed immense strain on host families and temporary shelters, where overcrowding and limited facilities exacerbate risks to health, safety, and dignity. With 1,685 men and 2,019 women affected, the storms have disrupted livelihoods, undermined community resilience, and exposed households to heightened vulnerabilities such as respiratory infections and malaria. Immediate donor support is critical to provide emergency shelter, non-food items (NFIs), and psychosocial assistance, while enabling recovery efforts that strengthen preparedness and resilience against future climate-related hazards.

The windstorms caused widespread destruction across 11 communities. In total, 213 households were affected, directly impacting approximately 3,704 people. The storms broke down in different categories of fragile housing structures, leaving families without shelter or basic household items. The impact was particularly severe in rural communities where infrastructure is weak, and recovery capacity is limited.

The scale of the disaster is significant, with 1,685 men and 2,019 women affected, including large numbers of children, elderly persons, pregnant women, and individuals with disabilities. These vulnerable groups face heightened protection risks in overcrowded temporary shelters and host family arrangements. The storms have not only displaced families but also disrupted livelihoods, undermined community resilience, and exposed households to increased risks.

The scope of humanitarian needs is broad and urgent. Immediate priorities include emergency shelter, non-food items (NFIs), early recovery and psychosocial support to stabilize affected households. At the same time, longer-term interventions are required to strengthen community preparedness and resilience against recurring climate-related hazards.

The impact of these incidents was particularly harsh on vulnerable groups, including women, children, persons with disabilities, and pregnant women, who face heightened protection risks in overcrowded temporary shelters. Many of these individuals are now exposed to unsafe living conditions, with limited privacy and increased susceptibility to exploitation, health complications, and psychological distress. The outbreaks underscore systemic challenges such as poor household fire management practices, inadequate infrastructure, and limited emergency response capacity. Addressing these gaps requires immediate humanitarian assistance—emergency shelter, non-food items, and psychosocial support—alongside long-term resilience-building initiatives to safeguard communities against future fire-related disasters. 

The fire outbreaks affected 150 households and 586 people across five counties. Women, children, persons with disabilities, and pregnant women were among the most vulnerable. The fires destroyed homes and belongings, leaving families displaced and exposed to harsh conditions. Risks include heightened protection concerns, loss of livelihoods, and increased health vulnerabilities due to inadequate shelter and lack of basic household items. Immediate humanitarian needs center on emergency shelter, psychosocial support, and NFIs, alongside community awareness and preparedness measures to reduce future fire risks.

The humanitarian crisis map in Iraq witnessed a critical shift with the continuation of the wave of heavy rains and devastating floods that struck large areas of Iraq's governorates until March 30, 2026. Updated field estimates indicate that approximately 5,218 families, equivalent to 31,308 people, were affected in the governorates of (Anbar, Wasit, Diyala, Dohuk, Kirkuk, Sulaymaniyah, Nineveh, Erbil, Muthanna, and Maysan). The damage varied from human losses and injuries to significant material losses. Accordingly, the Iraqi Red Crescent Society conducted intensive and comprehensive field assessments and prepared all human and logistical resources to achieve a direct and rapid response, the details of which are outlined below:

Loss and Damage Assessment
1- Wasit Governorate
The governorate recorded damage to more than 1,050 homes, with a clear variation in the impact. The damage was concentrated in areas with dilapidated infrastructure and informal settlements in the city of Kut, the capital of Wasit Governorate, specifically in the neighborhoods of Al-Hakim, Al-Jihad, Al-Sabha, and Oil Street. In Al-Suwaira district, a child died and all members of her family were injured, in addition to damage to homes in Al-Hay district. Furthermore, vast areas of agricultural land in the governorate were flooded as a result of the torrential rains.

2- Anbar Governorate
The total number of affected families reached 956. Al-Khalidiya district emerged as the most affected area, with more than 256 families losing all their belongings in the Al-Shuhada neighborhood. In Ameriyat Al-Fallujah, 700 families were displaced from the Bzeibiz camp for internally displaced persons and were temporarily housed in schools due to the destruction of their food and relief supplies by the floods.

3- Duhok Governorate
Approximately 347 families were affected (147 families in the governorate center, 100 in Zakho, 50 each in Amadiya and Aqrah districts) as a result of the rains. One death due to a lightning strike was also recorded in Zakho district.

4- Diyala Governorate: Approximately 575 families were affected (100 in Qazaniya, 150 in Baquba, 100 in Al-Muqdadiya, 75 each in Mandali, Khanaqin, and Al-Khalis).

5- Maysan Governorate: More than 650 houses were damaged in rural areas of the districts of Ali Al-Gharbi, Qalat Saleh, Al-Musharrah, and Al-Maymuna. Most of these houses were dilapidated and on the verge of collapse.

6- Salah Al-Din Governorate: 50 houses were damaged in Baiji District due to flooding, in addition to more than 70 houses in Al-Alam District.

7- Nineveh Governorate: More than 1,000 families were affected by flooding in their homes due to rain in the neighborhoods of Al-Rabee (200 families) and Al-Mazari (800 families). This forced more than 300 families to flee to host communities outside their areas.

8- Kirkuk Governorate: More than 120 houses were damaged in In the districts of Laylan, Zab, and Abbasi, a house collapsed, three citizens were injured, and one death occurred in Hawija district due to the floods.

9- Erbil Governorate: Material damage occurred to homes affected by the floods in the areas of Kalkand, Tirawa, Birzin, Shaqlawa, Dartu, Soran, Khabat, and Sidakan, affecting a total of 400 families. Additionally, one citizen died from a lightning strike.

countries.name: Syrian Arab Republic

name: SYR: Flood - 03-2026 - Al-Khabur River Floods, Al-Hasakah – 2026
summary:
Situation Overview

Since mid-March 2026, northern and north-eastern Syria, particularly Al-Hasakah Governorate, has been affected by a strong and prolonged weather system characterized by heavy rainfall, thunderstorms, and strong winds. Within a short period of time, significant precipitation was recorded across the region, leading to a rapid rise in water levels in rivers and tributaries. As a result, the Al-Khabur River overflowed its banks due to the combined effect of local rainfall and increased upstream inflows, with discharge rates exceeding 50 cubic meters per second. This led to widespread flooding across low-lying areas and riverbed settlements, particularly in the neighborhoods of Al-Mirdian, Ghweiran, Al-Nashwa, and surrounding areas in Al-Hasakah city, as well as rural communities along the river corridor.

Floodwaters entered homes and forced families to evacuate, while agricultural lands were extensively inundated, resulting in damage to crops and loss of livelihoods. Critical infrastructure was also affected, including the disruption of sections of the M4 road and the temporary closure of key access points such as the Semalka crossing, limiting movement and humanitarian access. The floods also impacted areas already affected by previous weather events earlier in the year, further compounding vulnerabilities.

At the broader level, the ongoing weather system has affected multiple governorates, including Aleppo and Raqqa, with reports indicating that approximately 10,000 people across displacement sites have been impacted, alongside casualties, including the reported deaths of children due to weather-related incidents. Displacement sites and informal settlements have been particularly affected, as floodwaters inundated tents and fragile shelters, exposing already vulnerable populations to harsh conditions, including cold weather, water contamination, and limited access to basic services.

In Al-Hasakah, the most affected populations include families residing along the riverbanks, many of whom were already living in precarious conditions, as well as displaced households and vulnerable groups such as children, older persons, and persons with disabilities. The situation remains fluid, with continued weather instability and forecasts indicating additional rainfall, raising concerns about further flooding and the potential expansion of humanitarian needs.

Response by Syrian Arab Red Crescent (SARC)

The Syrian Arab Red Crescent (SARC) has initiated an immediate response to the Al-Khabur River flooding in Al-Hasakah, focusing on life-saving interventions and rapid needs assessment.

1.      Evacuation and Emergency Support

SARC teams evacuated families living along the riverbanks whose homes were flooded or at risk. Evacuations were carried out to safer areas, particularly in the neighborhoods of:

  • Ghweiran
  • Al-Nashwa
  • Al-Mirdian
  • Dolab Al-Awais

Teams were deployed overnight to respond to the rising water levels and ensure the safety of affected communities.

2.      Relief Distribution

Based on the emergency response to families affected by the Al-Khabur River flooding, and following initial rapid assessments conducted on 17 and 18 March 2026, the Syrian Arab Red Crescent (SARC) targeted the most affected neighborhoods with non-food item (NFI) distributions.

The following areas were reached:

Al-Mirdian: 85 households

Ghweiran: 229 households

Al-Nashwa: 76 households

This brings the total number of assisted households to 390 families.

The distributed items included essential non-food items aimed at addressing immediate needs and supporting affected families in coping with the impact of flooding.

3.      Needs Assessment

SARC teams are continuing to conduct rapid needs assessments in affected areas, particularly in:

  • Western Ghweiran
  • Al-Nashwa
    to identify priority needs and guide further response.

summary:

The contamination entered Moldovan territory downstream and was first detected on 10 March near Naslavcea and Otaci. Initial monitoring confirmed the presence of oil slicks on the river surface, prompting early precautionary measures by national authorities.

 

From 11 March onwards, the situation escalated as contamination levels fluctuated and the pollution plume moved downstream. Authorities implemented preventive suspension of water abstraction from affected intake points to avoid contamination of water treatment systems. This led to temporary disruption of piped water supply, most notably in Bălți and surrounding areas supplied by the Soroca–Bălți aqueduct. Additional districts affected include Soroca District, Florești District and Sîngerei District.

 

On 15–16 March, the Government of Moldova declared an environmental state of alert across the Dniester River basin, enabling enhanced coordination, monitoring, and response measures. Containment actions, including the installation of booms and absorbent materials, were implemented, while continuous water quality monitoring was carried out along the river.

 

The humanitarian impact of the incident is primarily related to disruption of access to safe drinking water. Approximately 100,000 people are estimated to be affected, based on the population of Bălți and surrounding areas experiencing water supply interruptions. While no casualties, injuries, or displacement have been reported, the temporary loss or reduction of water supply has created significant operational challenges for affected communities, particularly in urban areas heavily dependent on centralized water systems.

 

Vulnerable groups, including older persons and people with disabilities, are disproportionately affected, as they face greater difficulties in accessing alternative water sources or reaching distribution points. In response, authorities have activated alternative supply measures, including water tankers and distribution points, while public health guidance has been issued to limit the use of potentially contaminated water.

 

At the time of reporting, the situation remains dynamic but controlled. Water supply has been partially restored in some areas following improvements in water quality; however, monitoring continues as contamination levels may vary and additional pollution waves from upstream cannot be excluded. The incident continues to pose localized humanitarian needs in the WASH sector, while broader impacts remain contained through ongoing response and coordination efforts.

countries.name: Australia
dtype.name: Flood
name: AUS: Flood - 03-2026 - QLD Central Coast Flood
summary:
In early–mid March 2026, the City of Bundaberg experienced a major flood event following prolonged and intense rainfall across the wider Burnett River catchment. The resulting rise of the Burnett River led to widespread inundation of residential, commercial, and community assets, large‑scale evacuations, and significant disruption to transport and essential services.

The incident was triggered by a slow‑moving tropical low‑pressure system producing sustained heavy rainfall across inland and coastal Queensland, including the upper and lower Burnett River catchments. Catchment soils were heavily saturated prior to the peak rainfall, resulting in rapid runoff and high river inflows.

Flooding in Bundaberg developed progressively as upstream floodwaters moved downstream over several days, with river levels continuing to rise after rainfall had eased locally. Drainage to the ocean was further constrained by coastal conditions, contributing to elevated river levels within the city.

The flood represented the most severe flooding in Bundaberg since the January 2013 record event, with river heights reaching major flood levels and causing substantial impacts across low‑lying and flood‑prone areas of the city.

The event demonstrated that major impacts can occur well below record flood heights, particularly where communities remain exposed on the floodplain.

Evacuation orders and warnings were issued for multiple suburbs, with council‑supported evacuation centres activated, while the closure of major river crossings temporarily isolated large sections of the city, including parts of North Bundaberg, impacting approximately 10,000 residents through restricted access during peak flood conditions. Authorities advised that flood conditions remained hazardous during the recession phase due to damaged infrastructure, submerged obstacles, and unstable road surfaces.

Authorities also noted that for many residents this was the fourth major flood in little more than 15 years, compounding financial and psychological stress.

countries.name: Suriname
dtype.name: Other
name: SUR: Other - 03-2026 - Chikungunya outbreak Suriname
summary:
According to CARPHA "Watching Brief on Re-Emerging Diseases dated March 4, 2026 CARPHA has elevated the relative risk of Chikungunya outbreaks across other CARPHA Member States from "Moderate" to "Moderate to High". This because of the given high degree of exposure to Aedes mosquitoes, the ease of movements of persons across the Caribbean and the significant increase in Chikungunya cases in Suriname. CARPHA notes that Suriname remains the only Member State reporting confirmed cases in 2026, with over 1,000 cases already documented regionally. In January 2026, Suriname started reporting confirmed cases of Chikungunya. The chikungunya virus, which is transmitted through mosquito bites, has re-emerge in the country after serveral years of relative absence.  The Ministry of Health offically announced the outbreak following the rapped increase of confirmed ChikV cases. 

According to information from PAHO in conjuction with the Suriname Ministery of Health, Welfare and Labour 1357 positive confirmed cases were identified. None of the infected individuals had recently traveled abroad, indicating that the virus is spreading locally. The confirmed cases were identified by both the Cenbtral Laboratory of the Buro of Public Health (BOG) and the Laboratory of the Academic Hospital Paramaribo (AZP). Based on reported cases and observed patterns of spread serveral communities of eight (8) of the 10 district of Suriname have been clasified as High-Risk areas. These are communities District Marowijne, Commewijne, Paramaribo, Para, Nickerie, Coronie, Wanica and Saramacca. These areas as mentioned are closely being monitored due to the increased reports of infections and environmental factors that may support mosquito breeding and transmission.

In the brief of the CARPHA report and information from the PAHO and MOH Suriname it is said that the number of infected persons is much higher, given typical health‑seeking behavior patterns, it is believed that the true number of infections may be up to three times higher, meaning the actual caseload could be approximately 4,000 cases. This aligns with regional observations that many ChikV‑infected individuals do not present to a health facility unless symptoms are severe. Surveillance data primarily reflects laboratory-confirmed cases, and community transmission may be underestimated due to incomplete capture of milder cases.

Epidemiological situation and vector control challenges:

The epidemiological trend obderved from the initial reported cases through the most recent CARPHA alert briefing indicates a rapid and concerning escalation in infections. This upward trajectory suggests that the absence of timely and adequate public health interventions may have contributed to the accelerated rise in new cases.

The Ministry of Health has reported a significant challenge: the primary mosquito vector has developed resistance to Malathion, a pesticide previously utilized for vector control interventions. As a result, Malathion is no longer effective in suppressing mosquito populations. ath the present, the Ministry is awaiting the procurement and delivery of alternative pesticides that are for use under the current resistance conditions and capable of reducing vector density.

Compounding these challenges is the prevalence of bulk waste at the household level. Such waste materials creat numerous stagnant-water environments that serve as ideal breeding sites for mosquitoes. The widespread presence of these breeding grounds significantly indermines vector control efforts and contributes to sustain transmision within high risk and or affected communities.

Suriname's wet season is expected to begin around mid-April 2026, creating ideal breeding conditions for Aedes mosquitoes, including Aedes aeqypti and Aedes albopictus. If vector control  measures and environmental management are insufficient, rainfalldriven proliferation of breeding sites may significantly accelerate transmission.

countries.name: Iran, Islamic Republic of
countries.society_name: Red Crescent Society of the Islamic Republic of Iran
dtype.name: Complex Emergency
name: IRN: Complex Emergency - 02-2026 - Iran Complex Emergency
summary:
Disaster Overview

Since 28 February 2026, the Iran has experienced a rapid escalation in hostilities, marked by large-scale strikes affecting over 130 cities and the majority of provinces, including major urban centres. The scale and geographic spread indicate a nationwide complex emergency, with widespread impacts on densely populated areas. The crisis has resulted in significant civilian casualties, large-scale displacement, and extensive damage to critical civilian infrastructure, disrupting essential services such as health, water, and energy systems. This escalation is occurring in a context of pre-existing socioeconomic fragility, including sanctions-related constraints, inflation, and environmental stressors, which have significantly reduced coping capacities. Overall, the situation reflects a high-severity, multi-sectoral humanitarian crisis with rapidly evolving needs and compounding vulnerabilities across the country.

The situation is further exacerbated by severe economic deterioration, including high inflation and rising prices, significantly limiting access to essential goods such as food and medicines, while service disruptions in some areas have resulted in water and electricity cuts.

Actions Taken

IRCS Response – Key Highlights

  • Activated nationwide emergency response, deploying teams across 31 provinces and major urban centres to address large-scale impacts.
  • Activated crisis management mechanisms and operations centres from the onset of the escalation
  • Large-scale mobilization of responders nationwide (up to 100,000), ensuring continuous emergency response coverage
  • Conducting search and rescue, technical rescue, and emergency medical response, including first aid, evacuations, and frontline life-saving interventions.
  • Delivering relief assistance, including distribution of essential household items and support to affected households facing infrastructure damage and service disruption.
  • Scaling up mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) through hotline services and community outreach to address widespread trauma.
  • Maintaining operations despite access, security, and infrastructure constraints, adapting response modalities to ensure continuity of assistance.
  • Humanitarian response capacity is under pressure due to direct impacts on IRCS assets, including damage to facilities and emergency medical services

IFRC Response

The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) is supporting the Iranian Red Crescent Society (IRCS) through its country delegation, the MENA Regional Office, and Geneva headquarters.

Initial financial support:

·       CHF 1.5 million allocated from the IFRC Disaster Response Emergency Fund (DREF) to support immediate response activities.

·       This enabled the rapid procurement of essential health supplies and protective equipment to support frontline responders.

Emergency Appeal:

·       On 6 March 2026, IFRC launched an Emergency Appeal for CHF 40 million to scale up humanitarian assistance and support approximately 5 million people affected by the crisis.

Operational support focuses on:

·       Information management and operational analysis

·       Logistics and supply chain support

·       Operational coordination with Movement partners

·       Remote coordination and analytical support through the MENA Regional Office to ensure continuity of information flow despite connectivity disruptions

·       Strengthening localized response capacities and pre-positioning of supplies to maintain operational continuity under access constraints

·       International procurement and delivery of critical medical supplies and relief items through IFRC global supply chain mechanisms.

Movement Coordination

·       The Iranian Red Crescent Society (IRCS) maintains close coordination with the IFRC and the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) to ensure a coherent Movement response.

·       Strategic coordination mechanisms between Movement partners have been established to support:
- Operational planning
- Resource mobilization
- Alignment of humanitarian action in response to the evolving crisis

Surge Support

·       IFRC has issued surge alerts to strengthen operational capacity, including deployment support for procurement and coordination functions, as well as additional surge capacities to support logistics, resource mobilization, and communications.

countries.name: Israel

name: ISR: Complex Emergency - 02-2026 - Israel: Missiles Attack and a State of Emergency
summary:
On Monday, March 9, the attacks on Israel continued, with many missiles and drones launched towards the entire country from Iran and Lebanon. Rockets from Lebanon were fired towards the center of the country, and not only to the north. One person was killed, and another was critically injured today when a missile hit a construction site near Tel Aviv. The Home Front Command extended the current defensive policy for the public until tomorrow evening. 

During the weekend, the attacks on Israel continued with constant attacks in the north of Israel by Hezbollah (from the Haifa area to the north). In one incident, more than 30 rockets were fired at once towards the town of Kiryat Shmona. A drone landed at the parking lot of Naharia Hospital. Several missile attacks from Iran targeted the north, center, and south of Israel. One casualty was severely injured, and several suffered considerable injuries from sharpnnel. Other casualties with minor injuries were injured while running for shelter. The Home Front Command's defensive policy for the public changed- workplaces are allowed to resume activities, as long as they have shelters in place to host employees and visitors, and the same applies to commerce. School activities are conducted remotely, with no clear date for resuming face-to-face activities. Israeli airlines are conducting a massive repatriation operation, through Ben Gurion Airport (with very limited capacity), Aqaba (Jordan), and Taba (Egypt), followed by organized land crossing.

As of Friday midday, the attacks on Israel continued, with many missiles and drones launched towards the entire country from Iran and Lebanon. There is no change in the defensive policy for the public of the Home Front Command. The health care system is in a state of emergency. Repatriation flights have been initiated, departures from Israel will be limited to 50 passengers per flight, upon special permits, and are expected from Sunday. According to the government announcements, 1,000 people have been evacuated from their houses due to damage from the attacks.

On Thursday, March 5, the attacks on Israel continued, with many missiles and drones launched towards the entire country from Iran and Lebanon. Several hits were reported in the center of Israel. The Home Front Command instructed on easing in the defensive policy for the public, and from today at 12:00 PM, gatherings of up to 50 people and working from workplaces is allwoed, as long as there in a safe room or shelter in reasonable distance. Educational activity is still not allowed. Ben Gurion Airport opened this morning for repatriation flights only. One airplane per hour will land over the next 24 hours. The airport will be operating 24/7. Repatriation flights through Aqaba and Taba airports continue. Passengers cannot fly out of Israel. Exit is possible through the land crossings. 

On Wednesday, March 4, the attacks on Israel continued, with many missiles and drones launched towards the entire country from Iran and Lebanon. Several hits were reported in the north and center of Israel. No change in the defensive policy for the public. 

On Tuesday, March 3, the attacks on Israel continued, with many missiles and drones launched towards the entire country from Iran and Lebanon. Several hits were reported in the north, center, and south of Israel. No change in the defensive policy for the public. 

On Monday, March 2, the attacks on Israel continued, with many missiles and drones launched towards the entire country. At night, for the first time during the current escalation, rockets and drones were fired from Lebanon towards the north of Israel. In a direct hit by a missile from Iran in Beit Shemesh on Sunday, 9 were killed, and 65 were injured. In Jerusalem, another 5 people were injured when a missile hit a main road. On Monday, in a direct hit by a missile from Iran in Beer Sheva, several people were injured. According to media reports, around 500 people have been evacuated to hotels, following damage to their homes.

The Israeli government approved the extension of the "Emergency under Civil Defense Law" until March 12, and the defensive policy for the public remains as before.

As of Sunday morning (March 1), MDA treated 121 casualties, and two persons were killed as a result of the missile attacks. There is no change to the public's defensive policy. The Israeli airspace is closed until further notice. This is in addition to the measures in place since Saturday morning – cessation of all public events and non-essential work.

On February 28, several missile hits were reported in different locations in Israel. In some of the sites, casualties were treated by MDA, and one person was killed. Home Front Command forces were rescuing trapped casualties from the debris. 

Since around 10:30 AM, many missile alarms have sounded across Israel following multiple launches of missiles and drones from Iran, as reported in the media and by officials. The public was called to remain in the vicinity of protected spaces and rocket shelters. The Home Front Command instructed on a strict defensive policy for the public, switching from "full activity" to "essential activity"- no educational activities, no gatherings, and no workplace activities are allowed. 

Earlier, at 08:15 AM, alert sirens followed by a broad cell broadcast sounded all over Israel.

The Israeli Defense Force (IDF) spokesperson informed that this is a preventive alarm, as the USA and Israel initiated an attack against Iran, in preparation for a retaliation by Iran.

The Minister of Defense signed the declaration of "Emergency under Civil Defense Law" for the entire Israeli Territory. All unnecessary activities are suspended, and public gatherings are prohibited.

countries.name: Afghanistan
dtype.name: Other
name: Afghanistan: Complex Emergency, 2026
summary:
The ongoing political tension between Afghanistan and Pakistan has turned into clashes between these two countries, which resulted in significant civilian casualties and large-scale displacement in provinces located near the border point of the country (Kuanr, Nuristan, Nangarhar, Paktika, Paktiya, and Khost). As a result, 66 people lost their lives, and 72 were injured. A total of 13,531 families were displaced, while 63 houses were destroyed and 33 were partially damaged. Additionally, one mosque and one clinic sustained damage. Heavy bombing and cross-firing during the conflict have severely impacted local communities, disrupted livelihoods, and increased humanitarian needs.  The Initial rapid assessment shows that Immediate humanitarian assistance is required to address urgent life-saving needs and prevent further deterioration of the humanitarian situation in the areas/provinces most affected. 

 Humanitarian Impact

A total of 13,531 families who were residing near the border line have been displaced, and among the families,  a number are staying with host communities, while others are living in open areas, including public spaces without adequate shelter. Many households have lost access to their homes, personal belongings, and primary sources of income. In addition, markets in the affected areas remain closed, restricting access to food and essential supplies. Areas where people previously worked have become conflict zones, severely limiting mobility and economic activities. As a result, in this holy month of Ramadan, families are unable to earn a daily income, access to food and non-food items is highly constrained, and the prices of essential commodities have significantly increased nationwide due to the border closure with Pakistan and Iran, which has also contributed to the inflation in Afghanistan Market. The humanitarian situation is particularly critical, leaving many displaced families with little or nothing to eat and unable to meet their basic nutritional needs. Children, elderly people, and people with disability including people with chronic diseases, are experiencing psychological shocks due to the absence of medical services like medicine Afghanistan used to import from Iran and Pakistan.

 Priority Needs

  • Food parcels
  • Emergency shelter (tents)
  • Cash assistance
  • Nutritional support for children
  • Safe drinking water
  • Essential medicines and medical support

 Response Gap and Recommendations

The scale of displacement and the rapid deterioration of living conditions require an immediate and well-coordinated humanitarian response. Timely intervention is essential to prevent further vulnerability among internally displaced persons (IDPs), support host communities that are under increasing strain, stabilize food security conditions, and provide life-saving assistance during the holy month of Ramadan. Humanitarian actors are strongly encouraged to mobilize emergency resources and conduct rapid needs assessments to ensure that assistance is effective, timely, and appropriately targeted to those most in need.

 Conclusion

The ongoing conflict has significantly impacted civilian populations, resulting in casualties, displacement, and economic disruption. Without urgent humanitarian intervention, the situation may further deteriorate, particularly for vulnerable groups such as women, children, and elderly people, including people with chronic disorders. 

Immediate action is required to address urgent needs and reduce the suffering of affected communities.

countries.name: Uruguay
dtype.name: Drought
name: URY: Drought - 02-2026 - Water deficit
summary:
Uruguay is going through a scenario of sustained water deficit that began to manifest itself more clearly during the last quarter of 2025, particularly in the south, center-south and east of the country. The technical monitoring carried out by official agencies showed a progressive decrease in the moisture content in the soils, accompanied by accumulated rainfall below the expected values and average temperatures between normal and above normal. 


As a result of this deterioration, in February 2026 the Ministry of Livestock, Agriculture and Fisheries declared an Agricultural Emergency for an initial period of 90 days, covering the entire departments of Canelones, Montevideo and Maldonado, as well as specific sections of Durazno, Flores, Florida, Lavalleja, Rocha, San José y Treinta y Tres. The measure is based on technical indicators such as the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) and the Percentage of Water Available in the Soil (PAD), monitored by INIA-GRAS and Inumet. 


The current impact is mainly concentrated in the agricultural production sector. The reduction of moisture in soils has caused a decrease in the availability and quality of pastures, an impact on summer crops, a lower capacity for forage recovery and pressure on water reserves for animal consumption.

This has led to an increase in operating costs, mainly in food supplementation and water logistics, and an increase in the economic vulnerability of small and medium-sized producers. 
Although there is no consolidated official figure of people affected, the territorial scope of the emergency includes departments with a high concentration of livestock, dairy and fruit and vegetable farms. Consequently, the potential impact includes thousands of rural producers, workers dependent on agricultural activity and families whose economy is directly linked to these production systems. 


The context of water deficit has increased the risk of forest and rural fires. Low soil moisture and dry vegetation increase the flammability of the environment, while high temperatures and the possible presence of seasonal winds favor the ignition and spread of fire. Official monitoring of the forest fire risk index indicates high conditions in several areas of the south and southeast of the country. 


This combination configures a composite risk scenario: drought not only impacts agricultural production, but also increases the probability of fires that could generate additional damage to rural infrastructure (fences, sheds, machinery), loss of livestock, damage to productive forests, and risk to communities in urban-rural interface areas. 


So far, the impact is predominantly productive and economic. However, if conditions persist, more far-reaching indirect impacts could be observed, such as deterioration of rural economic resilience, increased indebtedness, psychosocial stress in productive communities, and increased pressure on local fire response systems. 


As for the evolution, official seasonal trends do not show clear signs of immediate water recovery. An increased probability of normal to above-normal temperatures remains, which could sustain both water stress and fire risk if significant rainfall is not recorded in the short term. MGAP authorities have indicated that the emergency could be extended depending on climate change. 


In summary, the country is facing a slow-evolving event, with a current impact concentrated in the agricultural sector, but with potential intensification if prolonged drought, high temperatures and the occurrence of large-scale forest fires converge. Continuous monitoring and anticipatory preparedness are key to avoiding an escalation towards a scenario of greater humanitarian impact.

countries.name: Pakistan

countries.name: Pakistan

name: PAK: Complex Emergency - 02-2026 - PAK: Complex Emergency - 02-2026 - Global Crisis – Repatriation of Pakistan’s from Iran
summary:

countries.name: Peru
dtype.name: Flood
name: PER: Flood - 02-2026 - PER: SITUATIONAL REPORT ON RAINFALL IN TUMBES AND PIURA
summary:
As part of the rainy season, the Government of Peru declared a state of emergency due to imminent danger from intense rainfall in districts of several departments, including Piura and Tumbes, to enable immediate risk reduction, response, and rehabilitation measures. The first relevant declaration for both regions is Supreme Decree No. 005-2026-PCM (17 January 2026), which establishes a 60‑day validity and provides for the execution of actions by regional and local governments, with coordination and monitoring by INDECI and participation of sectors such as Health, Housing, among others.[1]

For Piura and Tumbes, DS 005-2026-PCM includes (among others) districts such as Ayabaca, Huancabamba, Morropón, Paita, Piura, Sechura, and Sullana (Piura); and Corrales, La Cruz, Pampas de Hospital, San Jacinto, San Juan de la Virgen, Tumbes, and Aguas Verdes (Tumbes).

Subsequently, the declaration was expanded through Supreme Decree No. 019-2026-PCM (4 February 2026), also for 60 days, incorporating new districts under the same response framework. For the north, this DS includes in Piura: Sapillica (Ayabaca), El Carmen de la Frontera and Lalaquiz (Huancabamba), and Chalaco, La Matanza, Santa Catalina de Mossa, Santo Domingo, and Yamango (Morropón); and in Tumbes: Zorritos and Casitas (Contralmirante Villar), and Zarumilla and Matapalo (Zarumilla).[2]

CURRENT SITUATION:

As of 23 February 2026, meteorological advisories and reports indicate continued rainfall in the north. SENAMHI reported for this period rainfall accumulations on the northern coast of 20–40 mm/day and warned of previous episodes of rain from light to extreme intensity on the coast, with accumulations of 50–85 mm/day in Tumbes and Piura, as well as the possibility of localized rains along the coast of both regions.[3]

In Tumbes, during the early morning of 23 February, intense rain with thunderstorms left flooded streets and waterlogged roads in different parts of the region, with the most affected districts reported as Tumbes, Canoas de Punta Sal, Zarumilla, and Aguas Verdes. The event generated water accumulation in streets and homes, with requests for support for water evacuation (motor pumps) and access rehabilitation; the Zarumilla and Tumbes rivers increased their flow and are being monitored.[4]

Hydrological advisories from SENAMHI on 23 February show a red alert condition at key stations of the Tumbes River, consistent with a dangerous rise scenario. At the El Tigre station (San Jacinto district), SENAMHI reported 1122.3 m³/s (05:00), exceeding the red threshold (1000 m³/s), with potential impact on riverside population centers (including, among others, Tumbes and nearby sectors), and recommended protection measures in areas near the channel.[5] Likewise, at the Cabo Inga station (also in San Jacinto), 1222.22 m³/s (01:00) was reported, also above the red threshold (1000 m³/s), with possible impacts on population centers such as Cabo Inga, Rica Playa, Brunos, Loyola, El Naranjo, and La Capitana.[6]

In Piura, SENAMHI issued a red alert due to the increase in the Chira River flow at the La Ardilla station (Lancones) with 2712.79 m³/s (06:00), exceeding the red threshold (1798 m³/s), and indicating potentially affected population centers in the area (Alamor, Sipiones, Solana Alta/Baja, El Puquio).[7] Press reports as of 20 February indicated the death of a merchant by drowning and ‘almost a thousand affected’ in the context of the rains, in addition to landslides and activation of ravines.[8] An additional news report (22 February) indicated more than 7,000 affected and damage to homes in Piura.[9]

THREAT SUMMARY

Today’s (23/02) prevailing meteorological threat is concentrated in precipitation associated with Meteorological Advisory No. 055 (orange level), valid from Sunday 22/02 (00:00) to Monday 23/02 (23:59). In terms of expected impact, INDECI warns that this advisory includes Tumbes and Piura and that, in addition to precipitation in the highlands, relevant rains are expected on the northern coast and localized light to moderate rains on the coast of Tumbes and Piura, with associated risks of pluvial flooding and activation of ravines (huaicos) in vulnerable areas through the end of 23/02. From 24/02 (00:00) to 25/02 (23:59) Advisory No. 059 (orange level) will be in force as an extension, with persistent risk due to saturated soils and the possibility that new rains may reactivate critical points (drainages, slopes, and ravines). In short-term warning bulletin No. 08-2026 regarding the possible activation of streams, the Regional Emergency Operations Center (COER) in Tumbes mentions the possibility of streams being activated due to the rain forecast for the next 24 hours, considering the rain over the previous seven days and the susceptibility to mass movements. [10]

In parallel, the most immediate threat is hydrological, due to red‑threshold river rises (risk of overflow and flooding in low-lying areas). In Tumbes, SENAMHI maintains the advisory for the Tumbes River, and in Piura, for the Chira River.

countries.name: Mongolia
dtype.name: Cold Wave
name: Mongolia: Snowstorm, 2026
summary:
Between 21-23 February 2026, hazardous strong winds, dust storms, and snowstorms affected multiple provinces across southern, eastern, and northern Mongolia, significantly worsening the ongoing dzud conditions. Sustained winds of 18–24 m/s, with gusts up to 31 m/s, combined with snowfall and extreme cold temperatures ranging from –30°C to –48°C, resulted in reduced visibility, blocked roads and mountain passes, and widespread disruption to movement. The event occurred during the Lunar New Year holiday period, when travel across the country was significantly higher than usual, contributing to an increased number of weather-related incidents and prolonging search, rescue, and assessment operations. According to forecasts, unstable weather conditions are expected to continue until 25 February, maintaining heightened risk levels in affected areas.

Human impact includes five confirmed fatalities due to exposure and hypothermia, including herders who became lost during snowstorms. At least one child sustained second-degree frostbite and required hospitalization. More than 100 people, including adults and children, were rescued after becoming stranded, lost, or trapped in snow, while numerous emergency calls were registered for snow entrapment, missing persons, and vehicle breakdowns. More than 10,000 herder households across Dornod, Khentii, Sukhbaatar, Dundgovi, Dornogovi, Umnugovi, Govi-Altai, Bayankhongor, Tuv, Selenge, Darkhan-Uul, and Khuvsgul provinces are experiencing severe wintering conditions, with many isolated due to snow-blocked access routes.

Livelihood impacts directly attributed to the 21-23 February storm are significant, with reported livestock mortality exceeding 4,900 head to date, particularly among large livestock, representing substantial economic losses for herder families. In several affected soums, repeated snowfall and ice-layer formation have made grazing impossible, and local hay and fodder reserves are depleted or critically low. Overall, the severe weather event has intensified pre-existing dzud vulnerabilities, increased humanitarian risks, and placed additional strain on already fragile herder livelihoods.

countries.name: North Macedonia
countries.society_name: Red Cross of the Republic of North Macedonia
dtype.name: Flood
name: MKD: Flood - 02-2026 - Flash floods North Macedonia 2026
summary:
Prolonged and intense rainfall between 14 and 16 February 2026 led to the rapid rise and overflow of several rivers, including the Zajashka and Slupčanka rivers, resulting in flooding across multiple municipalities in North Macedonia, particularly Kičevo, as well as parts of Tetovo, Gostivar, Lipkovo, Saraj (Skopje region), and surrounding settlements. In Kičevo, the Zajashka River overflowed its banks, inundating residential neighborhoods, streets, basements, yards, business premises, agricultural land, and segments of local road infrastructure, severely disrupting daily life and mobility.

Several low-lying areas experienced significant water accumulation, while localized landslides and damaged road corridors further limited access to essential services and hampered movement. Transport routes, including sections of the Tetovo Popova Šapka and Tetovo Jeduarce roads, were temporarily disrupted due to flooding and debris.

The floods disproportionately affected vulnerable groups, including low-income households, elderly persons, people with disabilities, single-parent families, and families with young children living in flood-prone or substandard housing. Many households experienced damage to living spaces, loss of household belongings, and temporary displacement. More than 250 residents were evacuated in the Kičevo area, including 187 persons supported directly by the Red Cross in evacuation procedures to temporary accommodation provided by the Municipality.

The situation remains dynamic, with continued monitoring of hydrological conditions due to the risk of additional rainfall. Emergency services, municipal authorities, the Crisis Management Centre, and Red Cross branches in Kičevo and other affected areas remain actively engaged in response activities, including evacuation support, pumping operations, shelter assistance, relief distribution, and coordination with local crisis management structures.

In response to identified immediate needs, the Red Cross Branch in Kičevo provided emergency assistance to approximately 200 households, including food parcels, hygiene parcels, blankets, sleeping bags, and drinking water. The Red Cross of North Macedonia remains in close coordination with the Crisis Management Centre and municipal authorities, which have indicated that continued humanitarian support will be required for affected populations during the recovery phase.

Weather forecasts for the coming weekend indicate a significant drop in temperatures across the affected regions, with colder conditions expected following the recent heavy rainfall. The anticipated temperature decline may increase hardship for displaced and flood-affected households, particularly those with damaged homes, limited heating capacity, or inadequate insulation. The colder weather raises concerns regarding health risks, especially for elderly persons, young children, and other vulnerable groups. As a result, there is an increased need for winterization support, including warm blankets, heating assistance, winter clothing, and other essential items to ensure safe and dignified living conditions during the recovery phase.
