summary:
A rapidly worsening humanitarian situation has resulted from severe flooding in Lagodekhi municipality caused by heavy rainfall since September 28, 2025. Rising waters destroyed households' vital food supplies and stocks as they flooded residential areas, flooding many homes' first floors. Farmlands and livestock have been severely impacted, endangering local livelihoods even more, and roads and other vital infrastructure have been damaged. The floods have had a direct impact on about 10300 people, or  households.

The impact on impacted families is profound, despite the fact that no fatalities or injuries have been reported. Road damage has left many isolated, and efforts to clean up and clear the area are still ongoing. There is an urgent need for food, drinking water, personal hygiene products, medical supplies, and safe housing for vulnerable populations, such as children and the elderly. To support the recovery of households that have lost both their essential stocks and their sources of income, immediate assistance is needed.

countries.name: Pakistan
dtype.name: Flood
name: Pakistan: Riverine Floods EAP, 2025
summary:
Pakistan is a country with diverse landscapes and a fluctuating climate. While typically hot and dry, it has shown significant variations in recent years. The country is prone to hazards such as floods, droughts, cyclones, heatwaves, and earthquakes. Floods occur frequently due to the summer weather system that develops in the Bay of Bengal during the monsoon months of July to September. According to the Climate Risk Index 2025, Pakistan was the most affected country in 2022, primarily due to exceptionally high relative economic losses.
 
Flooding in the Indus River and its tributaries cause substantial damage by inundating low-lying areas. This impacts lives, livelihoods, housing, and infrastructure, while also contributing to riverbank erosion. In the lower Indus Basin, where the river flows at a higher elevation than surrounding lands, breaches in embankments lead to prolonged inundation, causing extensive damage and delayed recovery

An impact survey conducted for this EAP covering 341 households across 50 vulnerable communities along the Indus River in Sindh and Punjab used quantitative and qualitative methods, including household interviews, FGDs, and KIIs. 
 
The Early Action Protocol (EAP) was developed with technical support of German Red Cross (GRC), Red Cross Climate Centre (RCCC), and IFRC, in close coordination with National/Provincial Disaster Management Authority, Pakistan Meteorological Department (PMD), Flood Forecasting division (FFD), Provincial Irrigation Department (PID), and the Federal Flood Commission (FFC). The design process involved multi-stakeholder consultations, risk
assessments with HeiGIT, and community surveys, ensuring evidence-based prioritization of early actions.  
 
The EAP aims to reach 15,000 households (approximately 105,000 individuals) across 29 tehsils in 18 highrisk districts along the Indus River and its tributaries (Kabul, Chenab).

countries.name: Philippines
dtype.name: Earthquake
name: Philippines: Earthquake and Typhoons 2025
summary:
On 30 September 2025 at approximately 9:59 PM local time, a powerful magnitude 6.9 earthquake struck off the
coast of Bogo City, Cebu making it one of the strongest recorded earthquakes in Cebu to date. The epicentre was
located near Bogo City in northern Cebu with an estimated shallow depth of about five kilometres, where intense
ground shaking led to the collapse of buildings, destruction of roads, and power outages. Neighbouring
municipalities, including Daanbantayan, Medellin, San Remigio, and even parts of Cebu City also felt the severe
impact of the earthquake. The event’s aftermath affected two regions, Central Visayas (Region VII) and Eastern
Visayas (Region VIII), with Northern Cebu in Region VII bearing the brunt of the impact and damages.


Based on the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (NDRRMC) situational report issued on
24 October 2025, a total of 217,901 families, or 754,733 individuals, were affected by the earthquake across 18
cities and municipalities in Cebu province, which comprises 281 barangays. The disaster resulted in at least 70
confirmed fatalities and 559 injuries, with the death toll expected to rise as rescue operations continue. The
number of people displaced has reached 26,638, most of whom are staying outside evacuation centres due to
safety concerns, limited access to shelter, clean water, or medical care. A total of 160,662 houses were reportedly
affected, including 7,410 destroyed and 153,252 partially damaged.


The earthquake also caused significant damage to 955 critical infrastructures, including bridges, concrete roads,
government facilities, schools, cultural heritage sites, and commercial establishments. Hundreds of sinkholes also
appeared in the municipality of San Remigio following the quake. Classes remain suspended in the hardest-hit
areas, including Bogo City, San Remigio, Daanbantayan, Borbon, and Medellin, while local governments conduct
structural assessments of schools and public buildings.


As affected communities in Cebu were still grappling with the earthquake’s aftermath, a storm threatened to
undermine the fragile recovery. On 2 November 2025, Typhoon Tino (international name: Kalmaegi) entered the
country’s monitoring domain, rapidly intensifying into a typhoon as it moved across the waters of the Philippine
Sea. Between 4 and 5 November, Tino made multiple landfalls across the Visayas islands region and Palawan,
bringing strong winds and torrential rains. The typhoon caused widespread flooding across Mimaropa, Regions 6
and 7, the Negros Islands Region (NIR), and Caraga, with the most severe destruction in Central Cebu, where
residential areas were heavily inundated.


Based on the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council report issued on 18 November 2025, a
total of 1,505,834 families, or approximately 5,383,323 individuals, have been affected across 447 cities and
municipalities in 33 provinces nationwide. Among these, 141 cities and municipalities have been placed under a
State of Calamity due to the extensive damage caused by Typhoon Tino. Based on the report, 271,329 people have
been displaced, with 191,194 individuals currently sheltering in evacuation centres. Prior to Tino’s arrival, local
government units carried out pre-emptive evacuations of 409,300 individuals across nine regions, including
Calabarzon, Mimaropa, Region 5, Region 6, Region 7, Region 8, Region 10, Caraga, and the Negros Islands Region
(NIR). The heavy rains brought by Tino triggered widespread flooding, storm surges, and rainfall-induced
landslides, affecting a total of 312,650 houses – 42,646 of which were completely damaged, while 270,004 were
partially damaged. The event also damaged 423 critical infrastructures, including government facilities, bridges,
roads and health facilities. The widespread flooding resulted in unverified casualty reports, with 253 dead and 502
injured.


While communities were still coping with the compounded effects of the Cebu earthquake and Typhoon Tino,
another tropical cyclone threatened the already dire living conditions.


On 9 November 2025, Super Typhoon Uwan (international name: Fung-wong) swept through Luzon, unleashing
destructive winds and heavy rainfall. This resulted in widespread power interruptions, storm surges, flooding in
low-lying and coastal areas, and damage to houses across the Bicol Region, Northern Luzon, and nearby coastal
provinces.


On 18 November 2025, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council reported that Uwan
affected approximately 2,100,220 families, or 7,414,164 individuals, across 72 provinces in 16 regions. As the
country’s weather bureau warned of the destructive nature of Uwan prior to its landfall in Luzon, local government
units implemented the pre-emptive evacuation of approximately 1.5 million individuals across 15 regions,
including Region 1, Region 2, the Cordillera Administrative Region (CAR), Region 3, Calabarzon, Mimaropa, Region
5, Region 6, Region 7, Region 8, Region 9, the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM),
Caraga, and the NIR. Over 400,000 individuals remained displaced, temporarily seeking shelter in 3,433 evacuation
centres.


Tropical Cyclone Uwan damaged 267,612 houses and caused widespread flooding in 674 areas. Major lifelines
were disrupted – power outages affected 549 cities and municipalities, with only 40 per cent of supply restored,
while communications lines in 169 cities and municipalities were partially down, with 30 per cent restored. A total
of 784 roads and 74 bridges were damaged, with 151 roads and 27 bridges still impassable. Unverified casualty
reports were significantly lower, reflecting the effectiveness of early warning systems and evacuation measures.
However, severe flooding, the limited restoration of utilities, and agricultural losses continue to strain affected
communities.

dtype.name: Flood
name: LAO: Flood - 09-2025 - Flood - Impact of BUALOI tropical storm
summary:
According to local governement, from 29–30 September, heavy to very heavy rainfall is expected with rainfall totals may reach 50–80 mm/24h, some areas exceeding 140 mm/24h. Bualoi weakened as it moved inland but still posed significant threats to northern, central and some province in the southern part of Laos. Many province were placed on high alert due to the risk of flash floods, landslides, and infrastructure damage. Heavy rainfall and strong winds disrupted daily life, particularly in mountainous and low-lying areas where communities are most vulnerable.

Savannakhet Province: Savannakhet experienced extensive flooding in low-lying districts, damaging homes, schools, and agricultural land. Several villages were temporarily isolated due to submerged roads and collapsed bridges. Local authorities coordinated evacuation efforts and distributed emergency relief supplies to affected families.

Attapue Province: In Attapue, mountainous terrain amplified the risk of landslides and erosion. Heavy rains caused road blockages and damaged critical infrastructure, including irrigation systems and rural health centers. Remote communities faced temporary isolation, prompting urgent delivery of food, water, and medical aid.

Houaphan Province: Houaphan experienced flash flooding and river overflow, impacting schools, health facilities, and residential areas. Landslides in hilly terrain posed risks to transport and safety. Emergency shelters were activated, and health workers were deployed to prevent disease outbreaks.

Bolikhamxay Province: Bolikhamxay reported moderate flooding in several districts, with damage to crops and livestock. Local response teams focused on clearing debris, restoring access to affected areas, and supporting vulnerable populations with food and hygiene kits.

Vientiane Province:Vientiane Province saw heavy rainfall and localized flooding, particularly in peri-urban and rural zones. Transport services were temporarily disrupted, and precautionary measures were taken to protect public infrastructure and ensure community safety.

Other Affected Provinces: Additional provinces including Luang Prabang, Khammouane, Saravane, Sekong, and Bokeo experienced varying degrees of impact. These ranged from crop destruction and livestock loss to temporary suspension of transport services such as the Lao-China Railway.

countries.name: Kenya
dtype.name: Complex Emergency
name: Kenya -  Complex Emergency
summary:
Kenya is increasingly vulnerable to climate extremes, with cycles of severe drought often followed by intense rainfall and flooding. Beginning in November 2023, El Niño-enhanced rains triggered widespread flooding that persisted into early 2024, displacing thousands and damaging infrastructure. However, the October– December 2024 short rains underperformed significantly across arid and semi-arid lands

(ASALs), disrupting cropping cycles, delaying replanting, and worsening food and nutrition insecurity. ASALs cover nearly 90 per cent of Kenya’s land and are home to approximately 16 million people (30 per cent of the population). These regions support 70 per cent of the country’s livestock, primarily through pastoralism and small-scale farming. However, they face chronic challenges including poverty, weak infrastructure, limited services, and frequent climate shocks such as droughts, floods, and land degradation.

By January 2025, the National Drought Management Authority (NDMA) reported deteriorating drought conditions in most ASAL counties, with Wajir, Kilifi, and Kwale entering the “Alert” phase due to inadequate rainfall. The combination of floods followed by failed rains disrupted agriculture, depleted water sources, and led to rising livestock losses – highlighting the growing volatility of Kenya’s climate.

The NDMA’s September 2025 food and nutrition assessment found that while the March–May long rains were near to or above average in most regions, over 1.8 million people – including 500,000 children and 100,000 pregnant women – remain in urgent need of food assistance (IPC Phase 3 or higher). Of these, approximately 179,000 are in IPC Phase 4 (Emergency), mainly in Baringo, Mandera, Marsabit, and Turkana. The situation is expected to worsen between October 2025 and January 2026 due to forecasted belowaverage short rains and rising temperatures, potentially pushing 2.1 million people into IPC Phase 3 or above. Eleven ASAL counties are projected to experience increased food insecurity, with Garissa, Tana River, and Wajir shifting from IPC Phase 2 to Phase 3.

As of October 2025, malnutrition remains critical. Between April 2025 and March 2026, an estimated 741,884 children aged 6–59 months are expected to suffer from acute malnutrition, including 178,938 with severe acute malnutrition (SAM) and 562,946 with moderate acute malnutrition (MAM). Additionally, 109,462 pregnant and lactating women are in need of treatment.

countries.name: Viet Nam
dtype.name: Cyclone
name: VNM: Cyclone - 09-2025 - Typhoon BUALOI
summary:
14:00 – 27 September
TYPHOON NO. 10 IS ABOUT 270KM FROM THE PARACEL ISLANDS; HEAVY RAIN TO START THIS EVENING IN NORTHERN VIETNAM AND FROM THANH HOA TO QUANG NGAI

✅ According to the National Center for Hydro-Meteorological Forecasting, at 13:00 on 27 September, the center of Typhoon No. 10 was located at approximately 15.0°N latitude and 114.0°E longitude, about 270 km east-southeast of the Paracel Islands.

  • Intensity: Level 11–12 (103–133 km/h), gusting up to level 15.
  • Direction and speed: Moving west-northwest at about 30–35 km/h.

HEAVY RAINS FROM TYPHOON NO. 10’S CIRCULATION CUT OFF MANY VILLAGES IN CENTRAL VIETNAM

The circulation ahead of Typhoon Bualoi has caused heavy rainfall in Thanh Hoa, Nghe An, and Quang Tri provinces, flooding low-lying areas (0.2–1 meter deep) and isolating several villages and roads.

✅ In Thanh Hoa, about 30 villages in Van Xuan, Tan Thanh, and Tam Thanh communes were cut off due to heavy rains from last night until this morning. The most severe impact was recorded in Xuan Chinh commune, where 9 out of 14 villages were isolated. Many spillways on inter-village and inter-commune roads were submerged 60–70 cm, with some areas over one meter deep. Local police have set up warning signs, stationed checkpoints at dangerous sites, and prohibited residents and vehicles from crossing to prevent accidents.
In Van Phu and Hoa Quy communes, multiple landslides occurred on hillsides, threatening nearby villages and forcing local authorities to evacuate residents and relocate property to safe areas.

✅ In Nghe An, from the night of 26 September to the morning of 27 September, prolonged heavy rains inundated many streets in Vinh City, paralyzing traffic.
By late morning on 27 September, floodwaters on Nguyen Van To Street (Vinh Phu ward) rose nearly 50 cm, causing widespread vehicle breakdowns and forcing residents to push their motorbikes through fast-flowing water.
Since the night of 25 September, widespread rains had already cut off several mountainous communes in Tuong Duong and Ky Son districts. In the past two days, upstream flows swelled rivers and streams, while landslides blocked roads and washed away crops and community infrastructure.

✅ In Quang Tri, rainfall in the past six hours reached 50–70 mm, with exceptionally heavy totals in some areas: Dong Hoi (109 mm), Viet Trung – Nam Trach commune (80 mm), and Vinh Kim – Cua Tung commune (115 mm).
Floodwaters from upstream isolated several spillways and mountain roads. In Ba Long commune, the Ba Long spillway on Provincial Road 558A was submerged nearly one meter, with swift currents cutting off access to six villages.
In Kim Ngan commune, floodwaters at spillway 25 on National Highway 9B rose 50–70 cm. In Truong Son commune, the road from the commune center to Trung Son and Doc May villages was submerged more than 50 cm, isolating local communities.
In Dong Ha city, sections of Tran Hung Dao Street (in front of Dong Ha market) and Dang Dung Street (intersection with Ngo Sy Lien Street) were 20–40 cm under water. Many vehicles broke down, forcing residents to push them home through flooded streets.

name: THA: Flood - 09-2025 - Impact of the storm BUALOI
summary:
Tropical Storm BUALOI has intensified prevailing weather systems across Thailand, contributing to widespread flooding. Between 28–30 September 2025, the storm has strengthened both the southwest monsoon over the Andaman Sea, Thailand, and the Gulf of Thailand, as well as the monsoon trough extending across the lower North, upper Central, and Northeast regions. According to the Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation (DDPM), Ministry of Interior, Thailand, as of 29 September 2025, flooding has impacted:17 provinces,71 districts,413 sub-districts and 2,247 villages. Affected areas span across the northern, northeastern, central, and eastern regions of the country. Local authorities are actively responding, and coordination with humanitarian partners is ongoing to assess needs and support affected communities.

  • Total affected households: 82,222 (approx. 269,351 people)
  • Fatalities: 7 (Phitsanulok – 1, Phetchabun – 1, Phichit – 1, Ayutthaya – 4)
  • Most severely affected provinces: Ayutthaya (38,132 households / 141,088 people / 4 deaths), Suphan Buri (13,704 households), and Phetchabun (7,383 households).
  • Water levels in several areas are stable or receding, though central provinces remain under high risk.

countries.name: Malawi
dtype.name: Epidemic
name: MWI: Epidemic - 09-2025 - Cholera Outbreak
summary:
On 26th September, the Ministry of Health, through Bwaila Hospital, confirmed two new cases of cholera in Lilongwe District, in the central region of Malawi. Both patients, a 30-year-old male from Chinsapo township and a 27-year-old male from Nathenje area, have been admitted to Bwaila Isolation Camp following positive test results. While the cases are currently isolated, the emergence of cholera signals continued vulnerability within the district, particularly in peri-urban and rural communities with limited access to safe water, sanitation, and hygiene services.
The primary effect on the health system has been the need for rapid mobilisation of isolation facilities and coordination between Bwaila Hospital, Kamuzu Central Hospital, and the District Medical Office. Secondary effects may include strain on already limited health resources, disruption of routine service delivery, and heightened risk of transmission in surrounding communities if containment measures are not sustained. For the affected population, the confirmation of cholera cases raises concerns about exposure to unsafe water sources and poor sanitation, highlighting the urgent need for intensified community engagement, surveillance, and preventive WASH interventions. Both patients are now under isolation and receiving appropriate care.
MRCS is coordinating closely with health authorities to monitor the situation and support response efforts.

countries.name: Kazakhstan
countries.society_name: Red Crescent Society of the Republic of Kazakhstan
dtype.name: Fire
name: KAZ: Fire - 09-2025 - Landfill Fire in Alatau
summary:
On 15 September 2025, a large fire broke out at a municipal solid waste landfill near the village of Alatau, located along the Almaty–Ust-Kamenogorsk highway. The fire has affected approximately 10 hectares of the 35-hectare landfill site. Following the escalation, the Akimat of Alatau declared a state of emergency of technological character at local level to enable the mobilization of additional firefighting and rescue resources.

The fire has not resulted in casualties, injuries, or displacement of the population. However, air pollution has been recorded in nearby settlements. Initial sanitary-epidemiological monitoring on 15–16 September showed exceedances of permissible concentrations of certain pollutants; follow-up tests on 17 September returned to within safety norms. As a precaution, residents have been advised to limit time outdoors to reduce exposure to smoke and air contaminants.

The landfill is operated by ADC Taza Alem LLP. The Ministry of Emergency Situations (MoES), supported by military units and regional fire brigades, is coordinating the response. More than 200 personnel and over 90 units of specialized equipment are engaged in firefighting efforts, with reinforcements mobilized from several regions. Road traffic in the affected area has been restricted due to reduced visibility and operational needs.

The affected population has not required evacuation or immediate assistance, but vulnerable groups (children, elderly, and people with chronic respiratory diseases) remain at risk if smoke and air quality conditions deteriorate. Authorities continue monitoring the situation closely.

countries.name: Ecuador
dtype.name: Civil Unrest
name: ECU: Civil unrest - 09-2025 - Demonstrations Ecuador 2025
summary:
On September 12, 2025, President Daniel Noboa issued Executive Decree No. 126, eliminating the
subsidy on automotive diesel and raising its price from USD 1.80 to USD 2.80 per gallon. The government said that the measure seeks to consolidate public finances, reduce smuggling and allocate resources to social programs . As compensation, the government announced bonuses for vulnerable groups, support for public transport and agricultural technification programs, in addition, it assured that the fare will not increase.
Faced with the beginning of the demonstrations against the elimination of the diesel subsidy, on September 16, 2025, President Daniel Noboa issued Executive Decree No. 134, declaring a state of emergency in seven provinces: Carchi, Imbabura, Pichincha, Cotopaxi, Bolívar, Azuay and Santo Domingo de los Tsáchilas.

The measure, initially in force for 60 days, was based on the existence of a "serious internal commotion" and includes the restriction of the right to assembly in public spaces and the participation of the Armed Forces and the National Police for the control of public order. Subsequently, on September 18, 2025, Executive Decree No. 146 was issued, which extends the state of emergency to the province of Chimborazo and incorporates the restriction of freedom of movement between 10:00 p.m. and 5:00 a.m. in five provinces: Cotopaxi, Imbabura, Chimborazo, Bolívar and Carchi.

 The government clarified that the right to peaceful protest is not prohibited, but warned that road blockades, interruption of services or acts of violence could constitute crimes punishable under current legislation. On September 18, 2025, the CONAIE convened an extraordinary national assembly in Riobamba, in which it was resolved to initiate an indefinite national strike, demanding the repeal of Decree 126.

The organization argued that the elimination of the diesel subsidy increases transportation and production costs, directly affecting indigenous, peasant and working communities. During the assembly, it was also resolved to declare a state of community emergency in indigenous territories, which implies restricting the entry of state security forces and activating traditional mechanisms of territorial protection, such as community guards. Likewise, the CONAIE rejected a possible Constituent Assembly and denounced state persecution of its leaders. The Indigenous and Peasant Movement of Cotopaxi (MICC), through its president Rafael Negrete, called for a peaceful march called for 10:00 a.m. on Monday, September 22, called "taking Latacunga".

During the night of September 20 and the early morning of September 21, 2025, there were demonstrations by the indigenous sector, with the closure of first-order roads that connect several provinces and cantons, which generated heavy traffic congestion and forced many people to travel on foot to their destinations.

countries.name: Malaysia
dtype.name: Flood
name: MYS: Flood - 09-2025 - flood
summary:
The floods that began on 11 September 2025 have continued to impact several districts in Sabah. According to official statistics from the Social Welfare Department (JKM) evacuation centers, a total of 923 individuals from 286 families have been recorded as evacuees. Penampang district reported the highest number, with 375 people across six temporary evacuation centers (PPS). Beaufort follows with 273 people at the Selagon Permanent Evacuation Center, the largest number recorded at a single PPS. Putatan recorded 212 evacuees at Dewan Sri Serigai, exceeding its original capacity by 141 percent, while Papar accommodated 63 evacuees across two PPS.

In addition to the floods, landslides since last Friday have claimed 12 lives, including five children, across several locations in Inanam, Papar, Penampang, and Tuntul. One individual remains missing, and authorities are actively conducting search and rescue operations.

The Malaysian Red Crescent (MRCS) Sabah continues to monitor the situation and coordinate with local authorities while remaining on standby at evacuation centers. The team is providing emergency ambulance services at the Penampang Sports Complex Hall. As of 16 September, 14 volunteers have been deployed in Penampang, while in Beaufort, MRCS teams are assisting in managing evacuees at PPS Selagon and distributing donated clothing to flood-affected families. The operation is further supported by 1 staff member, 4 additional volunteers, and a four-wheel-drive vehicle (Navara).

In terms of humanitarian assistance, MRCS Sabah previously distributed food baskets (Nestlé packs), hygiene kits (Guardian packs), bottled water, and blankets to families evacuated to three PPS locations around Penampang on 12 September 2025.

countries.name: Afghanistan
dtype.name: Earthquake
name: Afghanistan : Southeastern and Northern Earthquake, 2025
summary:
Situation

Afghanistan has experienced two significant earthquakes within a span of two months, compounding humanitarian needs and increasing vulnerability in affected regions. Both events caused widespread destruction to homes and infrastructure, disrupted access to essential services, and left thousands of people in urgent need of assistance ahead of the winter season.

On 31 August 2025 at 11:47 PM local time, a 6.0-magnitude earthquake struck southeastern Afghanistan. The epicenter was approximately 27 km east-northeast of Momand Dara district in Nangarhar province and Nurgul district in Kunar province, near the border with Pakistan. Occurring at a shallow depth of 8–10 km, the quake caused severe shaking across Kunar, Nangarhar, and Laghman provinces, destroying or damaging around 600 houses, primarily in mountainous areas. Key road access routes were disrupted, leaving affected households in urgent need of shelter, food, and essential non-food items.

On 3 November 2025 at 12:59 AM local time, a second earthquake measuring 6.3 magnitude struck northern Afghanistan. The epicenter was near Kulam and Hazrat Sultan districts in Samangan province and Marmol and Keshende districts in Balkh province, about 28 km east-southeast of Mazar-e-Sharif. The tremor was strongly felt across Balkh and Samangan provinces, resulting in casualties and extensive structural damage, further straining local coping capacities.

Overall impact

As per the reports indicate more than 2,000 fatalities with over 1,000 people sustaining injuries due to the southeastern Afghanistan. Currently, there is no confirmed data regarding missing persons.  An estimated 600 houses have been destroyed or damaged with a considerable number of families displaced. 

The initial reports from the Afghan Red Crescent Society (ARCS), for the northern Afghanistan earthquake, 11 people have lost their lives and approximately 183 others have been injured. Among the injured, 88 are from the provincial center and 53 from Kulam District in Samangan province. In the Hazrat Sultan District of Samangan Province, one fatality and eight injuries have also been reported. Overall, more than 580 houses were either totally or partially damaged.

Action taken

ARCS field assessments are currently ongoing, and current figures continue to be updated as more information becomes available. Ambulances from districts in Nangarhar continue to arrive to transport injured people to medical facilities for urgent care. The Nangarhar Regional Specialist Hospital has reached full capacity having received an overwhelming number of women and children suffering from injuries in the aftermath of the quake. One IFRC staff is being deployed with European Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations (ECHO) Afghanistan team to conduct an aerial assessment and gather initial field assessments in Jalalabad on the immediate needs. 

The Afghan Red Crescent Society (ARCS) has deployed its teams to the affected areas to support with aerial and field assessments and immediate response efforts.

Immediate needs identified include:

  1. Search and rescue teams and equipment.
  2. Emergency healthcare support (medicines, trauma care, blood supplies).
  3. Food and clean water. 

Roads have been severely disrupted due to landslides, blocking vital access. 

Information and data continue to be updated and will be shared in subsequent reports.

countries.name: Gambia, Republic of The
dtype.name: Flood
name: GMB: Flood - 08-2025 - The Gambia 2025 Flash Flood
summary:
The 2025 seasonal rainfall began on 28 June 2025 with massive torrential downpours characterised by sporadic windstorm affecting scores of marginalized people in the Upper River and Central River Regions, West Coast Region, Lower River Regions and Kanifing Municipality.

However, from the 30th of August to 2nd September 2025, heavy rains turned roads into rivers, marketplaces into muddy pools, and homes into waterlogged neighbours, causing collapse of houses/buildings, culverts and critical infrastructure, and increase to floodplain vulnerability in the affected regions. This situation is getting wores as rains on the 7 and 8th september increases the vulnerability of the affected population.

The situational report of The Gambia Government through the National Disaster Management Agency (NDMA) indicates that, 1,321 households representing 10,560 people are affected. Three thousand one hundred and twenty-nine (3,129) houses are affected, out which 908 are completely destroyed and 2,221 are partialy destroyed. Several communities have been impacted by flood disaster in all regions in the country notably Upper River, Central River, West Coast, Lower River Regions and Kanifng Municiaplity. Reports has also indicated WASH challenges in some of the flood prone areas. 

The floods killed 1 child, injured  more than 50 others, with 75 water points and approximately 161 sanitary facilities destroyed by the floods.  The precipitation intensifies causing more destruction and devastation. Therefore, these figures are expected to rise significantly.

Food, household items and some rominants are reported been lost in the floods with little or no support. Most of the affected people have no coping mechnism and are hosted by their relatives and neighbours. GRCS volunteers are currently on the ground conducting assessment and how best to support the affected people.

summary:
According to local authorities, Typhoon Kajiki made landfall in Viet Nam on 25 August with winds up to 120 km/h before weakening into a tropical depression over Lao PDR on 26 August. The storm continues to bring heavy rainfall, with some areas expected to receive up to 90 mm within 24 hours, raising risks of flash floods and landslides.

Flooding has already affected communities in Khammouane and Bolikhamxay provinces, where villages were inundated and access routes cut off. Vientiane Capital has also reported flooding risks, with authorities warning that continued rainfall could worsen conditions. Communities in at-risk areas are urged to remain vigilant and take precautionary measures.

countries.name: Democratic Republic of Congo
countries.society_name: Red Cross of the Democratic Republic of the Congo
dtype.name: Epidemic
name: DRC - Ebola Virus 16 Outbreak - 2025
summary:
This is the 16th Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) since 1976. It comes after almost three years without a confirmed outbreak in the country. The previous outbreak was declared on 15 August 2022 in Beni, North Kivu Province, where a single case was reported and later died; the Ministry of Health declared the end of that outbreak on 27 September 2022. In Bulape district—the epicentre of the current outbreak—the last recorded EVD outbreak dates back to 2007.

According to official data from MOH , as of 12 September 2025 the provisional toll stands at 43 suspected cases, 30 Confimed case and 27 deaths, with a case fatality rate estimated at 56%. 

This outbreak is unfolding in a complex epidemiological and humanitarian context. The country is simultaneously facing outbreaks of mpox, cholera, and measles, while also grappling with a prolonged economic and political crisis. These overlapping challenges are straining national resources and limiting response capacity.

The epicentre is located near Tshikapa city, the capital of Kasai Province, and close to the Angolan border (100–200 km depending on the crossing point). Although the affected district is a hard-to-reach rural area far from the main urban centres of Mbuji Mayi and Kananga, population movements are frequent, particularly between Bulape and Tshikapa, raising the risk of wider spread.

In response, the Government has activated the Public Health Emergency Operations Center (COUSP), mobilized rapid response teams, strengthened epidemiological surveillance, and established triage and isolation facilities. Safe and dignified burial practices are also being implemented to protect communities while respecting cultural norms.

summary:
According to Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation (DDPM), since August 24, 2025, Tropical Storm "Kajiki" has brought heavy rainfall across Thailand, triggering widespread floods and landslides. The situation has evolved into a significant humanitarian crisis, impacting communities in the northern and northeastern regions. As of today, the disaster has affected 12 provinces: Chiang Rai, Phayao, Nan, Phrae, Lampang, Lamphun, Chiang Mai, Mae Hong Son, Phetchabun, Uttaradit, Loei, and Nakhon Phanom.

A total of 1,808 households, or 6,354 people, have been directly affected by the floods and landslides. 5 confirmed deaths, 15 people injured, and 7 people missing.

countries.name: Ghana
dtype.name: Population Movement
name: GHA: Population Movement - 08-2025 - Chieftancy Dispute
summary: The Sawla–Tuna–Kalba land dispute has already escalated into violent clashes, resulting in multiple deaths, injuries, widespread destruction of homes, and displacement of over a thousand people. If the situation is not contained, there is a high risk of further escalation into a larger-scale communal conflict. This could spread to other parts of the Savannah Region and along the Black Volta corridor, affecting nearby border communities. Projected Impact Humanitarian Crisis Expansion: Rising displacement could quickly overwhelm host communities, public facilities, and available humanitarian resources. The current supply of tents and shelter materials is already inadequate, leaving many without safe accommodation. Public Health Risks: Poor shelter conditions, lack of WASH facilities, and food insecurity create a heightened risk of waterborne disease outbreaks (cholera, diarrhea), malnutrition, and secondary infections among the injured. Protection Concerns: Vulnerable groups (women, children, elderly, disabled) face increased risks of violence, exploitation, and psychosocial trauma due to displacement and loss of livelihoods. Economic & Food Security Impact: With farms, food stocks, and motorbikes destroyed, affected families may face long-term livelihood losses, further driving poverty and food insecurity in the region. Security Instability: Continued clashes may stretch security forces and undermine peace in the district. Prolonged tensions could destabilize cross-border trade and movement, worsening regional fragility. Without immediate humanitarian assistance and sustained conflict resolution, the land dispute could evolve into a protracted humanitarian and security crisis.

name: VNM: Cyclone - 08-2025 - Kajiki
summary:
At 07:00 on 24 August, the center of Typhoon Kajiki was located at approximately 17.5°N latitude and 111.4°E longitude, over the northwestern waters of the Paracel Islands, about 620 km east-southeast of Nghe An and about 600 km east of Ha Tinh. The maximum sustained wind near the center was level 12, gusting up to level 15. The typhoon is moving westward at about 20 km/h.

Forecast track (next 24 to 60 hours):

 

  • By 07:00 on 25 August: The typhoon is expected to be at 18.3°N – 107.1°E, over the southern Gulf of Tonkin, about 160 km from Nghe An and 140 km from Ha Tinh to the east. Moving west-northwest at around 20 km/h, with winds of level 12–13, gusting to level 15, and may strengthen further.
    • Danger zone: between latitudes 16.0°N – 20.0°N and longitudes 106.5°E – 114.5°E.
    • Disaster risk level 3: western part of the northern East Sea (including the Paracel Islands), Gulf of Tonkin, southern waters of Quang Tri – Thua Thien Hue (including Hon Ngu Island, Con Co Island).
    • Disaster risk level 4: coastal waters from Thanh Hoa to Quang Tri.

 

  • By 07:00 on 26 August: The typhoon is expected to be at 18.9°N – 103.3°E, over the upland region of Laos. Moving west-northwest at 15–20 km/h, gradually weakening, with winds at level 6, gusting to level 8.
    • Danger zone: between latitudes 16.0°N – 20.0°N, west of longitude 108.5°E.
    • Disaster risk level 3: Gulf of Tonkin, southern waters of Quang Tri – Thua Thien Hue (including Hon Ngu Island, Con Co Island).
    • Disaster risk level 4: coastal waters from Thanh Hoa to Quang Tri, mainland areas from Thanh Hoa to northern Quang Tri.

 

  • By 19:00 on 26 August: The typhoon is expected to be at 19.2°N – 101.3°E, over the upland region of Laos, with winds below level 6.
  • China National Meteorological Center (NMC): The intensity of 🌀Kajiki has been raised to 45 m/s (172 km/h), equivalent to level 15 on the Beaufort scale used in Viet Nam. The forecast landfall location is directly over Vinh City (Nghe An–Ha Tinh border).

 

  • Hong Kong Observatory (HKO): The intensity of 🌀Kajiki has been upgraded to 155 km/h, equivalent to level 14 on the Beaufort scale used in Viet Nam. The forecast landfall location is also directly over Vinh City (Nghe An–Ha Tinh border).

 

  • Meanwhile, the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) maintains Kajiki at the upper end of level 13, near level 14, with gusts up to level 17. The U.S. Navy’s Joint Typhoon Warning Center (JTWC) differs slightly from JMA, forecasting gusts up to level 16.

Expected impacts

 

Western waters of the northern East Sea (including the Paracel Islands): Winds at level 8–10; areas near the typhoon’s center reaching level 11–13, gusting to level 15. Wave heights 5.0–7.0 m, rising to 7.0–9.0 m near the center. Sea conditions: extremely rough. From the afternoon of 24 August, coastal waters from Thanh Hoa to Thua Thien Hue (including Hon Ngu Island and Con Co Island) will experience gradually strengthening winds at level 6–8, later increasing to level 9–10, and near the center up to level 11–13, gusting to 15. Waves 4.0–6.0 m, rising to 7.0–9.0 m near the center. Sea conditions: extremely rough. From the afternoon of 24 August, the northern Gulf of Tonkin (including Cat Hai, Co To, Van Don) will experience strengthening winds at level 6–7, gusting to level 9; particularly in the southern part of the northern Gulf of Tonkin (including Bach Long Vi Island), winds will reach level 8, gusting to level 10. Wave heights 2.0–4.0 m. Sea conditions: rough.

 

Coastal areas and islands from Hai Phong to Ha Tinh: Storm surge of 0.5–1.5 m. Expected water levels at tidal stations: Hon Dau (Hai Phong) 3.3–3.8 m; Ba Lat (Ninh Binh) 1.7–2.1 m; Sam Son (Thanh Hoa) 3.2–3.7 m; Hon Ngu (Nghe An) 3.2–3.6 m; Cua Nhuong (Ha Tinh) 2.2–2.6 m. There is a high risk of inundation in low-lying coastal and estuary areas due to storm surge and high waves in the afternoon and evening of 25 August.

 

Onshore impacts: From the night of 24 August, inland areas from Thanh Hoa to Quang Tri will experience gradually strengthening winds at level 7–9, with areas near the typhoon’s center reaching level 10–12, gusting to level 14–15. Coastal provinces from Quang Ninh to Ninh Binh will experience winds strengthening to level 6–7, gusting to level 8.

 

Tides: At Cua Hoi, tide levels are expected to reach 2.0 m at 13:00 on 25 August, coinciding with the projected landfall of the typhoon.

countries.name: Mauritania
dtype.name: Flood
name: MRT: Flood - 08-2025 - Mauritania: Floods / River Flood 2025
summary:
The populations along the Senegal River are facing an unprecedented situation. The rising waters, caused by heavy rainfall in Mauritania, Senegal, Mali and especially Guinea, where the river originates, has considerably raised the water level, leading to overflows and devastating floods. Many villages were flooded, causing the destruction of homes, loss of crops and livestock, and plunging the already precarious inhabitants into immense distress, tens of thousands of people living in the localities of the Senegal River valley. over an area of 700 kilometres, suffered a major disaster caused by flooding. On the Mauritanian side of the river, four regions are affected: Gorgol, Guidimakha, Brakna and Trarza. According to these weather data, the probability of heavy rains will persist over the next few days, which indicates a significant risk of rising water levels in the river. The warnings received from the OMVS and the OMVS show a high probability of flooding in several places in Mauritania with a peak expected at the end of August and September 2025, the rainiest month in general. The potential risk of localized flooding, overflow, low water is very high at the Matam Toufoundé civé and maghama stations in Gorgol as well as the Gouraye station at Guidimakha, the alert level has been crossed. The flood wave continues to advance downstream.

From August 19 to 22, 2025, the Gorgol region was hit by floods, especially in the departments of Kaedi and Maghama following heavy rains, causing population displacement, material damage and the isolation of neighborhoods such as Wandama and Dar Salam. One child died by drowning; The waters also invaded part of the asphalt road coming from Nouakchott via Boghé.

In addition, several villages in the Guidimakha region of southeastern Mauritania experienced torrential rains that exceeded the barrier by 100 mm in several localities in the departments of Ghabou and Wompou as well as the district of Gouraye bordering Bakel in Senegal. These villages have suffered heavy rainfall, these are the villages of Ghavou, Diaguily and Gouraye. The road from Seilibaby to Ghabou is unreachable, the only means of transport of people and goods is the maritime logistics means (traditional canoes)

countries.name: Mauritania
dtype.name: Population Movement
name: Mauritania Population Movement 2025
summary:
Since January 2025, the MRC has reported a growing humanitarian crisis at the Rosso border crossing with Senegal. Migrants
intercepted inside Mauritania—over 30 000 between January and April—are expelled to Rosso and refused onward passage. Local reports
observer up to two buses of 60–70 people arriving each day, some of which are left stranded with irregular administrative situation. The
caseload includes mainly young men but also some unaccompanied minors and women (numerous pregnant or caring for infants).

The recent MSF assessment confirmed no international actors on-site and found that the few local organisations, including the MRC, are overstretched.
This continuous influx has plunged the migrant population into a situation of acute humanitarian distress. Many lack access to clean
water, food, essential medicines, and adequate shelter. A significant number are forced to sleep outdoors or in makeshift facilities,
exposed to harsh weather conditions, particularly during Ramadan and periods of extreme heat.

countries.name: Cabo Verde
dtype.name: Flood
name: Cape Verde - Floods 2025
summary:
On the night of 10–11 August 2025, torrential rains triggered devastating flash floods across São Vicente and Santo Antão islands in Cabo Verde, with partial impacts also reported in São Nicolau. The heavy rainfall, occurring within just a few hours, caused widespread flooding, landslides, and extensive destruction of homes, infrastructure, and essential services.

 Preliminary assessments suggest that approximately 119,000 people may have been affected, representing the combined population of the two worst-hit islands. At least 12 people have been confirmed dead, with five missing, while over 5,500 households have been severely impacted, including 1,500 displaced people in São Vicente alone.

 The floods has severely disrupted essential services. Health infrastructure was heavily damaged, with the main hospital in Mindelo and several clinics flooded, while critical vaccine stocks were lost in São Vicente and partially in Santo Antão and São Nicolau. Water and sanitation systems were also disrupted, creating acute drinking water shortages that now require daily ferry transport of potable water (150 m³) from Santo Antão to São Vicente. Power and communications networks were intermittently affected, complicating coordination and response efforts.

 Infrastructure damage is extensive, with 2,500 buildings damaged, five bridges destroyed, and several kilometres of roads affected according to the currently information available. Flooding also devastated local markets and supermarkets, limiting food access and damaging small businesses. Several areas remain difficult to access due to blocked or damaged roads, isolating affected communities.

 The Government of Cabo Verde has declared a national emergency, activating national disaster response mechanisms. The Cabo Verde Red Cross (CVRC), supported by the IFRC and partners, has mobilised volunteers to provide immediate relief, including the distribution of non-food items (NFIs) to 300 families.

Affecting 68 neighborhoods in rural areas near the epicenter, it caused the demolition of 16 buildings, out of which 12 were not habitable during the Earthquake.  The Search and Rescue Teams from the National Disaster Management Agency have been operational with 781 staff, 170 vehicles, and have rescued 4 people from under the rubble. MoH has mobilized 258 staff and 76 vehicles for medevac and medical response. The Logistics Centers in Balıkesir, Bursa, and Manisa are operational and ready to send  46,540 family-type tents to the affected area.

summary:
In the early morning of August 8, 2025, following a heavy torrential rain, a landslide occurred in the district of Foumban, department of Noun,  simultaneously in the villages of said Mapouoche par Njintout, Njilom, Machinka, Koudounka). It should be noted that this same locality had already been subject to a landslide in 2018. The district and departmental committees of the Red Cross of the Noun department immediately went down to the field to assess the situation. The toll to date is nearly 3600 people directly affected, i.e. 500 households.  There is no loss of human life but significant material damage is to be deplored, namely: 165 households without shelter because their houses have been completely destroyed as well as household items, damaged community infrastructure (roads, bridges, places of worship, graves, easements, commercial buildings; toilets).

The rainy season is in full swing and the national weather forecast announces an increase in rainfall that could lead to a series of floods in several parts of the country, including the West region. There is an urgent need for action to save lives.

En effet, les fortes pluies du samedi 02 août 2025 qui se sont poursuivies pendant plus de 09 heures ont provoqué de graves inondations dans la ville de Luba, capitale de la province de Bioko Sur. En outre, certains quartiers de la capitale du pays, Malabo, tels que Pérez, Timbabe, Vicatana, entre autres, sont également touchés plus modérément par les pluies.

Selon  des premieres evaluations rapide faites par la CR et certaines sources d'information en ligne, les degats matérielles sont nombreux, certains ont même perdu des voitures qui ont été emportées par les eaux, la plupart ont tout perdu, en effet, les maisons n'ont rien récupéré qui puisse avoir de la valeur.  Certaines  populations ont ete relogees dans un site temporaire.

countries.name: Viet Nam
dtype.name: Pluvial/Flash Flood
name: VNM: Pluvial/Flash Flood - 07-2025 - Viet Nam - Pluvial/Flash Flood - 08/2025
summary:
Between late July and early August 2025, prolonged heavy rainfall associated with Storm Wipha triggered widespread flooding, flash floods, and landslides across three northern provinces of Viet Nam: Nghệ An, Điện Biên, and Sơn La. The most severely affected areas are remote mountainous communes where rainfall exceeded seasonal norms and overwhelmed already fragile infrastructure. As a result, at least 19 people have died, one is missing, and over 11 others injured. More than 2,000 houses were either damaged or destroyed, while major roads and bridges were washed away, isolating dozens of communities.

Approximately 76,600 to 85,600 people have been directly affected, including thousands who lost homes, access to clean water, food sources, and means of livelihood. In Nghệ An alone, over 58,000 people across 132 villages in 15 communes have been cut off due to road blockages and rising river levels. In Điện Biên and Sơn La, many families were forced to evacuate or take shelter in temporary locations as flash floods inundated homes and farmland. Livelihoods have been heavily disrupted, with thousands of hectares of rice, crops, and livestock lost. Immediate humanitarian needs include shelter, food, safe water, and access to healthcare for displaced and isolated households.

countries.name: Japan
dtype.name: Earthquake
name: JPN: Tsunami - 07-2025 - Tsunami warning issued for Japan's Pacific coast triggered by the M8.8 earthquake in Kamchatka Peninsula, Russia
summary:
Overview:
An earthquake with a magnitude of 8.8 at a depth of 20.69 km has occurred at 136 km east-southeast of Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky, Russia, as reported by the National Earthquake Information Center (NEIC) of the USGS on July 29, 2025 08:24 local time（JST）.
A tsunami warning of up to 3 meters has been issued along Japan's Pacific coast from Hokkaido to Wakayama. Officials are calling on people to stay evacuated until all alerts are lifted despite the hot weather. Tsunami have been observed over wide areas along the coast, including a 1.3-meter wave at Kuji Port in Iwate Prefecture.（As of 16:30 local time on 30 July 2025）

Impact:
Tsunami waves have reached several Pacific coastal areas of Japan after the earthquake.

  • A 1.3-meter tsunami was recorded at Kuji Port in Iwate prefecture, while a 80 centimeter wave was observed at Nemuro, Hokkaido and 70 centimeter tsunami at Ishinomaki Port in Miyagi.
  • High waves have also been observed in the Tohoku and Kanto regions. A 30 centimeter wave was recorded at Yokohama Port.

Runways at Sendai Airport in Japan's northeast have been closed after an earthquake in Russia triggered tsunami warnings.

  • The transport ministry said the runway shutdown began around 9:40 a.m., and that some flights bound for the major coastal hub were rerouted.
  • Flights to and from the airport were suspended. Airlines are urging customers to stay updated by checking their websites.

countries.name: Costa Rica
dtype.name: Tsunami
name: ITT: Tsunami - 07-2025 - Strong currents on the Pacific coast due to the effect of the 8.8 earthquake in Russia
summary:
The Volcanological and Seismological Observatory of Costa Rica, National University (OVSICORI-UNA), published an international earthquake report at 17:24 on July 29, 2025, with an epicenter 131km SE of Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky, Russia, with a Magnitude of 8.8Mw, cataloging it as a "Megaearthquake"

At 8:43 p.m., the National Tsunami Monitoring System, National University (SINAMOT-UNA) indicates that according to the information available so far, strong currents caused by the tsunami caused by the seismic movement are expected from 7:50 a.m. on July 30, 2025, extending until 2:00 p.m., for which it issues a report of Dangerous Currents for the Pacific coast and rrecommends not sailing or carrying out activities at sea during the indicated period of time.

In view of this, the National Commission for Risk Prevention and Emergency Attention (CNE), activated the Emergency Operations Center (COE) with the participation of the Costa Rican Red Cross and declared Yellow Alert 25-2025 in the cantons of the entire Pacific coast, namely La Cruz, Liberia, Carrillo, Santa Cruz, Nicoya, Hojancha, Nandayure in the North Pacific region. Puntarenas, Esparza, Garabito, Parrita, Quepos and Cocos Island in the Central Pacific region, as well as Osa, Puerto Jiménez, Golfito in the South Pacific Region.

In view of this, the DINARE of the Costa Rican Red Cross , in accordance with the provisions of the National Emergency and Disaster Response Plan (PLANRED), decreed Response Level #2 for the Guanacaste, Puntarenas and South Pacific regions, activating the internal mechanisms of anticipation and response, representation in Municipal Emergency Committees, in addition to providing information to help the population of the Pacific coast.

name: GTM: Earthquake - 07-2025 - Sensitive Earthquakes in Guatemala
summary:
On July 29, 2025 at 3:21 p.m., the first of several sensitive earthquakes was recorded in much of the national territory, with an epicenter in the department of Jutiapa, bordering El Salvador.  The aftershocks continue and many of them of intensity greater than 3.6 on the Richter scale and with shallow epicenter depth. 

Preliminary reports indicate that there is damage to homes, buildings and 2 health facilities. Some of the injured are being treated by local health services and rescue services.

The authorities of CONRED have declared a national orange alert.

countries.name: Portugal
dtype.name: Fire
name: PRT: Fire - 07-2025 - Forest fire
summary:
Since the beginning of 2025, wildfires in Portugal have burned an estimated 60,000 hectares across multiple districts, with 6,393 rural fire incidents recorded up to 11 August. Numerous large-scale events have led to preventive evacuations and significant damage to rural areas. The most affected regions have been in the North and Centre of the country, where mountainous and forested landscapes, combined with hot and dry weather, have created critical fire conditions.

The National Civil Protection issued Rural Fire Danger warnings on 17 and 27 June and 25 July, based on forecasts of hot and dry weather and an increased wildfire risk. A State of Alert was declared for the entire mainland from 3 to 7 August 2025, later extended to cover the period from 8 to 13 August 2025.

The Portuguese Red Cross has been actively engaged in the response, providing rest areas for firefighters, emergency transport and victim evacuation support, and logistical assistance in affected regions. The Red Cross has also activated a Crisis Room to coordinate its operations and responses effectively.

As of 12 August, the National Society has been present in 15 operational theatres since 27 July, deploying 222 operational staff and 29 logistical personnel, supported by 15 vehicles and 28 activated local branches. The Emergency Operations Center has been operating 24/7. As a preventive measure, logistical trailers (for setting up population support areas), a drone team, and a command and communications vehicle are on standby.

name: COG: Epidemic - 07-2025 - CHOLERA EPIDEMIC
summary:
This confirmation of the cholera epidemic in our country comes in a regional context marked by the resurgence of cholera in neighboring countries, particularly in Angola, with confirmed cases in the province of Kabinda and in the Democratic Republic of Congo with confirmed cases in Kinshasa and in the province of Equateur (Loukoléla zaire).
In any case, suspects and even confirmed are quarantined in the nearest health centers with a great need for appropriate medical assistance.
This situation is once again affecting the Congolese health system, which on the eve of its independence day is confronted with this scourge. 
To date, the rapid and unusual increase in the number of cases is possible in the localities of the island of Mbamou, Loukoléla and Mossaka due to the period of fairground markets.

countries.name: Greece
dtype.name: Fire
name: GRC: Fire - 07-2025 - Wildfires in Greece, 26-28, July, 2025
summary:
Greece experienced one of its most intense wildfire outbreaks in recent years, with over 50 wildfires reported in just 24 hours. The fires were fueled by a prolonged heatwave (temperatures reaching up to 45°C) and strong winds (6–7 Beaufort), creating extreme fire conditions across the country.

The primary affected areas were Kryoneri (Attica), Pedini - Ioannina (Epirus Region), Patra (Achaea Region), Temenia and surrounding villages (Chania, Crete), Polithea, Monastiri, and Aetos (Messinia, Peloponnese), Serres (Northern Greece), and Central and Northern Euboea (Evia).

Thousands of residents were evacuated across multiple regions. In numbers over 32,000 people were displaced nationwide, with many seeking shelter in schools, community centers, and temporary shelters.

Over 1,100 firefighters were deployed nationwide. Moreover, Greece requested six additional water-dropping aircraft from the EU Civil Protection Mechanism. One hundred forty-five firefighters, 44 vehicles, 7 helicopters, and 10 aircraft were active in Attica alone.

Many firefighters were hospitalized due to burns and smoke inhalation while battling the fires. These injuries occurred during intense efforts to contain fires threatening residential areas, with some fire trucks also damaged in the process. Moreover, civilians were injured, suffering from burns, respiratory problems, and other injuries.  

The extensive damage influences the forests, agricultural land, animal pens, houses, cars, and more.

countries.name: Thailand

name: THA: Other - 07-2025 - Tensions between Thailand and Cambodia
summary:
According to several sources, tensions between Thailand and Cambodia have rapidly escalated since 24 July 2025, near the Prasat Ta Muen Thom (Ta Muen Thom) temple in the Oddar Meanchey and Preah Vihear provinces in Cambodia, and in Ubon Ratchathani, Surin and Si Saket provinces in Thailand.

Impact In Thailand,

  • Over 138,000 Thai civilians from four border provinces (Surin, Sisaket, Burirum and Ubon Ratchathani provinces) have been evacuated to nearly 300 temporary shelters.
  • 14 Thai civilians and one Thai soldier died
  • One damaged hospital – Phanom Dong Rak hospital in Suring Province
  • Affected Provinces and Hospitals: Ubon Ratchathani Province: Three medical facilities affected, with two hospitals completely shut down and one partially closed. Sisaket Province: Two hospitals completely shut down, including Kantharalak Hospital, which evacuated approximately 170 patients due to the town being a high-risk zone. Surin Province: Two hospitals partially closed and two fully closed down. Phanom Dongrak Chalerm Phrakiat in Phanom Dongrak District was specifically reported to have suffered significant damage , leading to the urgent evacuation of injured patients. Buriram Province: One hospital closed, while two are partially closed.

Impact in Cambodia

  • More than 20,000 people have fled from the northern border province of Preah Vihear, and Preah Vihear with many relocations to temporary shelters.
  • 01 civilian died and 05 injured

The situation has drawn urgent international attention. Both the UN and ASEAN have issued statements calling for the immediate cessation of hostilities and urging both governments to exercise restraints, pursue diplomatic channels and prioritize civilian protection.

countries.name: Mongolia
dtype.name: Storm Surge
name: MNG: Storm Surge - 07-2025 - Severe Wind Storm-Flash Rainfall
summary:
On the night of 24–25 July 2025, Mongolia was struck by a sudden severe windstorm reaching up to 33 m/s, followed by short but intense rainfall, hailstorms, and thunderstorms. The event caused widespread damage across 15 locations in Ulaanbaatar, Sukhbaatar Province, and Tuv Province, severely impacting household dwellings, public infrastructure, and essential services.

The most extensive damage was recorded in Songinokhairkhan District, Ulaanbaatar, where 113 traditional homes collapsed, including two rendered completely uninhabitable. In addition, 60 fences and 9 vehicles were damaged, two kindergartens lost parts of their roofs, and four residents sustained minor injuries. Power outages were reported in five khoroos, with 13 utility poles downed, including four in the 32nd khoroo where electricity remains cut off.

In Sukhbaatar Province, the soums of Halzan, Uulbayan, and Tumentsogt experienced heavy rainfall and strong winds. Khalzan received up to 65 mm of rain and reported damage to 27 traditional homes, 20 fences, and 3 house roofs, along with the collapse of a flood embankment that led to the inundation of five households. Playground equipment, greenhouses, and sanitation facilities were destroyed, and multiple vehicles became stuck in mud. Uulbayan and Tumentsogt reported additional household losses and vehicle damage.

In Tuv Province, storm activity affected Bayankhangai, Argalant, Lun, Erdenesant, and Zuunmod soums, with some areas experiencing hail. Over 80 traditional houses collapsed across these locations. Public structures, including school dormitories, kitchens, and bathhouses, were damaged. In Lun soum, a fallen 35kV transmission pole led to a power outage affecting 483 customers, including businesses and households. Livestock deaths and widespread fence destruction were also reported.

countries.name: Indonesia
dtype.name: Earthquake
name: IDN: Earthquake - 07-2025 - Earthquake Disaster in Poso District, Central Sulawesi Province
summary:
On Thursday, July 24, 2025, at 20:06 WITA, an earthquake with a magnitude of 6.0 SR struck Poso District, Central Sulawesi. The epicenter was located at a depth of 10 km, with coordinates 2.03°S, 120.70°E, approximately 70 km southwest of Poso.

The earthquake was felt across several regions, with the following intensities based on BMKG analysis:

  • MMI IV-V in Poso,

  • MMI III-IV in Bungku,

  • MMI IV-V in Kolonodale,

  • MMI II-III in Palu,

  • MMI IV-V in Mangkutana,

  • MMI III-IV in Mappadeceng.

Fortunately, the earthquake did not generate a tsunami threat.

Impact of the Disaster

The most severely affected area was Pamona Tenggara District in Poso Regency. The earthquake impacted 1,560 households (approximately 4,680 people). The casualties include:

  • 4 individuals with severe injuries,

  • 5 individuals with minor injuries,

  • 4,680 displaced individuals,

  • 52 houses severely damaged,

  • 248 houses lightly damaged,

  • 5 places of worship,

  • 2 schools.

Post-Earthquake Situation

As of July 31, BMKG recorded 208 aftershocks with magnitudes ranging from 3.0 to 4.0 SR. Although the situation has stabilized, many residents remain concerned about potential aftershocks and have chosen to seek refuge with relatives for safety.

Health Reports

According to Puskris Kemenkes, 106 health-related cases have been reported following the earthquake, with a variety of conditions including:

  • Hypertension

  • Vertigo

  • Cold/flu

  • Asthma

  • Gastritis

  • Dyspepsia

  • Myalgia

  • Arthritis

  • Parotitis

  • Hypotension

  • Common cold

The most frequently reported condition is hypertension, with 20 reported cases.

countries.name: Pakistan
dtype.name: Pluvial/Flash Flood
name: Pakistan: Monsoon Flood, 2025
summary:
Since 26 June 2025, heavy monsoon rains have caused severe flash flooding across Pakistan including Gilgit Baltistan (GB), Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJ&K), while Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) province being among the worst aected. The districts of Buner, Swat, Shangla, Mansehra and Swabi have suered extensive loss of life, widespread damage to infrastructure, and disruption of essential services. The situation worsened dramatically on 14 and 15 August due to intense cloudbursts, particularly in Buner, where rainfall reached 150 mm per hour. According to PDMA, 358 people have died across KP, with Buner for 225, Swat 20, Shangla 36, Bajur 22 and Swabi 17 accounting fatalities. Thousands of homes, schools, shops, and infrastructure such as roads, bridges, and water systems have been destroyed or damaged. In Swat, Village Golkada, UC Landi Kas Tehsil Babuzai 80 per cent infrastructure such as roads, bridges, and water sources have also been damaged, while in Shangla (Village Shahi Dand and Kuz Palaw), Bajur, Swabi and Mansehra, multiple villages report extensive losses to housing, agriculture and livelihoods. 

According to the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), over 693 fatalities and nearly 1,000 injuries recorded to date, more than 2,707 houses damaged and 1,005 livestock have perished. 

The Pakistan Meteorological Department (PMD) warns of continued heavy rainfall through 21 August 2025 heightening the risk of additional flooding, landslides, and glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) in mountainous regions. With over 7,000 glaciers, GB is acutely exposed to sudden GLOF events. The World Weather Attribution initiative has found that global warming has made monsoon rains in Pakistan 10–15 per cent heavier, intensifying the impact of cloudbursts, rapid snowmelt and river overflows.

The overall situation is still unfolding and actual data remains unclear. The National Society is planning to conduct rapid and detailed need assessments and based on the findings of the assessments and damage details the operational strategy will be revised to scale up the response and interventions to better respond to the needs of the affected population.

countries.name: Viet Nam
dtype.name: Other
name: VNM: Other - 07-2025 - Typhoon Wipha-Heavy rain and flash flood
summary:
As of the morning of July 21, Typhoon Wipha remains at Category 9 but is forecast to strengthen to Category 10-11 as it enters the Gulf of Tonkin, then directly impacts provinces from Quang Ninh to Nghe An.

According to the National Center for Hydro-Meteorological Forecasting (NCHMF), at 7:00 AM today, the typhoon's center was located over the northern part of the Leizhou Peninsula (China), about 220 km east of Quang Ninh – Hai Phong. The maximum wind speed reached 88 km/h, equivalent to Category 9, with gusts up to Category 11. The storm is moving west-southwest at a speed of 15–20 km/h. By 7:00 AM on July 22, the typhoon is expected to strengthen to Category 10–11, with gusts reaching Category 14, while located over the northern Gulf of Tonkin, and may continue to intensify. It is then forecast to move inland over the provinces from Thanh Hoa to Nghe An and weaken into a low-pressure system over the Upper Laos region.

Forecasted impacts

At Sea:

  • East Sea & Gulf of Tonkin: Winds force 7–11, gusts up to 14; waves 2–6 m; extremely rough seas.
  • High risk in Bạch Long Vi, Co To, Cat Hai, Hon Dau, Hon Ngu with dangerous winds and high waves.

Storm Surge & Coastal Flooding:

  • Surge of 0.5–1.0 m along Hai Phong–Quang Ninh.
  • High tide levels: Hòn Dấu up to 4.1 m, Cua Ong ~4.8 m.
  • Flooding risk from afternoon July 22 in coastal and estuarine zones.

Onshore Hazards (from night July 21):

  • Winds force 7–11, gusts 14 from Quang Ninh to Nghe An; inland gusts up to 8.
  • High damage potential: uprooted trees, power outages, roof damage.

Rainfall & Severe Weather:

  • Heavy to extreme rain July 21–23:
    • NE, Red River Delta, Thanh Hoa–Nghe An: 200–350 mm (locally >600 mm).
    • Hà Tĩnh, northern regions: 100–200 mm (locally >300 mm).
  • Flash flood, landslide, tornado, hail, and lightning risks remain high.
  • Rain persists through July 25 in northern and north-central areas.

Between 19 and 20 July, severe weather—including lightning, tornadoes, and hail—caused significant impacts across 14 provinces in northern, central, and southern Viet Nam. Four fatalities and 11 injuries were reported, primarily due to falling debris, collapsed structures, and lightning strikes. A total of 19 houses were completely destroyed and over 1,700 others sustained damage or were unroofed. Damage was also reported to 32 schools and over 280 hectares of agricultural land, including rice, vegetables, and perennial crops. Additionally, 36 boats were reported capsized. Local authorities are actively responding to the situation and continuing damage assessments.

countries.name: Thailand
dtype.name: Flood
name: THA: Flood - 07-2025 - Heavy rainfall and flash floods
summary:
Widespread flooding has affected parts of Nan and Chanthaburi provinces in Thailand following days of heavy rainfall and flash floods between 16 and 17 July 2025. According to the Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation (DDPM), a total of 150 households (555 people) across 9 districts, 15 sub-districts, and 24 villages have been impacted. While there have been no reports of injuries or fatalities, the floods have caused temporary displacement and disruption to communities.

In Chanthaburi province, heavy rainfall on 17 July led to flash floods across four districts – including Khlung, Laem Sing, Mueang, and Makham – affecting 20 households (74 people). The floodwaters have since receded.

In Nan province, continuous rainfall from 16 to 17 July triggered flash floods across five districts – including Thung Chang, Chalerm Phrakiat, Song Khwae, Tha Wang Pha, and Pua – affecting 130 households (481 people). Water levels remain steady in some areas, and localized flooding persists.

summary: According to the MOIS, from July 16 to 18, 2025, prolonged and intense rainfall caused severe flooding, landslides, and infrastructure damage across multiple regions of the country. Accumulated rainfall exceeded 400mm in several areas, including Naju, Gwangju, and Honseong, leading to widespread disruption. The hazard has had a substantial impact on both public infrastructure and private properties. As of July 18, a total of 5 people were reported dead or missing, with one individual still unaccounted for in Gwangju. Public infrastructure sustained over 490 incidents of damage, including flooded roads, landslides, collapsed dikes, and river overflows. Private property damage includes the flooding of over 200 buildings in Gwangju alone, structural collapes in Seoul and Gyeonggi Province, and significant agriculture losses in South Chungcheong. A total of 3,413 hhs - comprising 5,192 people - were forced to evacuate their homes, with over 4,500 people still unable to return as of the latest update. The majority of the displaced population is currently staying in temporary shelters set up in schools and public facilities, while some are residing with relatives. These families are among the most vulnerable, with many lacking the means to quickly recover or secure alternative accomodations.

name: ETH: Storm Surge - 07-2025 - Wind storm
summary:
Based on the Emergency Rapid Assessment Report of the joint team of Ethiopia Red Cross Society Regional branches and Regional Disaster Risk Management Commission of Amhara and Afar regions,  Severe windstorm with high intensity has struck the Afdera town of Kilbati Rasu Zone of Afar Region, and Five woredas of Amhara region mainly two weredas in West Gojam ( sekela and Finote selam wereda) and three weredas in North Gojam Zones ( North mecha, South Achefer and North Achefer weredas) Between late June and mid of July 2025.

The wind storm has caused a widespread destruction to 5368 homes, injured 87 people with 1person death and displaced a total of 38,537 peoples in both of the region. It has also destroyed 34 Hactar of crops, 50 goats and key social infrastructure like Salt Processing factories, schools, health facilities including Government offices.

It has severely affected the life’s and livelihoods, and resilience of communities in these affected weredas because they have experienced a heavy burden due to prior climate-induced drought, internal displacement and conflict. The re-occurrence of wind storm accompanied by heavy rain is imminent because Ethiopian heavy rainy season called “ Kiremit” is starting and will be stretching to September 2025. It will exacerbate the situation and more people will be affected due to the fact that More shelters and homes are destroyed and poor access to basic service.

countries.name: Bangladesh
dtype.name: Cold Wave
name: Bangladesh: Cold Wave EAP, 2025
summary:
Though Bangladesh is in a subtropical monsoon region, due to being situated close to the Himalayan, the northern especially north-western part of Bangladesh faces extreme weather conditions during winter. Bangladesh has recently been experiencing cold waves, which often result in adverse impacts on the livelihoods of the most vulnerable people. Due to the historical climatic condition, the people of the country are not prepared for the sudden drop in temperature, especially below 10°C, with their present household structures and livelihood patterns. Additionally, rural houses have no heating system and are designed for ventilation in summer. But there are no measures to protect the inhabitants from cold waves.
 
In Bangladesh, the cold wave is affecting the livelihood of vulnerable people mostly in the northwest and northeastern parts. Health risks like- respiratory problems or breathing issues, pneumonia, hypothermia, diarrhea, and other cold-related illnesses are a common situation for the elderly and children during the period of cold waves. Study shows that from 2009 to 2021 on average more than 100 people died during this period due to coldrelated sicknesses. In addition to agriculture activities, crop production, livestock and poultry farms, transport system, and education sector, overall day-to-day activities and economic activities are hampered during cold waves. 
 
The cold wave is a complex weather phenomenon. Though the minimum temperature is one the primary factors for expressing cold waves, maximum temperature, sudden drop, and feeling like temperature are not negligible as they intensify the impact of cold waves. Therefore, to understand the hazard of cold waves, historical analysis has been done for temperature and wind speed.

summary:
On 15 July 2025 at 2:00 PM, a Low-Pressure Area (LPA 07F) was monitored inside the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) with a "medium" potential to develop into a tropical depression within the next 24 hours.

 By 3:00 PM, LPA 07F was estimated to be located 1,040 km east of Southeastern Luzon. Meanwhile, the Southwest Monsoon was affecting the rest of the country.

 On 16 July 2025 at 8:00 AM, LPA 07F developed into Tropical Depression “CRISING”. By 11:00 PM, it had slightly intensified as it moved northwestward over the sea east of the Bicol Region.

A total of 7,501 families or 23,918 individuals were affected in 56 barangays in region 6, 7, and 12. Of which, 115 families or 117 individuals were served inside 6 ECs and 106 families or 526 individuals were served outside ECs.

countries.name: Bangladesh
dtype.name: Epidemic
name: BGD: Epidemic - 07-2025 - Dengue Situation
summary:
Dengue remains a major public health concern in Bangladesh, with recurrent outbreaks posing a significant threat. The dengue virus has the potential to cause widespread epidemics with high morbidity and mortality.

As of 17 July 2025, the total number of fatalities this year is 60. Additionally, on average, 300 new patients are hospitalized in the month of July, bringing the cumulative number of dengue cases to over 16,000 in 2025.

The current surge of cases, which began in June 2025, has affected all eight divisions, with Barisal being the hardest-hit. From 1 January to 13 July 2025, Barisal Division alone reported 6,286 cases, accounting for 41% of the total nationwide. The second and third highest numbers were reported in Dhaka (4,921) and Chattogram (2,193), respectively. Sylhet Division reported the lowest number of cases.Deaths were reported highest in Dhaka (31), while Rangpur and Sylhet divisions reported zero fatalities.In May 2025, there were 1,773 reported cases and 3 deaths, followed by a significant fivefold increase in June, with 5,951 hospital admissions and 19 confirmed deaths.

According to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), male patients accounted for 58.8% of total cases, compared to 41.2% in females.Similarly, the mortality rate was higher among males (53.4%) than females (46.6%).This trend is in contrast to 2023, when female deaths outnumbered male deaths.

The surge in cases is attributed to the onset of the monsoon season (May–September), which creates favorable breeding conditions for Aedes mosquitoes. High temperatures, increased humidity, and inadequate mosquito control measures further exacerbate the situation. Climate change, with intensified rainfall and heat waves, has extended the dengue transmission season and geographic reach.[1]

Unlike previous years, when Dhaka was the primary epicenter, in 2025, cases have been reported across all 64 districts, indicating a broader geographic distribution. Urban areas, particularly Dhaka and Chattogram, remain high-risk zones due to dense populations and rapid urbanization

The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) is actively monitoring cases through daily situation reports. The government has implemented measures like dedicated dengue wards and mosquito control programs, but challenges remain due to limited resources and insufficient surveillance in rural areas

[1] [1] https://www.who.int/southeastasia/activities/integrating-one-health-approach-to-surveillance-prevention-and-control-of-dengue-fever-in-bangladesh
