name: MOZ: Cyclone - 12-2024 - Tropical Cyclone Chido
summary:
On 15 December 2024, Tropical Cyclone (TC) CHIDO has made a landfall in the district of Mecufi in Cabo Delgado, northeastern Mozambique, at a maximum windspeed of 200km/h and windgust of 250km/h. It arrived from South Indian Ocean, crossing above Madagascar and through Mayotte and Comoros. As of 16 December, Mozambique’s National Institute for the coordination of Disaster Risk Reduction (INGD) has identified more than 175 thousand people in humanitarian need. 

As of 16 December, the number of confirmed deaths and injured is 27 and 36 in TC affected provinces. More than 24,000 shelters have been completely destroyed, leaving several thousands of families without a home. While CVM’s Early Action Protocol has been activated prior to the TC landing, their distributions of shelter kits have not arrived on time to support families before impact. CHIDO has landed earlier than the expected TC season and with greater impact due to La Nina climate phenomenon. Additionally, the TC hit amid a very unprecedented and unstable political period in Mozambique history, with nationwide protests and civil unrest following the results of presidential election in October.

countries.name: Africa Region
dtype.name: Cyclone
name: Africa - Cyclone Chido
summary:
Tropical Cyclone Chido was the first cyclone with a significant and destructive impact in the Southwest Indian Ocean region during what was forecasted to be an early and above-average cyclone season, with particular risk to the Mascarene Islands, east Madagascar, and Mozambique. Chido intensified into an intense tropical cyclone on 11 December, reaching category 4 - equivalent status with sustained winds of 220 km/h and gusts of up to 250 km/h, and an extreme central pressure of 929 hPa. As of 22 December, Tropical Cyclone Chido has resulted in at least 142 confirmed deaths – 94 in Mozambique, 35 in Mayotte, and 13 in Malawi – and over 3,300 reported injuries.

The first country impacted was Madagascar, where Cyclone Chido’s path crossed about 100 km from its northern tip – the Diana Region. An estimated 135,838 people were projected to be affected. Its strength was felt across several districts, causing significant damage to infrastructure and displacing residents. Heavy rains triggered flooding in several areas and impacted crops. Authorities, with the support from the Malagasy Red Cross, issued imminent danger warnings and took preventive measures, including the evacuation of at-risk communities.

The Comoros government declared a week-long mourning following the crossing of the devastating cyclone on 14 December, which has affected 64,167 people in the islands of Anjouan and Moheli, including 171 families who lost their homes. Schools and houses were damaged or destroyed while an average of 45 per cent of agricultural crops were affected.

Tropical Cyclone Chido caused extensive devastation in Mayotte, with approximately 70 per cent of its population – around 230,000 people – severely impacted. About 35,000 houses were destroyed, and the main hospital and airport were damaged, disrupting essential services and trade. There are roughly 100,000 people temporarily housed in 70 accommodation centres without water, food, or adequate hygiene and safety conditions.

In Mozambique, approximately 622,000 people have been affected by the cyclone, according to the latest reports. In Cabo Delgado alone, some 509,800 individuals have experienced severe damage to shelters and critical infrastructure, with significant impacts also reported in Tete, Nampula, and Niassa provinces. Over 130,000 shelters were damaged or destroyed, and the cyclone has caused widespread destruction to livelihoods, deepening existing vulnerabilities in the affected regions.

In Malawi, nearly 45,000 people have been affected due to the cyclone’s remnants, highlighting the need for continued disaster management and humanitarian aid.

These figures are preliminary, as assessments are ongoing to determine the full extent of the damage to infrastructure and agriculture. The National Societies of the Red Cross and Red Crescent are on the ground, fulfilling their humanitarian mandate by supporting search and rescue operations, providing first aid, and assisting with family reunifications and relocations.

name: FRA: Cyclone - 12-2024 - Mayotte Cyclone CHIDO
summary:
The intense tropical cyclone CHIDO struck Mayotte at full intensity in the middle of the day on December 14, before making landfall in northern Mozambique on the morning of December 15 as an intense tropical cyclone.

Usually spared by cyclones, Mayotte faced an unprecedented event, the likes of which had not been seen in over 90 years. Winds recorded by Météo France during Chido's passage exceeded an average speed of 176 km/h, with gusts reaching 226 km/h.

The situation report shared by the government on the 16th of December 2024 count with :

  • 21 Fatalities
  • 830 Injured people
  • 100 000 Sheltered people
  • 70 Emergency shelters
  • 7 816 Affected buildings 
  • 15 000 people are without access to electricity

However, as most roads remain inaccessible and some neighborhoods have been completely destroyed by mudslides and the collapse of bangas (precarious housing in slums), a much higher toll is feared.

Water, electricity, and telephone networks (with the exception of the Orange network) have been cut, making it particularly difficult to assess the human and material toll due to the lack of information coming from the field.

Precarious housing, which affects at least one-third of the archipelago's population, has been completely destroyed.

Infrastructure has also been impacted:

  • The airport's control tower is inoperative
  • The barges connecting Grande-Terre and Petite-Terre have been destroyed
  • The Prefecture (govt bulding), the Mayotte Hospital Center, the prison, and the Mayotte media studios have been damaged.

Commercial air connections are suspended (only military flights operative), the airport is expected to reopen by Thursday, December 19.

As a reminder, the socio-economic context in Mayotte before the impact of Cyclone CHIDO was as follows:

  • Official (legal) population estimated at 321,000 people. Very young population: average age 23.
  • At least 100,000 undocumented migrants, mainly from the Comoros, living in Mayotte, according to the Ministry of the Interior.
  • Approximately 77% of the Mahoran population living below the poverty line (compared to 14% in mainland France).
  • An economy heavily reliant on the public sector.
  • A context of significant insecurity characterized by the presence of gangs and frequent social unrest.
  • A persistent water crisis for several years, marked by prolonged water cuts affecting access to drinking water for many residents.
  • Mayotte recently experienced a Cholera outbreak, in April 2024.

countries.name: Myanmar
dtype.name: Heat Wave
name: Myanmar: Heatwave sEAP, 2024
summary:
There has been a general increase in temperatures across Myanmar over the last six decades. This has resulted in an increase in extreme high temperature days and thus the prevalence of heat-related disorders. Prolonged exposure to extreme heat, resulting in heat stress, is expected to increase in the next five years in all regions and states of Myanmar. According to the Department of Meteorology and Hydrology of Myanmar (DMH), there is high confidence that warming is very likely to continue across Myanmar. Climate change is leading to more frequent and severe heat waves. As global temperatures rise, the occurrence and intensity of heat waves are expected to increase in Myanmar.
 
The MONREC (Ministry of Natural Resources and Environmental Conservation of the Republic of the Union of Myanmar), in Myanmar's National Adaptation Programme of Action 2016-2030, reports 1,482 cases of heatrelated disorders and 260 heat-related deaths during the summer of 2010 across the country. As a so-called silent killer, heatwave deaths are likely underreported. In addition, the report highlights that local populations in Mandalay are experiencing heat-related stresses and diseases more frequently. It adds that extreme heat days in Mandalay forced all schools to close in 2015.
 
In 2010, a heatwave in Mandalay, reaching a daily maximum temperature of 47°C on 20 May 2010, reportedly killed 230 people. On 20 April 2014, during a heatwave with a daily maximum temperature of 41.7°C, 49 heatstroke cases were reported in Mandalay city3 , of which 9 resulted in death.
In Yangon, during a heatwave with a daily maximum temperature of 42.2°C in April 20194 , 8 people died from heat-related illnesses.
 
Additionally, while the people of Myanmar are accustomed to high temperatures throughout the year, deadly heat extremes have been increasingly recorded in recent years. This poses a problem as people may believe they are prepared for high temperatures, leading to a false safety perception. Some experiences indicate that individuals who did not seek information on heat-related illnesses during heatwaves are potentially at higher risk.
 
Rapid industrialization and urbanization in the country are leading to higher temperatures in urban areas, In urban areas located in
wet climate zones, such as Yangon, the impacts of the UHI are further intensified by high humidity levels in the air, which heighten the impact on human health.

countries.name: Haiti
dtype.name: Flood
name: HTI: Flood - 12-2024 - Inondations Grand-Anse decembre 2024
summary:
Durant la période allant du 30 novembre au 2 décembre 2024, de fortes pluies se sont déversées sur le département de la Grand-Anse provoquant des dégâts importants. 

Jérémie, la principale ville du département, a été la plus durement affectée, les intempéries ayant causé l’inondation de près de 80 % du territoire communal, entraînant la mort de deux enfants et de treize blessés, deux disparitions, à la suite d’un éboulement et au débordement de la ravive de Tipiman. Par ailleurs, les inondations ont touché 32 familles et provoqué le déplacement d’environ soixante personnes. Selon l’information fournie par l’administration de l’hôpital de Saint-Antoine de Jérémie, du 30 novembre au 2 décembre, plus de dizaines de personnes blessées sont hospitalisées. La commune de Dame-Marie quant à elle déplore deux pêcheurs portés disparus.

Les inondations ont également détruit deux maisons et endommagé environ vingt autres. Des infrastructures du département, notamment des routes intercommunales, ont été également dégradées. Plusieurs rues à Jérémie sont jonchées de boues, d’alluvions et de déchets.

countries.name: Bolivia
dtype.name: Other
name: BULL: Other - 11-2024 - Landslides
summary:
On November 23, an event was recorded due to the overflow of the Pasajahuira River in the area of Bajo Llojeta in La Paz, causing flooding and landslides in the area which caused the death of a minor, where 32 people were also evacuated, of which 14 are injured, around 30 houses are reported damaged and 40 affected (report of the Civil Vice Ministry)
The SENAMHI (National Meteorology and Hydrology Service) on November 26 declared an orange alert in 5 departments (La Paz, Cochabamba, Potosí, Chuquisaca and Tarija) in the country. Where on November 30, as a result of the constant rains, the Pasajahuira River overflowed again despite the fact that the local mayor's office had placed defensive walls and was with heavy machinery in the area, this was not an impediment for the water to re-enter the area.
 On December 1, the rains began to be felt in other departments as well, such was the case of Cochabamba where as a result of the rainfall it caused a landslide in the tropical area causing the crushing of 2 houses where unfortunately 4 people died and the cutting of the road that connects Cochabamba with Santa Cruz.
 It is expected that as it is in the rainy season, rainfall will increase, causing flooding and overflowing of rivers, as well as landslides in different areas.

name: BOL: Pluvial flood / flood - 11-2024 - Floods La Paz Bolivia
summary: In recent months November, December and January , the department of La Paz, Bolivia, has been affected by heavy rains that have caused flooding in several regions, especially in rural and urban areas near rivers and streams. The floods have caused thousands of people to evacuate their homes, as floodwaters have flooded homes, farmland and roads. More than 20,000 families have been directly affected, with a significant number of victims losing their homes, belongings and livelihoods. At least 16 deaths have been reported due to overflowing rivers and landslides. The situation has also generated a high risk of disease spread, as contaminated waters could affect people's health.

countries.name: Malaysia
dtype.name: Flood
name: Malaysia: East Coast Monsoon Flood - 2024
summary:
The Northeast Monsoon (MTL) began in early November 2024 and is expected to end by March 2025, during which Malaysia is forecasted to experience five to seven episodes of heavy rainfall. Continuous heavy rain lasting several days has resulted in flooding in low-lying and flood-prone areas, such as Kelantan, Terengganu, and several other regions in Peninsular Malaysia.

According to official statistics as of November 28, 2024, a total of 31,798 individuals from 9,613 families have been affected by the Northeast Monsoon floods in both the East and West Coasts. The affected states include Kelantan, Terengganu, Kedah, Perlis, Johor, and Perak. Official reports from the Social Welfare Department (JKM) indicate that 296 Temporary Evacuation Centers (PPS) have been established to accommodate those impacted. In Kelantan, electricity supply has been cut off in 17 areas across four districts due to worsening flood conditions. To date, only one fatality—a 33-year-old victim in Kelantan—has been reported, caused by electrocution.

Additionally, six major rivers in Kelantan have surpassed danger levels and are showing rising trends. These include Sungai Lanas in Jeli at 31.28 meters, Sungai Kelantan in Kuala Krai (25.41 meters), Sungai Kelantan in Machang (20.27 meters), Sungai Golok in Rantau Panjang (10.94 meters), Sungai Melor in Bachok (9.85 meters), and Sungai Semerak in Pasir Puteh (3.69 meters).

In Terengganu, the number of flood victims has risen sharply to 3,768 compared to 1,851 yesterday evening, with a total of 69 Temporary Evacuation Centers (PPS) opened across the districts of Besut, Setiu, Dungun, Hulu Terengganu, Marang, and Kemaman. Besut is the most affected district, recording 2,335 victims housed in 33 PPS, followed by Hulu Terengganu (513 people in 19 PPS), Setiu (388 people in 11 PPS), Dungun (246 people in two PPS), Kemaman (215 people in two PPS), and Marang (71 people in two PPS).

River levels at 11 stations in the state have also recorded readings exceeding the danger level, including Sungai Besut at Jambatan Keruak and Sungai Besut at Kampung La in Besut; Sungai Nerus at Kampung Langkap and Sungai Setiu at Kampung Besut in Setiu; Sungai Setiu at Jambatan Permaisuri; and Sungai Chalok at Jambatan Chalok in Setiu

METMalaysia also has release latest warning and weather alert as follow:
The Continuous Rainfall Warning (DANGER) is in effect until November 29, 2024, for the following areas:
i) Kelantan;
ii) Terengganu; and
iii) Pahang (Jerantut & Kuantan).

The Continuous Rainfall Warning (SEVERE) is in effect until November 29, 2024, for the following areas:
i) Perlis;
ii) Kedah (Kubang Pasu, Kota Setar, Pokok Sena, Padang Terap, Pendang, Sik & Baling);
iii) Perak (Hulu Perak); and
iv) Pahang (Cameron Highlands, Lipis, Maran, Pekan & Rompin).

The Continuous Rainfall Warning (ALERT) is in effect until November 29, 2024, for the following areas:
i) Kedah (Langkawi, Yan, Kuala Muda, Kulim & Bandar Baharu);
ii) Penang;
iii) Perak (Kerian, Larut, Matang and Selama, Kuala Kangsar, Kinta & Kampar);
iv) Pahang (Raub, Bentong, Temerloh & Bera);
v) Johor (Segamat, Mersing & Kota Tinggi); and
vi) Sabah: Sandakan (Telupid, Beluran & Sandakan) and Kudat

name: UGA: Landslide - 11-2024 - Uganda Landslide Eastern Region - Bulambuli District November 2024
summary:
Following heavy rains that occurred on 27th November 2024 from morning at 10:00AM up to evening 6:00PM across Bulambuli and the neighbouring districts, various disaster events occurred.

Flooding occurred in the sub counties of Simu, Muyembe, Bukhalu, Bunalwere, Nbongo and Buyaga and Bulambuli Town Councils. River Simu bursted its banks affecting several households nearby, cutting off Sironko-Kapchorwa road and Tororo cement truck was witnessed to have overturned as a result of the large volume of water on the road. The bridge also on Simu River connecting Simu sub county and Soti sub county had been swept off as well and Nabongo river along Muyembe- Nakapiripit road was cut off affecting people’s homes. The total estimated of households affected in terms being partially submerged and crop destructed is 751 across the 05 subcounties and the 02 town councils.

The landslides also occurred yesterday 27th November 2024 at between 7pm and 9pm, affecting 8 villages (Masugu, Namacele, Mamolo, Taagalu, Lula, Buzemolili, Lusolo and Nakacene) in Buluganya parish, Buluganya sub-county; Sooti sub-county affecting 2 villages (Bunambale, Nabude); Sisiyi and Bulago sub-counties affecting 1 village; in Bulambuli District.

The total population affected stands at 1,540 persons from the 220 households. 125 households were totally destroyed; So far 15 dead bodies have been retrieved (10 male, 5 female; 7 children (6 male and 1 female), 22 people were injured and were taken to Buluganya H/C III and Muyembe H/C IV and 125 people are missing and unaccounted for. 750 people have been displaced with 534 living with their relatives and neighbours and 216 have been displaced to Masugu Primary school. The search for the missing persons continues by the UPDF, URCS and the community.

It should be noted that data presented above on landslides are recorded only from Buluganya subcounty while the assessment are yet to assess and establish the statistics on losses and damages from the other subcounties later and will be reported in the next situation report.

countries.name: Syrian Arab Republic
dtype.name: Complex Emergency
name: SYR: Complex Emergency - 11-2024 -
summary:
The escalating hostilities that have recently occurred in the northern governorates of Syria, specifically Aleppo, Idlib, and Hama, have led to the displacement of approximately 500,000 individuals inside and outside these governorates in search of safety and protection. This increase in violence has exacerbated the vulnerabilities of communities already struggling with the prolonged crisis, earthquake repercussions, economic difficulties, the recent influx of displacement from Lebanon, and direct environmental pressures in densely populated areas.

All governorates, especially those directly affected, are currently facing a severe shortage of humanitarian assistance and basic necessities due to the protracted crisis, which is considered one of the longest and most complex in the world. Already weakened communities in these areas are now grappling with the aftermath of a devastating earthquake that struck the region in 2023, further worsening their already dire situation. Additionally, neighboring areas previously inundated by waves of displacement are now under additional strain on their resources and services. The onset of winter has exacerbated vulnerabilities, leaving families without adequate shelter, heating, or essential non-food items.

Moreover, the recent displacement has disproportionately affected women, children, and the elderly, increasing their needs compared to other demographics and exposing them to additional risks. Despite efforts to alleviate the crisis, maintaining resilience in the most vulnerable families becomes increasingly challenging within the fragile context of limited and often absent resources.

In areas like Aleppo and Idlib, the gap between life-saving basic needs and resources accessible to the affected populations widens due to conflict and the lack of safe access to service providers and supplies, despite facilitation by many stakeholders and interest parties.

The military operations are not over as of the drafting of this report and further escalation could be expected in the coming days. The area of conflict has widened through Aleppo and rural Aleppo, Eastern and southern Idleb, and northern Hama. The population living in the currently affected areas is estimated at 3,170,000 people. Isolated incidents have also been recorded in other governorates which would increase the risk of further displacement within these governorates or in-between different governorates. As information starts to trickle in, there will be more clarity on numbers and specific needs It is to be noted that the situation remains extremely fluid.

Immediate response efforts focus on the following:

- Establishing safe evacuation corridors and providing life-saving assistance, including food and NFIs

- Ensuring a safe supply of water sources and coordinating with sector workers for safe passage

- Providing emergency healthcare and medical aid,

- Supplying hospitals with essential materials and providing safe passage for medical supplies across conflict lines

- Family reunification services and dead body management

- Enhancing coordination between local and international actors to address aid gaps and ensure fair distribution

-Sanitation and Waste management

-  Enhanced targeting of most vulnerable populations, and expansion of services to include Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS), protection services

countries.name: Lithuania
dtype.name: Transport Accident
name: LTU: Transport Accident - 11-2024 - Cargo flight crash
summary: Around 4 AM local time on 25 November 2024, a DHL cargo flight crashed approx. 2 kms short of the runway. One crew onboard died, another was found injured. Burning debris from the plane impacted a 2-story residential building housing a 12 people. The house and terrain in the impact area has caught fire, while fire was extinguished by responding rescue services, and the 12 inhabitants were evacuated, the residential building has become uninhabitable.

countries.name: Botswana
dtype.name: Storm Surge
name: BWA: Storm Surge - 11-2024 - Storm
summary:
On Monday, the 25 November 2024, Francistown experienced heavy rains accompanied by strong winds, which caused widespread destruction. Cars, houses, office buildings, and informal business structures operated by street vendors at the bus rank were signific damaged. Another severe storm struck the same area and Tumasere on 03rd of December 2024, resulting in further damage, such as trees falling on parked cars and interruptions to electricity and communication networks.
In response, government authorities and the Botswana Red Cross Society (BRCS) initiated an assessment to evaluate the extent of damage to roads and infrastructure. The most severely affected areas included Kgaphamadi, Somerset, Area W, Gerald Estate, a Galo/Old Mall in the Francistown.
The impact extended beyond private properties to include government offices, a junior school, a public clinic, and the civic center. Francistown, approximately 460 households comprising around 2,300 people suffered significant damage. 57 business destroyed, impact n surroundings and infrastructures affecting the life of 23,000 people.

countries.name: Tanzania, United Republic of
dtype.name: Flood
name: TZA: Flood - 11-2024 - TANZANIA TARIME FLOODS
summary:
Tragic news from Tarime District in the Mara Region of Tanzania confirms that nine members of one family have drowned following heavy rains that caused severe flooding. The floods swept away their home, along with three other houses, leaving several families homeless.

Acting Regional Fire and Rescue Commander Augustine Magere stated that unplanned construction near the river contributed significantly to the tragedy, as the affected houses were located close to the waterway.

This incident highlights the dangers of building in flood-prone areas and underscores the importance of following construction regulations to minimize the risks associated with natural disasters. Authorities are urging residents to prioritize safety and adhere to official guidance in such vulnerable locations.

countries.name: Trinidad and Tobago
countries.society_name: The Trinidad and Tobago Red Cross Society
dtype.name: Pluvial/Flash Flood
name: TTO: Pluvial/Flash Flood - 11-2024 - Intense localized rainfall cased massive flash floods - Northwest Trinidad
summary: On Saturday 23rd November 2024, around 11am, local weather forecast indicated the approach of a trough system that would bring intense thunderstorm activity across much of Trinidad. Rains began falling across Trinidad on the eastern coast arond noon and the system quickly made its way across Trinidad within a couple of hours. Intense rainfall was concentrated in the northern part of the island while most of the country experienced some amount of rainfall. From 2pm initial reports came in of water levels rising in rivers in the major watercourses in Diego Martin and San Juan/Laventille and flash flooding occuring in typical places across both regions. By 3pm several watercourses began overtopping and flooding nearby street and communties. The Ministry of Rural Development at Local Government began posting notices of flooded areas and warning to avoid areas. Within the Diego Martin area the communties Carenage, Blue Basin, Morne Coco Road, Saddle Road, Maraval and Petit Valley were among the communties affected with street and flashflooding and very localized riverine flooding. A major landslide was reported on the Northcoast Road which leads to popular beaches stranding motorists on either side, and smaller landslides in hilly areas around St. James. As of this time the TTRCS does not have confirmed reports of the possible number of households affected and the extent to flooded communities.

countries.name: United Kingdom
dtype.name: Flood
name: GBR: Flood - 11-2024 - Storm Bert
summary:
Storm Bert hit the UK on Saturday 23 November, bringing heavy rain and snow, together with strong winds to large swathes of the country.

Heavy rain across the UK has led to widespread flooding, and multiple flood warnings were issued.

The National Society deployed teams across the UK to support those impacted by Storm Bert. Our support focussed on rest centres or door knocking following flooding, and volunteers have also provided emotional and practical support to those impacted.

Support continued across Rhondda Cynon Taf and volunteers provided flood cleanup items, water, and Cash Based Assistance.

A telephone support line was set up to support households in specified Rhondda Cynon Taf regions who were not present when support was offered in-person. The support line ran Monday 2 December – Friday 6 December from 10:00 – 14:00

countries.name: Belize
dtype.name: Cyclone
name: BLZ: Cyclone - 11-2024 - TD 19 (Invest 99L)
summary: Tropical Depression TD 19 is forecasted to intensify to Tropical Storm or even Category 1 Hurricane Sara by Sunday, November 17, potentially impacting Belize with winds up to 140 km/h and heavy rains. Belize, already saturated from Tropical Storm Nadine, which has caused significant flooding faces heightened risks of flash floods and widespread flooding, especially with additional surges expected from Honduras. NEMO has issued a national advisory, activated standby protocols, and is preparing the Emergency Operations Center in Ladyville. Residents are urged to finalize emergency plans and follow NEMO’s updates as the storm approaches. Those in flood-prone areas are advised to stay prepared for possible evacuations. At present it is uncertain which part of the country will be affected but the entire country is expected to receive heavy rains. Presently NEMI is responding to localized floods in the north, central and south of the country

countries.name: Tanzania, United Republic of
dtype.name: Other
name: TZA: Other - 11-2024 - Urgent Response to Kariakoo Building Collapse: Lives Lost and Rescues Ongoing
summary:
Situational Overview: Kariakoo Building Collapse in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania

Date and Location: On November 16, 2024, a multi-story building in the Kariakoo district of Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, unexpectedly collapsed. Kariakoo is a bustling commercial area, making this incident particularly devastating due to its dense population and high activity.

Impact:

  • Casualties: At least 13 people have been confirmed dead.
  • Injuries: Over 84 individuals have sustained injuries, ranging from minor to critical.
  • Rescued: Emergency teams have rescued more than 84 individuals from the rubble, with efforts ongoing to locate any remaining survivors​
     
    ​
     

Actions Taken:

  • Tanzania Red Cross:
    • Provided immediate first aid and psychosocial support to survivors and families.
    • Assisted in search-and-rescue operations, supplying oxygen, water, and other essentials to trapped victims.
    • Supported local hospitals with medical assistance for the injured.
    • provided pyscho social services and mental health services to the affected families and individuals 
  • Government Efforts:
    • President Samia Suluhu Hassan has ordered a comprehensive inspection of buildings in Kariakoo to prevent similar incidents.
    • Authorities are providing free medical care for victims and assistance with burial arrangements for the deceased​
       
      ​
       
      Current Challenges:
  • The risk of further collapse in adjacent buildings poses a safety concern for responders.
  • Heavy machinery is being deployed to speed up rescue operations, though debris clearance remains a complex task.
  • Families of the victims are in urgent need of psychological and material support.

Urgent Needs:

  • Continued support for search-and-rescue operations.
  • Medical aid for the injured.
  • Shelter and psychosocial assistance for affected families.

countries.name: Guatemala
dtype.name: Flood
name: GTM: Flood - 11-2024 - Tormenta Tropical Sara
summary:
La tormenta tropical Sara se dirige por el océano Atlántico rumbo a Belice y las bandas de lluvias afectarán, según los pronósticos, gran parte del territorio de Guatemala.

 

Las autoridades han establecido alerta anaranjada a nivel nacional, lo que implica la preparación para una posible respuesta humanitaria, especialmente por inundaciones, deslizamientos y eventos relacionados con el exceso de lluvias que afectarán a la población en zonas de riesgo.

countries.name: Guatemala
dtype.name: Cyclone
name: GTM: Cyclone - 11-2024 - Tormenta Tropical Sara
summary:
A pesar de su deformación por el acercamiento del frente frío, la tormenta tropical Sara continúa dejando importantes precipitaciones en Izabal, Alta Verapaz y Petén además de varias lluvias espontaneas y lloviznas fuertes tipo temporal sobre casi toda Guatemala. 

Las condiciones continuarán así hasta el día lunes. Mañana domingo se espera que se adentre a tierra y se degrade a depresión tropical.

Se registra la afectación a 33 familias por inundaciones en Petén y Escuintla.

countries.name: Honduras
dtype.name: Cyclone
name: HND: Cyclone - 11-2024 - Tormenta Tropical Sara
summary:
El día miércoles 13 de noviembre se comenzó a monitorear un disturbio que se encontraba a unos 600 km al este del cabo de Gracias a Dios. En horas de la tarde se convirtió a depresión tropical 19. Equipo de la Sociedad Nacional se reunió con el Centro Nacional de Estudios Atmosférico, Oceanográficos y Sísmicos para el monitoreo de dicho fenómeno, donde se concluyó que afectaría la zona atlántica y Gracias a Dios. La Secretaría de Estado en los Despachos de Gestión de Riesgos y Contingencias Nacionales (COPECO) emitió alerta amarilla por 72 horas para los departamentos de Gracias a Dios, Islas de la Bahía, Atlántida y Colón; alerta verde para Cortés, Olancho y Yoro.

 el pronóstico del Centro Nacional de Huracanes (NOAA), donde el fenómeno tiene un 50-60% de probabilidad de que la depresión tropical llegue a convertirse en la tormenta tropical “Sara”. El jueves 14 de noviembre a las 11:50 AM se convirtió en tormenta tropical con vientos máximos sostenidos de 35 nudos. 

COPECO elevó a alerta roja por 72 horas a los departamentos de Islas de la Bahía, Atlántida, Colón y Gracias a Dios; alerta amarilla para Yoro, Olancho y Cortés; y alerta verde al departamento de Santa Bárbara.

Según el mapa de intervención, los Departamentos con mayor posibilidad de afectación son Colòn Atlantida, Gracias a Dios y Cortès.

Con estos datos Cruz Roja Hondureña ha activado el PAT Tormenta Tropicales focalizando su intervenciòn en el municipio de Tocoa departamento de Colòn

For much of the early morning rains have been falling and local ponding in low areas have caused some roadways especially in the more rural parts of Trinidad to be impassible as water levels reached 2 feet. countries.name: Brazil
dtype.name: Drought
name: BRA: Drought - 11-2024 - Droughts and Fires Florestais
summary:
In 2024, the Amazon is facing an unprecedented environmental crisis due to a combination of extreme drought, deforestation, and wildfires that are affecting both the environment and the local population. Regions such as Barcelos and Santa Isabel do Rio Negro have been without significant rainfall for more than 16 months, which has dried up rivers and left vegetation highly flammable. 

The intensification of the El Niño climate phenomenon: the rainfall pattern has been affected by the phenomenon that warms the waters of the Pacific Ocean. It peaked earlier this year and played a role in the onset of the drought; abnormal warming of the waters of the Tropical North Atlantic – the temperature in the maritime region, which is located above South America, could increase between 1.2 °C and 1.4 °C in 2023 and 2024; Record global temperatures - In July, the world broke the record for the highest temperature ever recorded in history. The scenario creates conditions for stronger heat waves, drastically reduces humidity and creates a favorable environment for the spread of flames, aggravated by the illegal use of fires to clean up deforested areas.

Fires, exacerbated by low humidity and high temperatures, are becoming increasingly difficult to control. The National Institute for Space Research (INPE) reported that despite a 24 per cent decrease in deforestation compared to the previous year, the area of forest affected by fire increased from 10 per cent to 35 per cent in the Amazon. The fires have intensified thanks to what experts call a "criminal strategy": instead of cutting down the forest, illegal invaders set it on fire directly, making it easier for the flames to advance in the middle of very dry vegetation. With 21,289 fires registered until September, this represents an increase of 75% compared to last year, according to the National Institute for Space Research (INPE).

The social impact is significant, with more than 747,000 people directly affected by drought and fires, which have jeopardized the supply of drinking water and the health and safety of the population. Data on injuries, deaths and displaced people are still limited.

In the Amazon, in addition to the fires, municipalities have not rained for almost a year. It is the longest drought on record. On 10/24/04, the level of the Negro River reached 12.66 meters, the lowest since monitoring began in 1902, according to data from the SGB (Geological Survey of Brazil). 

The weather forecast for the coming months is for the dry season to continue, which could further aggravate the situation.

countries.name: Brazil
dtype.name: Drought
name: BRA: Drought - 11-2024 - Droughts and Fires Florestais
summary:
The droughts affecting the state of Pará in 2024 have reached alarming levels, surpassing those of 2023, considered until then the worst in history. With rivers at extremely low levels, the situation directly affects traditional communities, commerce and tourism, sectors that employ thousands of people. According to the Climainfo website, low tides are the worst ever recorded, making it difficult to transport goods by river. The state government declared an emergency in September, affecting 38 municipalities and profoundly altering the lives of families who depend on rivers for their livelihoods and economic activity.

The decree considers that the drought is causing serious environmental damage, such as the death and migration of fauna species, the destruction of vegetation due to lack of water and the increased risk of fires, which pollute the air with toxic particles and gases. affecting air quality and contributing to climate change.
The document also highlights the impacts on public health, with respiratory problems worsening due to air pollution caused by fires.
The most affected regions are Araguaia, Bajo Amazonas, Carajás, Guajará, Guamá, Lake Tucuruí, Marajó, Río Caeté, Río Capim, Tapajós, Tocantins and Xingu.

As of July this year, at least 86 municipalities in Pará had declared a state of emergency due to droughts, but currently the state has 38 municipalities with drought decrees in force: Alenquer; Almeirim; Altamira; Anapu; Aveiro; Baião; Bannach; Belterra; Belém; Bom Jesús do Tocantins; Breu Branco; Curuá; Itaituba; Itupiranga; Jacareacanga; Juruti; Monte Alegre; Muaná; Novo Progresso; Oriximiná; Ourém; Pacajá; Pau D'Arco; Ponta de Pedras; Porto de Moz; Prainha; Río María; Santa Cruz do Arari; Santana do Araguaia; Santarém; Senator José Porfírio; São Félix do Xingu; Terra Santa; Trairão; Tucuruí; Vitória do Xingu; Xinguara; Obidos.

The river's descent directly affects the communities that depend on it for their livelihoods. River transport, essential for access to remote areas and for the transport of products, is increasingly limited. In several regions, such as around the community of Boim on the Tapajós River, school transport service providers report extreme difficulties in getting students to school, with episodes of children being carried on their shoulders so as not to miss classes.

The most affected people in the current scenario are the indigenous peoples of Pará and the population of São Félix do Xingu, who are facing great challenges due to fires and drought, which have deeply affected their way of life. With environmental degradation, many rivers and lakes, traditional sources of livelihood, are drying up or fish are becoming scarce. This not only jeopardizes fisheries, but also the food security of their peoples, who depend on this resource to nourish their communities and provide them with hydration, food, and transportation. 

Fires, often caused by agricultural expansion and the unbridled exploitation of natural resources, lead to biodiversity loss and air pollution, making it even more difficult for indigenous communities to survive. Water scarcity and deteriorating ecosystems make hunting and gathering food increasingly difficult.

Today, there are 8,536 people in the city and roundabout of São Félix do Xingu, 30 indigenous villages with about 2,000 indigenous people, 25 villages in Ourilandia do Norte with about 1,800 indigenous people, Aldeia de Bannach with about 150 indigenous people, 20 villages in Cumaru do Norte with around 1,500 indigenous people and Pau Darco with 4 communities of around 500 people, totaling 14,486 PEOPLE who are in a serious situation as they face water and food shortages.

countries.name: Colombia
dtype.name: Flood
name: COL: Flood - 11-2024 - Floods in Choco, La Guajira, Santander, Cundinamarca, Antioquia
summary:
The second rainy season in Colombia extends between September and November, where rainfall is more prolonged and constant, especially in the Andean region. In coastal areas, rainfall is also frequent, varying in intensity according to the region, influenced by climatic factors such as altitude, proximity to the sea and climatic phenomena such as La Niña. Additionally, during this season, the Caribbean region will experience the Tropical Cyclone Season, which may aggravate risk scenarios for the population. According to IDEAM's climate forecast report, a 71% ENSO La Niña phase is expected, which could last until the first quarter of 2025, altering conditions in the Caribbean, Pacific and Andean regions. Preliminary data from the National Risk Management Unit (UNGRD) indicates that during the last quarter more than 250 thousand people have been affected by adverse events derived from heavy rains. So far, the departments of Chocó, Antioquia, Santander, La Guajira and Cundinamarca have been significantly affected, aggravating the conditions of food security, safe access to drinking water, health and housing. The department of Chocó is the most affected.

In particular, the most recent situation report from the Governor's Office of Chocó informs that, due to the effects of the las few days, at least 27 municipalities are in an emergency situation, caused by heavy rains and the collapse of three river basins - Alto y Medio Baudó, the Atrato river basin and the San Juan river basin - (PMU Chocó). The department of La Guajira has been strongly impacted by the passage of Hurricane Rafael, as heavy rainfall has caused flooding in the municipalities of Uribia, Riohacha, Maicao, Manure and Dibulla
(PMU La Guajira). It is important to note that both departments have limited resources that limit adequate and immediate attention to all the victims, which is aggravated by the needs that the country is presenting in the rest of the territory.

Meanwhile, in the department of Santander, the Las Cruces stream rose, causing a torrential flood in the municipality of San Vicente de Chucurí, where so far it has been reported that five houses have collapsed, fifteen houses have been affected, four bridges and other tertiary roads have collapsed, the infrastructure of the municipal aqueduct has been affected, one person died and two people are missing (PMU Santander). Due to the increasing rains in the department of Norte de Santander, the Disaster Risk Management Office has declared maximum alert in 20 municipalities, where landslides, floods, damage to crops and household goods have occurred. In Antioquia, 87 municipalities are on alert for landslides and 9 municipalities have been affected by floods. In addition, the District Institute for Risk Management and Climate Change (IDIGER) of Bogota has reported the occurrence of 56 events in the last hours, in relation to the heavy rains that have occurred in the capital of the country, highlighting 16 floods, 23 reports of damage to utility networks, 3 situations due to mass movements, among others.

This scenario indicates that the effects will continue to increase during the next quarter, which requires the institutions that are part of the National Disaster Risk Management System to take response actions to meet the needs of the affected people in the country and mitigate the negative effects of heavy rains and floods.

Timeline:
- November 8, 2024: Governor's Office of La Guajira department issues Decree No. 0907 of 2024, declaring public calamity in the department.
- November 9, 2024: Governor of Chocó issues Decree No. 0282 of 2024, declaring public calamity in the department.
- November 10, 2024: The president of the Republic after convening a Unified Command Post (PMU in spanish), announced the decision to declare a National Disaster Situation due to climate variability.
- November 13, 2024: The president of the Republic issues Decree No. 1372 of 2024, declaring a National Disaster Situation

countries.name: Philippines
dtype.name: Cyclone
name: PHL: Cyclone - 11-2024 - Combined Effects of TCs Nika (Toraji) and Ofel (Usagi)
summary:
In less than a month, the Philippines experienced a series of six tropical cyclones that had devastating impacts on the country. Among these were Typhoons Kristine (international name Trami), Leon (Kong Rey), Marce (Yinxing), Nika (Toraji), Ofel (Usagi), and Pepito (Manyi), each contributing to the widespread destruction and challenges faced by the affected communities.

Please see Philippines: Typhoons and Floods - 2024 for details on the combined response to all six typhoons.

On November 9 at 2 AM, a low-pressure area (LPA) entered the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR), and PAGASA named it "NIKA" with the international name "TORAJI." By 8 AM, the LPA, located east of Southern Luzon, had developed into a Tropical Depression. On the same day at 5 PM, "NIKA" intensified into a Tropical Storm.

 

At 5 AM on November 10, "NIKA" intensified into a Severe Tropical Storm as it underwent rapid intensification.

 

On November 11 at 5 AM, "NIKA" strengthened into a Typhoon as it neared the boundary between Isabela and Aurora. By 8:10 AM that same day, it made landfall in Dilasag, Aurora, and started moving across Northern Luzon. On the evening of Monday, “NIKA” had weakened from a Typhoon to a Severe Tropical Storm and exited Luzon's landmass through Ilocos Sur.

 

PAGASA reported that Severe Tropical Storm “NIKA” exited the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) at 2 PM on November 12. However, another Tropical Storm, “OFEL,” which entered the PAR at 3 AM on the same day, slightly intensified as it moved northwestward over the Philippine Sea.

 

A total of 52,551 families or 195,532 persons were affected. Of which, 9,275 families or 28,104 persons were served inside 562 ECs and 4,658 families or 15,600 persons were served outside ECs.

A total of 325 damaged houses are reported in Region 1, Region 2, Region 3, CAR. Of which, 280 are partially damaged and 45 are totally damaged.

countries.name: Grenada
dtype.name: Flood
name: GRD: Flood - 11-2024 - Flash Flooding
summary:
On Tuesday November 12th, 2024 the Grenada Meteorological office issued an advisory related to possible thunderstorms during the day due to convective activities profuced by the inter tropical convergence zone. The rainfall began during the morning period and fell consistently for approximately 6 hours. It was reported after that the state experience two (2) months' worth of rainfall in six (6) hours.
 
As a result of this heavy rainfall, mass flooding and landslides were reported. Additonally, due to recent heavy rainfall, multiple water systems across mainland Grenada, especially in the parishes of St. David, St. George, St. Andrew, St. John, and St. Patrick, were out of commission as the the National Water & Sewearge Authority reported challenges with silted dams and damaged raw water mains. As such, some households were without water for quite a number of days. There was also a report of 1 death of a school teacher whose vehicle was washed away by flood waters, her body was found the next day in her van.
 
The restoration process was slow, but steady. However, in the process of clearing dams the state of Grenada experienced similar weather conditions on Tuesday November 18th, 2024 which significantly delays the process of water restoration to households affected. As of the morning of November 19th, 2024 there are more reports of flooding, landslides, broken pipes and silted dams.

countries.name: Jamaica
dtype.name: Cyclone
name: JAM: Cyclone - 11-2024 - Potential Tropical Cyclone 18
summary:
As of 5:00pm November 3, 2024, a Tropical Storm Warning has been issued for Jamaica. At 4:00pm on November 3, 2024, the potential tropical cyclone 18 was located 600 kilometers southwest of Negril Point and is moving towards the northeast. Maximum sustained winds are near 55km/h with higher gusts. This system is expected to become a tropical depression in the night and is expected strengthen steadily. 

This potential tropical cyclone 18 is expected to continue moving towards Jamaica and should be near Jamaica by late Monday evening. While this system is in the vicinity of Jamaica, it is expected to produce locally heavy rainfall and strong gusty winds, primarily over eastern and southern parishes on Monday and Tuesday. Landslides should also be anticipated. 

All small craft operators including fishers from the cays and banks should return to the mainland and start preparations for safe harbour. 
 
As at 8:00am on Monday, November 4, 2024, a bulletin issued by the Meteorological Office of Jamaica Service states that the potential Tropical Cyclone 18 is forecasted to strengthen into a Tropical Depression during the day. As a result, tropical storm conditions will begin to affect Jamaica within the next 24 hours.

countries.name: Costa Rica
dtype.name: Flood
name: ITT: Flooding - 11-2024 - Heavy rains - Costa Rica
summary:
On Sunday, November 3, the IMN Weather Advisory detailed that the Intertropical Convergence Zone is still very active over Costa Rica, causing rains from the early hours of that Sunday in the Central and South Pacific, with accumulated between 5 to 25 mm. With a low pressure system strengthening in the southwest of the Caribbean Sea, favoring the accumulation of moisture and instability towards the south of Central America, very rainy conditions are expected, especially towards the South Pacific and the rest of the Pacific slope, which would extend to other regions such as the Central Valley, North Zone and Caribbean.

 Faced with this scenario, the National Emergency Commission, at 12:00 p.m., decreed Alert #41 Yellow Alert in almost the entire country, raising the South Pacific region to orange alert due to such conditions, requesting the institutions of the SNGR, and the Municipal and Communal Emergency Committees to monitor local conditions based on the reports of the IMN. in addition to preparing the response mechanisms and keeping the operational units informed of situations that arise, as well as maintaining activation and monitoring.

 Despite the fact that the low pressure system evolved into what is now Hurricane Rafael, the influence of the phenomenon according to the IMN left the country on Wednesday, November 6, the Intertropical Convergence Zone remained over the country providing instability and humidity and the entry of Tropical Wave #45 was warned. warning that soil saturation, with extremely high percentages, is maintained in both Peninsulas, the entire North Pacific, South Pacific mountains, North Zone, Central Pacific and Central Valley, so it is recommended to take extreme measures since they are highly vulnerable to incidents.

Based on this climate perspective that insists on the problem of high rainfall accumulations and constant soil saturation, the CNE decided to raise the alert levels of the Central Pacific, North Pacific and Central Region to Orange, leaving the Northern Zone and the Caribbean Region on Yellow Alert.

Given the above, and according to the National Emergency and Disaster Response Plan, the Costa Rican Red Cross established Response Level 3, where there is a concentration of personnel in Auxiliary Committees, cancellation of activities and training, establishing CCOR and determining the deployment of personnel, to cope with the response to incidents related to this hydrometeorological event.

During the week there have been fires involving floods, trapped people, people who must be evacuated due to the damage to their homes and must be mobilized to shelters or relatives' rooms, as well as landslides that have affected homes and vehicles.

countries.name: Philippines
dtype.name: Cyclone
name: PHL: Cyclone - 11-2024 - Marce(Yingxing)
summary:
In less than a month, the Philippines experienced a series of six tropical cyclones that had devastating impacts on the country. Among these were Typhoons Kristine (international name Trami), Leon (Kong Rey), Marce (Yinxing), Nika (Toraji), Ofel (Usagi), and Pepito (Manyi), each contributing to the widespread destruction and challenges faced by the affected communities.

Please see Philippines: Typhoons and Floods - 2024 for details on the combined response to all six typhoons.

On November 3, at 5 PM, a low-pressure area located outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) developed into a tropical depression. It maintained its strength while accelerating northwestward.

As it entered the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) early in the morning of November 4, it intensified into a Tropical Storm and was given the local name "MARCE," with the international designation "YINXING." By 11 PM the same day, "MARCE" underwent further intensification, rapidly developing into a Severe Tropical Storm

By 11 AM on November 5, Tuesday, "MARCE" had strengthened into a Typhoon, marking a significant increase in intensity as it continued its northwestward movement.

Typhoon "MARCE" made landfall twice on Thursday, November 7, first in Santa Ana, Cagayan, at 3:40 PM, and later in Sanchez-Mira, Cagayan, at 9 PM

At 4 PM on November 8, Typhoon "MARCE" exited the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR), but its trough continued to bring scattered rains and thunderstorms to Ilocos Norte and Ilocos Sur over the next 24 hours.

A total of 76,622 families or 261,787 persons were affected. Of which, 4,559 families or 13,887 persons were served inside 230 ECs and 4,176 families or 12,916 persons were served outside ECs.

A total of 20,930 houses were damaged from Region 1, 2 and CAR, of which 20,038 are partially damaged and 892 are totally damaged. (NDRRMC Report #7)

countries.name: Panama

name: PAN: Flood - 10-2024 - Panama Flood
summary:
The National Civil Protection System (Sinaproc) informs the population that, in the face of a period of greater atmospheric instability over our region, a Yellow Alert is declared throughout the Panamanian territory, as of 6:00 p.m. this Thursday, October 31, 2024.

This preventive measure is due to a report on the weather conditions forecast by the Institute of Meteorology and Hydrology of Panama (IMHPA), which refers to the interaction of several atmospheric systems and the monitoring of a low pressure system in the Caribbean Basin with a potential cyclonic development of 50%, for the next 7 days.

From Friday, November 1 to November 5, 2024, persistent rains of varying intensity, electrical activity and gusts of wind are expected, indicates the IMHPA.

The Emergency Operations Center in view of this declaration reinforces its surveillance and monitoring throughout the national territory.

During today, November 2, river overflows have been recorded in the provinces of Chiriquí, Veraguas, Los Santos, Darién, Comarca Ngabe Bugle.

On the recommendation of the local authorities, the activities of the National Holidays scheduled for November 3 and 4 have been suspended in some provinces.

At the level of the Panamanian Red Cross, monitoring and surveillance is maintained by local committees, in some provinces the provincial coes have been activated. The National COE of SINAPROC has held a meeting with the institutional liaisons.

In the area of Sona, province of Veraguas, the search is underway for a member of the police who were affected by a landslide

countries.name: Spain
dtype.name: Flood
name: ESP: Flood - 10-2024 - Inundaciones DANA
summary:
The situation in the Valencian Community after the passage of the DANA (high level atmospheric depression - cold drop, acronym in Spanish) is very serious. So far, more than 70 deaths have been confirmed, most of them in the province of Valencia. In addition, several people are missing and numerous localities are affected by severe flooding.
Torrential rains have caused rivers to overflow, traffic cuts and coverage, building collapses and evacuations. Power outage are affecting more than 140.000 people. In Valencia, some population areas such as Chiva and Pedralba have registered historic accumulations of up to 490 liters per square meter.
The Government of the Generalitat Valenciana has activated the “multiple victims” procedure and emergency teams have been deployed, including the Military Emergency Unit (UME), to rescue trapped people and assist in recovery efforts. The situation remains critical, and reconstruction work is expected to take months due to the extent of the damage.

countries.name: Philippines
dtype.name: Cyclone
name: Philippines: Typhoons and Floods - 2024
summary:
In less than a month, the Philippines experienced a series of six tropical cyclones that had devastating impacts on the country. Among these were Typhoons Kristine (international name Trami), Leon (Kong Rey), Marce (Yinxing), Nika (Toraji), Ofel (Usagi), and Pepito (Manyi), each contributing to the widespread destruction and challenges faced by the affected communities.

Severe Tropical Storm (STS) Kristine (Trami) entered the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) as a tropical depression on 21 October 2024. It affected the entire Luzon and Visayas island regions extending to parts of Mindanao in the south. Even before making landfall, it caused severe flooding and landslides that impacted a significant number of people, especially in areas that were hit by the trough. The heavy rainfall led to lahar (destructive mudflows) flowing from Mount Mayon Volcano in the Bicol Region, which severely impacted both lives and livelihoods. 

On 24 October, STS Kristine made landfall in Isabela province in northeast Luzon, then crossed to Ifugao, Mountain Province, and Ilocos Sur province on the same day. Kristine exited Luzon through Ilocos Sur, however, the trough of the STS continued to unleash heavy rain and winds across vast areas, severely impacting Regions III, IV-A, and V. On 25 October, STS Kristine exited the PAR and made landfall in Vietnam on 27 October. In the Philippines, STS Kristine was the 11th tropical cyclone in 2024, out of an annual average of 20 tropical cyclones that typically affect the country. 

Following STS Kristine, Super Typhoon Leon (international name Kong-Rey) entered the PAR on 26 October. It passed over the far northern region of Luzon, affecting some of the remote islands in the area. Leon brought typhoon-strong winds, heavy rain, flooding, and landslides to the northern islands and the extreme northern mainland of the Philippines before exiting on 1 November.  

Tropical Storm (TS) Marce entered the PAR on 4 November and made landfall in Region II (Cagayan) on 7 November. The Cagayan Valley region experienced continuous heavy rains and widespread impacts due to Marce, which also affected parts of Region I, the CAR, and Region III. 

After the exit of TS Marce, Tropical Cyclone (TC) Nika (Toraji) entered the PAR as a Low-Pressure Area on 9 November 2024. Nika later intensified into a typhoon and made landfall in the vicinity of Dilasag, Aurora (Region II), causing significant effects in Region I, Region III, and Region IV-A while two other weather disturbances with significant TC potential were hovering outside the PAR. The onslaught continued with Super Typhoon Ofel (Usagi), which entered PAR on 12 November and struck Baggao, Cagayan on 14 November, and Super Typhoon Pepito (Man-Yi), which entered PAR on 14 November, making its first landfall in Panganiban, Catanduanes on 16 November, followed by a second landfall in Dipaculao, Aurora on 17 November.

In an unprecedented event, the Philippines experienced a succession of devastating tropical storms within a single month, a first in the nation's recorded history. As a result, the same areas have been impacted repeatedly, with multiple tropical cyclones and associated hazards significantly intensifying the disasters. This escalation is attributed to existing vulnerabilities and a limited capacity for recovery, compounded by the frequency and recurrence of these events. This rapid series of tropical cyclones has inflicted extensive damage across various regions, severely impacting communities that are already grappling with vulnerabilities and limited resources.

Summary of the disaster situation 

The sequence of 6 natural disasters has devastating staggering impact on 14.3 million people. A total of 174 deaths, 148 injuries and 25 cases of missing people have been reported to date. More than 1.4 million individuals have been displaced, and damage has been sustained to a total of 315,777 houses of which 36,000 houses are reported to be totally damaged. Affected communities are confronting critical shortages of water, sanitation, food, and healthcare.

As of 6 January 2025, two and a half months have passed since the first typhoon of the sequence struck the Philippines, according to the Report No 77 from the Department of Social Welfare and Development, a total of 11,520 families (47,275 individuals) remain displaced across Regions NCR, I, II, III, CALABARZON, MIMAROPA, V, VI, VII, VIII, IX, X, and XII. Of which, 3,091 families (12,436 individuals) are currently sheltered in 80 evacuation centers across Regions NCR, II, III, CALABARZON, MIMAROPA, V, VIII, IX, and XII; 8,429 families (34,839 individuals) are staying temporarily with relatives or friends.

In terms of shelter damage, Regions I, II, III, CALABARZON, MIMAROPA, V, VI, VII, VIII, IX, X, XI, XII, Caraga, and CAR are affected. To date, 205,319 houses have sustained damage of which 16,677 houses are totally damaged and 188,642 houses partially damaged. This data reflects the widespread and severe impact of the cyclones, highlighting the urgent need for continued support for displaced individuals and assistance in housing reconstruction.

In the past months, there has been an urgent need for immediate relief efforts, including the provision of clean water, food, shelter, and medical care to safeguard lives. The scale of the needs on the ground is immense, and the Philippine Red Cross, in partnership with public authorities and other organizations, is striving to assist as many individuals as possible with available resources. 

The cumulative impact of these typhoons has further weakened already vulnerable communities, indicating that recovery will be a prolonged process. The Philippines may expect additional cyclones and other weather disturbances in the coming months, which may affect the same regions, complicating recovery efforts and necessitating more resources.

Please see Appeal Documents tab for latest information about Philippine Red Cross' response and interventions.

countries.name: Bahamas
dtype.name: Cyclone
name: BHS: Cyclone - 10-2024 - Hurricane Oscar
summary: At 2 p.m. on Saturday, October 19, 2024, a hurricane warning was issued for the Southeast Bahamas, including the islands of Mayaguana, Inagua, Crooked Island, Acklins, Long Cay, and Ragged Island. Hurricane Oscar is moving west at 12 MPH, with maximum sustained winds of 80 MPH and higher gusts. Hurricane-force winds extend up to 5 miles from the center, and tropical storm-force winds extend up to 45 miles. The Bahamas Red Cross group leaders and volunteers on the affected islands have met with District Councils and Family Island Administrators to review and activate emergency plans. All shelters in the Southeastern islands have been opened, and the Royal Bahamas Defence Force stationed on Ragged Island will also be assisting at their shelter.  Residents are securing their property and making necessary preparations to protect their families and livelihoods.

countries.name: Guatemala
dtype.name: Cyclone
name: GTM: Cyclone - 10-2024 - Depresión Tropical
summary:
La tormenta tropical Nadine que posteriormente se convirtió en depresión tropical provocó lluvias en los departamentos de Alta Verapaz, Izabal y Petén, siendo este último el que mayor impacto registra en áreas inundadas, daño a medios de vida y afectación de la estructura vial. 

Las autoridades locales inician la evaluación de daños para establecer las acciones a realizar localmente.

countries.name: Cuba
dtype.name: Cyclone
name: CUB: Cyclone - 10-2024 - Hurricane Oscar
summary:
After previously passing through the Bahamas, Category 1 Hurricane Oscar made landfall Sunday in eastern Cuba at 17:50 local time (23:50 GMT), as the country continues attempts to restore the power grid amid a massive blackout.

The storm had already made landfall on Great Inagua Island in the Bahamas in the early morning, with winds of up to 130 kilometres per hour (80 mph).

Oscar's rapid increase in intensity from a tropical storm to a 135-kilometre-per-hour (85 mph) hurricane alerted the islands in its path.

The small cyclone is considered one of the smallest in size on record in the Atlantic Basin, which could mean rapid fluctuations in intensity due to its ability to take advantage of specific conditions such as dry air and shear.


Oscar, originally designated as Invest 94L, poses a significant threat to areas in its path. However, 'it is expected to weaken to a tropical storm as it moves across eastern Cuba during Sunday night and Monday,' the National Hurricane Center said.

Despite this expected weakening, torrential rains and high winds are still anticipated for the region, and hurricane warnings have been issued for the northern coast of Cuba's Holguín and Guantánamo provinces as far as Punta Maisí.

Cuba's Ministry of Energy and Mines (Minem) reported on Sunday the third total outage of the National Electric System (SEN) in less than three days.

'A few minutes ago there was another disconnection of the Electrical System, SEN. Immediately began the work of restoration,' Minem wrote on social networks.

The first total system outage, the first event of 'zero national energy coverage', according to the Minem, occurred on Friday morning, after an 'unforeseen' output of a key power plant for the SEN destabilised the entire system.

countries.name: Belize
dtype.name: Flood
name: BLZ: Flood - 10-2024 - Belize potential Floods
summary:
Tropical Storm conditions associated with Nadine are spreading over coastal pats of the Corozal, Belize and Stann Creek Districts. The National Meteorological Service's weather station at Half Moon Caye recently reported a wind gust of 43 mph. A general westward motion with an increase in forward speed is expected for the remainder of Saturday, October 19th, 2024, before the tropical storm makes landfall along the coast of Belize in a few hours. No significant strengthening is expected before the system makes landfall.

The main threat from Tropical Storm Nadine is heavy rainfall. Rainfall totals of 1 to 2 inches have already been recorded and an additional 4 to 6 inches are possible, especially over northern and central Belize. This could result in flooding.

Winds of 50 miles per hour with higher gusts will occur within the impact area. This may result in damage to weak structures, crops, and trees.

A minor storm surge generally less than 1 foot is possible just north of where the system makes landfall.

countries.name: Haiti
dtype.name: Population Movement
name: HTI: Population Movement - 10-2024 - Haitians migrants deported from Dominican Republic
summary:
Since the Dominican government announced on October 2, 2024, that it would implement its campaign to expel 10,000 immigrants per week, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) has recorded more than 7,800 expulsions of Haitians at three of the four official border crossings between Haiti and the Dominican Republic in less than a week, a 95% increase over the previous week.

Most people arrive at the border in a very precarious and vulnerable state, with limited or no resources or documentation, and in need of medical and/or psychological care. However, while Haiti has been facing a humanitarian crisis for several years, due to endemic gang violence in the metropolitan area of ​​the Haitian capital, the response capacities of the Haitian government, civil society, national and international NGOs, and the United Nations system remain underfunded.

Beyond capacity, the 2024 Humanitarian Response Plan for the Migrant Protection Working Group is only funded at 2%. As a result, the various actors at the border have only been able to assist approximately 7% of all people arriving at the border in 2023 (out of a total of over 215,000 expulsions over the year).

If expulsions continue at the current rate, approximately 130,000 people will arrive at the border by the end of the year (Advocacy Note - Migrant Protection Working Group). In order to preserve the dignity and human rights of these migrants and provide them with essential emergency assistance upon arrival. This assistance will include the following essential services:
- a meal
- transportation to their region of origin
- non-food items (clothing, shoes, hygiene items)
- medical assistance
- placement in emergency accommodation for one night

countries.name: Türkiye

summary: On October 16, 2024, a 5.9 magnitude earthquake struck the Kale district of Malatya, with no fatalities reported. Following the quake, some individuals were injured due to jumping from heights, resulting in a total of 9 injuries. In total, 187 people were affected by the earthquake.

countries.name: Mauritania
dtype.name: Pluvial/Flash Flood
name: MRT: Rain/Flash Flood - 10-2024 - Senegal River Flood
summary:
Significant rainfall has been recorded in the Senegal River Valley since the beginning of September 2024. These rains, coupled with the inflows of uncontrolled tributaries, have caused a rise in water. Alerts were reached on Thursday, September 12, 2024 by the OMVS via these information releases on the preventive measures to be adopted in order to allow the local populations to remain vigilant and to strengthen the system to fight against possible floods if river overflows were to occur in places.The OMVS, in collaboration with the technical services of the member countries, monitors the evolution of the water level in the Valley on a daily basis.

Guidimagha Region

Several villages in the departments of Ghabou, Wembou and Gouraye in Mauritania's Guidimagha region on the banks of the Senegal River have been damaged by rising waters on the Senegal River, forcing people to leave their homes for their lives, Temporary shelters are set up to accommodate the affected inhabitants. In addition, the Regional Emergency Committee, of which the Red Crescent is a member, has begun to visit the flooded areas and intervene to help the affected people in the district of Gourey and in some villages of the department of Gabo, particularly in the villages of Diyagili and Selo.More than 200 affected families have been registered and evacuated to safe and secure places, several agricultural fields have emerged, I recall that the Senegal River Investment Organization (OMVS) issued a statement on October 13, 2024 warning areas adjacent to the river of flooding and torrential rains expected due to the uncontrollable rise in the water level of the river due to the rain. 

Trarza Region

In the Trarza region of southwestern Mauritania, the waters resulting from the flooding of the Senegal River surrounded more than twenty villages in the department of Ntikan in the Trarza region, the localities of Ntikan, Oum Al-Qura and Lekseiba 2 were completely flooded by the waters of the river and completed the flooding of the river.most of the roads leading to these villages have been cut off and inaccessible.

The authorities have begun to evacuate residents of the affected localities, while the National Company for Rehabilitation and Agricultural Works (SNAT) is working to build a road for some villages to facilitate the evacuation process.

countries.name: Benin
dtype.name: Flood
name: BEN: Flood - 10-2024 - flood
summary:
Heavy rainfall has caused a rise in water levels in Benin, leading to flooding in several cities in the country. The forecasting and warning unit updates its bulletin daily, revealing worrying water levels. Following the recent rains in the department of Atacora and its surroundings, the Pendjari River burst its banks, flooding agricultural fields located in the neutral zone of Koalou on Sunday, October 13, 2014. A team of phytosanitary agents from the Ministry of Agriculture, Livestock and Fisheries (MAEP) went to the site to assess the extent of the damage, which extends over several dozen hectares.

Alert level for the next few days:
For the period from October 11 to 21, 2024, a rise in water levels is expected in Zagnanado, Bonou and Adjohoun, in the lower Ouémé valley. On the other hand, a slight decrease is expected in Athiémé, in the Mono basin, as well as in Malanville, in the Niger basin. As a result, disaster risks are high around Zagnanado, Bonou and Adjohoun in the lower Ouémé Valley. These risks are low in Athiémé, but remain high in Malanville and Karimama, in the Niger Basin.

According to the flood situation report (SITREP INONDATION N°65 MISP/ANPC), dated October 11 to 12, 2024 at 7 a.m., it is recommended that populations living in the flooded or flood-prone areas of Zagnanado, Bonou and Adjohoun leave these sectors. Those of Athiémé can continue their activities without fear. On the other hand, the inhabitants of Malanville and Karimama must also evacuate flooded or at-risk areas in the Niger Basin.

countries.name: Azerbaijan
dtype.name: Flood
name: AZE: Flood - 10-2024 - Hajigabul
summary:
Heavy rainfall and excessive flooding in the Hajigabul district have caused significant damage in the area.

According to Saleh Alasgarov, the chairman of the Hajigabul District Emergency Commission, who provided information, the natural disaster in Hajigabul began in the afternoon. Due to the heavy floods originating from Mount Mushov and the intense rainfall, there was a disruption in electricity supply to the city center. In addition to the district center, more than 300 households in the villages of "Qubalı Baloğlan", "Pirsaat", "Udulu", "Nəvahi", and "Qızılburun" were flooded.

Traffic on the city’s internal roads became difficult. Furthermore, the Shirvan-Hajigabul railway was affected by the floodwaters caused by the heavy downpour. Currently, around 50 different types of machinery and personnel have been deployed to the area to mitigate the damage.

countries.name: Mongolia
dtype.name: Fire
name: MNG: Fire - 10-2024 - Steppe fire
summary: Between October 11 and 14, a series of steppe fires erupted across 16 hectares in various locations within the Dornod and Sukhbaatar provinces of eastern Mongolia. Subsequently, from October 15 to 16, the fires spread to Khentii province. Tragically, two children under the age of five were found deceased, and one herder sustained severe burns. The fires destroyed six homes and resulted in the loss of over 1,000 livestock, along with significant damage to animal shelters, hay, fodder, and vehicles. In total, 76 individuals from 21 families have been directly affected, and six locations are currently without power.

countries.name: Burkina Faso

summary: Since October 7, 2024, Burkina Faso has received a series of dividian rains in several regions often accompanied by strong winds. The most affected regions are the Boucle du Mouhoun, the Cascades, the Hauts Bassins, etc. These rains, which continued until October 13, caused significant material damage in several localities in the country. Indeed, the communes of Founzan in the Boucle du Mouhoun, Bama and Karangasso Sambla in the Hauts-Bassins, Sindou in the cascases and Séguénéga in the north were particularly affected by floods that affected more than 1600 households. Among the damage are hundreds of collapsed houses and losses of property and property. It should also be noted that some localities have remained inaccessible due to the rise in water levels and the cutting off of the main access roads.

countries.name: United States
dtype.name: Cyclone
name: USA: Cyclone - 10-2024 - Hurricane Milton
summary: As of Wednesday, October 9, Hurricane Milton, a Category 5 storm, is in the eastern Gulf of Mexico, moving northeast at 14 mph (22 km/h). The storm is expected to accelerate as it continues northeast through tonight, with a turn to the east-northeast and east by Thursday and Friday. Milton is forecast to make landfall along Florida's west-central coast late tonight or early Thursday, before moving across the state and into the Atlantic Ocean by Thursday afternoon. With maximum sustained winds of 160 mph (260 km/h) and higher gusts, Milton's hurricane-force winds extend up to 30 miles (45 km) from the center, while tropical-storm-force winds stretch up to 125 miles (205 km). The central pressure is an intense 907 mb (26.78 inches). Experts warn that Milton could be one of the most destructive hurricanes on record for west-central Florida, with forecasts predicting more than a foot of rain and a 15-foot storm surge. This comes just two weeks after Hurricane Helene made landfall in Florida, compounding the state's challenges. Over 12 million people are currently under hurricane watches and warnings, and evacuation efforts are underway across the region.

countries.name: Bosnia and Herzegovina
countries.society_name: Red Cross Society of Bosnia and Herzegovina
dtype.name: Pluvial/Flash Flood
name: BIH: Pluvial/Flash Flood - 10-2024 - Flood
summary:
On the night of October 4, 2024, a series of flash floods struck five municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina: Jablanica, Konjic, Kreševo, Fojnica, and Kiseljak. In addition to the severe flooding, the municipality of Jablanica was further impacted by an earthquake, compounding the devastation.

The combined effects of the flash floods and earthquake triggered a landslide in the Donja Jablanica region, completely destroying large parts of the area. As of October 4, 2024, more than 18 individuals have been confirmed dead, and over 12 people remain missing. This number is not final, as several communities remain isolated and cut off from rescue and communication efforts due to the destruction of critical infrastructure.

In the affected municipalities, schools have been canceled, and roads have been severely damaged, with many rendered completely impassable. In the Jablanica region, phone and internet connections are unavailable, further complicating coordination and rescue efforts.

The situation remains fluid as rescue operations continue, and updated information is expected as access to the cut-off areas improves.
