countries.name: Panama
dtype.name: Flood
name: PAN: Flood - 09-2024 - Panama Flood
summary:
The National Civil Protection System (SINAPROC) in view of the intensification of rains and the saturation of the soils, issues a declaration of Yellow Alert in the provinces of Chiriquí, Bocas del Toro, Veraguas, Herrera, Los Santos and the Ngäbe Buglé region, as of Monday, September 30. from 11:00 p.m. The rest of the country and the regions of the Panamanian territory are raised to Green Alert, as a preventive measure against the rains in a considerable way. 

This measure obeys the technical-scientific criteria of the Institute of Meteorology and Hydrology of Panama (IMHPA), which refers to a low pressure system over the Panamanian Caribbean, north of the country and due to cyclonic development (10% in 48 hours and 40% in 7 days). which could induce the incursion of significant wind flows and rainfall. 

According to the IMHPA, accumulated rainfall is forecast in the next 48 hours, between 50-70 mm in the western region, Veraguas and Azuero. The Emergency Operations Center (COE) is constantly monitoring atmospheric conditions and collaborating with local authorities to provide support if needed.

To guarantee the safety of citizens during this period of climate instability, SINAPROC recommends:
   • Stay informed through official sources.
   • During this declaration it is preferable not to visit trails, mountains, rivers, streams and lakes.
   • Do not park vehicles, or camp in dry riverbeds, or on the banks of rivers, to avoid being surprised by a sudden flood of water.
   • The population, especially those living in risk areas, is recommended to stay informed and comply with the prevention measures of emergency institutions and security forces.

The population is urged to follow these recommendations to minimize risks and ensure their safety.

countries.name: Algeria
dtype.name: Epidemic
name: DZA: Epidemic - 09-2024 - South Algeria Malaria and Diphtheria 2024
summary: Since late September 2024, southern Algeria has faced significant outbreaks of malaria and diphtheria, severely impacting the wilayas of In Guezzam and Bordj Badji Mokhtar (those new provinces were part of Tamanrasset Province). Heavy rains in September led to stagnant waters, accelerating mosquito breeding and increasing malaria cases to 536 registered cases with 40 deaths. Diphtheria cases have risen to 115 registered cases with 28 deaths, largely due to vaccination gaps and strained healthcare resources. The health system is overwhelmed by shortages of medications, equipment, and personnel, hindering effective response. All age groups are affected, but children and unvaccinated individuals are particularly vulnerable to diphtheria. Secondary effects include potential spread to additional regions, economic disruptions, inadequate sanitation infrastructure posing future health risks, educational interruptions, and increased psychosocial stress within affected communities.

countries.name: Nepal
dtype.name: Flood
name: Nepal - Flood and Landslide 2024
summary:
On September 25, the Department of Hydrology and Metrology (DHM, GoN) issued a weather advisory for a new spell of monsoon, influenced by the moisture-laden winds from the Bay of Bengal and the local weather system, to remain active between 26 and 29 September with the potential to cause heavy rainfall in most of the provinces, triggering flash floods, landslides and overflow of rivers. This forecast turns into reality with heavy rainfall noticed in Bagmati and Gandaki provinces and moderately heavy rain in other provinces. In the last 24 hours, seven locations in Koshi province received above 120 to 140 mm rainfall, above 30 locations in Bagmati received above 140mm rainfall, and around 6 locations in Gandaki province received high to very high rainfall, while the rainfall in other provinces remains between moderate and high with minimal impact on lives and properties.

 The impact of this short but intensified rainfall across the country is evident from the real-time data: Over 101 of 272 real-time metrological stations observed the river crossing the danger level in the last 24 hours. The rainfall is expected to dissipate in the coming hours, with the possibility of scattered light to heavy rainfall throughout the country.

 In the early morning of 28 Sep. 24, multiple sources reported that nearly all streams and rivers in the Kathmandu Valley had overflowed, surpassing the danger levels and flooding nearby settlements along the riverbanks. Although there is no confirmed data on the extent of the damage yet, initial estimates suggest that over ten thousand people may be seeking refuge in open areas. It is expected that the floodwaters will take several hours to decrease.

 Reports of major and minor highways being washed away or severely eroded due to landslides and river erosion have emerged. The main highway – Kathmandu to Naryangadh – connecting Kathmandu to the rest of Nepal is currently inaccessible, with frequent mudslides at several locations, rendering it impassable for traffic and pedestrians. Similarly, massive blockages have been reported on other highways across the western and eastern Terai and in hilly areas. Kalikandaki corridor, a lifeline for at least three Syangja, Banglung and Parbat districts, is reportedly blocked due to several small to large landslides. Similarly, the Araniko highway is currently not passable due to numerous landslides along the road and a bridge collapse, a critical logistical corridor for Nepal to get supplies from China. 

 The water levels in the tributaries of the Koshi basin have increased, and the water level has reached both warning and danger levels. The flow of the Saptakoshi River was measured at 449,680 cusecs at 9 AM on Saturday. This is above the danger level. All 56 gates have been opened. We are actively trying to gather more information from the field. So far, DHM has already sent out 2 SMS alerts in the area since yesterday evening. Fortunately, the water has not yet entered the settlement areas (UN Situation Report, dated 28 Sept).

 The situation is expected to continue for several days, disrupting the supply of goods across the country as the festive season begins. This is likely to hike the price for essential commodities and may cause the stock to be out of stock if the roads remain impassable for several days. Debris cleaning remains challenging owing to the increasing number of sites requiring immediate attention and the severe lack of heavy equipment. 

 For the second time after 25 years, both gates of Kulekhani Dam were opened as the water level reached a hazardous level due to continuous rainfall in the catchment area. This caused havoc in low-lying areas of Makawanpur, Kathmandu, Sarlahi, and Mahottari. Extensive details of the damages to lives and properties are out of reach at this stage.

So far, there have been reports of around 22 districts affected by floods and landslides.

countries.name: Lebanon
dtype.name: Complex Emergency
name: Lebanon Complex Emergency - 2024
summary:
On 2 March 2026, Lebanon experienced a major escalation in hostilities marked by intense airstrikes across South Lebanon, Nabatieh, Beirut’s southern suburbs, Bekaa, Baalbek-El Hermel, and Mount Lebanon. The escalation followed displacement warnings issued for more than 50 villages, triggering widespread civilian movement and placing significant pressure on essential services and humanitarian systems.

The escalation occurred within an already fragile context. Since the beginning of hostilities in October 2023, Lebanon has experienced repeated cycles of violence resulting in casualties, displacement, and infrastructure damage. Although a ceasefire announced on 27 November 2024 reduced large-scale hostilities, intermittent strikes continued, maintaining a volatile environment leading up to the March 2026 escalation.

According to the Lebanese Disaster Risk Management (DRM) Unit, based on data from the Ministry of Public Health (MoPH), casualties have since risen to at least 687 deaths and 1,774 injuries, with the highest figures reported in Nabatieh Governorate.The growing number of casualties is placing increasing pressure on Lebanon’s already fragile health system.

The escalation has also triggered large-scale displacement across multiple governorates. According to the Lebanese Disaster Risk Management (DRM) Unit, there are approximately 822,600 registered displaced people nationwide, including 128,200 individuals currently sheltering across 596 collective sites. The actual number is likely significantly higher, as many community-run shelters are not yet included in official reporting systems and large numbers of families are hosted by communities or staying in informal locations.

Population movements have been characterized by large-scale displacement from southern and eastern districts toward Beirut, Mount Lebanon, and northern governorates. Many families experienced delays reaching safer areas due to heavy traffic congestion and access constraints. In response to the growing displacement, national authorities established over 170 collective shelters, primarily in public schools, many of which quickly reached capacity. The Ministry of Education and Higher Education (MEHE) also announced the closure of educational institutions nationwide, reflecting the severity of the situation.

Humanitarian needs emerging from the escalation are significant and include emergency medical care, blood supplies, shelter support, water, mattresses, blankets, food assistance, and fuel for generator-dependent facilities. Overcrowding in shelters and informal sites is also increasing concerns related to water and sanitation, health care access, and protection risks.

Lebanese Red Cross Response: In response to the escalation, the Lebanese Red Cross (LRC) activated its national emergency mechanisms and mobilized its emergency medical, blood transfusion, and relief capacities across affected areas. Emergency Medical Services (EMS) responded to conflict-related incidents, transporting injured people to hospitals and supporting evacuations from high-risk locations. At the same time, Blood Transfusion Services (BTS) continued collecting and distributing blood components to hospitals to support the treatment of the wounded. LRC teams also assisted displaced families through the distribution of essential relief items and supported response coordination with national authorities and humanitarian partners.

Operational priorities include sustaining nationwide emergency medical services coverage despite increasing operational pressure, scaling blood collection to meet growing demand, strengthening logistics and fuel supply to support response operations, and maintaining close coordination with national authorities and humanitarian partners.

 

SITUATIONAL OVERVIEW - 2024

Lebanon’s southern border has been the scene of continued conflict since 8 October 2023, evoking memories of the 2006 conflict and its profound impact on the region. Following the explosion of thousands of pagers on 17 September 2024, the hostilities have escalated dramatically. Southern Lebanon, the Bekaa region and Beirut’s suburbs have seen a massive increase in airstrikes and attacks, leading to over 2,710 deaths and 12,592 injuries as of 28 October 2024. This recent escalation has led to widespread destruction and mass displacement, exacerbating an already dire socio-economic situation in the country.

Lebanese authorities estimate that over 1.1 million individuals have been displaced, including many Syrian and Palestinian refugees, with some households being displaced multiple times. Many people left their homes quickly, without their essential items. Livelihoods are also severely disrupted, particularly for farming communities.

Around half of all displaced people are currently living in host settings, often in overcrowded conditions. The Lebanese Government has also opened 1,118 new collective shelters in public schools and other buildings that currently host over 188,690 displaced individuals (43,586 families), based on the household registration efforts of the Lebanese Red Cross and the Lebanese Government. However, limited access to safe and adequate shelter for internally displaced people (IDPs), as well as registration for displaced refugees and migrants, remains a challenge, particularly as winter approaches, increasing the humanitarian needs for those in makeshift housing and overcrowded centres. 

The large-scale displacement has heightened demand for essentials like bread, water, and shelter, placing the market system under pressure, and with prices already significantly inflated in some areas. Moreover, the hostilities have not only inflicted heavy civilian casualties, but have also severely damaged civilian infrastructure, including water and sanitation facilities, cutting off access to clean water for tens of thousands. The lack of effective sanitation services, with most wastewater treatment plants non-operational due to power shortages, heightens the risk of disease outbreaks like cholera, which had already severely affected Lebanon in late 2022.

Lebanon's healthcare sector, already strained by the economic crisis and COVID-19, faces critical shortages of medical staff and supplies, making it increasingly challenging to meet the needs of displaced people and those with chronic health conditions. Lebanese hospitals and health facilities are overwhelmed by the surge in casualties. Out of 207 primary health care centres and dispensaries in conflict-affected areas, 100 are already closed. Mobile Medical Units (MMU) from the Lebanese Red Cross have been deployed to mitigate this, but the overall healthcare system in Lebanon remains severely overwhelmed.

countries.name: Malaysia
dtype.name: Flood
name: MYS: Flood - 09-2024 - West Coast
summary:
Kedah is currently the most severely affected state, with the number of flood victims rising from 2,882 individuals last night to 3,441 from 978 families this morning, an increase of 559 compared to earlier figures. The seven impacted districts are Pasu (704 people), Pendang (429 people), Kulim (86 people), Pokok Sena (773 people), Kuala Muda (131 people), Kota Setar (1,205 people), and Bandar Baharu (113 people), all of whom are currently housed in 28 temporary relief centers (PPS).

Datuk Zulkhairi Zainol Abidin, Director of the Kedah Social Welfare Department (JKM), assured that sufficient supplies of basic necessities and food are available for evacuees, and that conditions at the relief centers remain stable despite the growing number of displaced individuals.

On the other hand, the Public Infobanjir website by the Drainage and Irrigation Department (JPS) reported that the number of rivers at dangerous levels in Kedah has decreased from 10 yesterday to seven today. 

The rivers currently at risk are Sungai Padang Terap in Kepala Batas; Sungai Bata in Kampung Bata; Sungai Laka in Kampung Padang Pasir, Kubang Pasu; Sungai Anak Bukit in Taman Aman; Sungai Anak Bukit at Jambatan TAR, Kota Setar; Sungai Titi Kerbau in Kubur Panjang, Pendang; and Sungai Perik in Kampung Perik, Padang Terap.

In Penang, eight relief centers across three districts have been opened, providing shelter to 586 victims from 163 families. Seberang Perai Utara remains the most heavily impacted area with 411 victims, followed by Seberang Perai Tengah with 95, and Seberang Perai Selatan with 62.

In Sabah, floods that began on 16 September have affected 303 people from 79 families, all of whom have been relocated to a relief center in the Tongod district.

Similarly, Perlis has maintained four PPS locations, accommodating 149 victims in total, with 113 in Arau and 36 in Kangar.

In Sarawak, where the floods began earlier on 22 August, one PPS in Betong remains open, sheltering 105 victims from 26 families.

As of 19 September 2024, at 4:45 PM, a total of 5,024 people (1,428 families) from seven districts have been displaced and are currently residing in 46 temporary relief centers.

countries.name: Chad
dtype.name: Flood
name: Chad - Floods 2024
summary:
Weeks of severe rains in Chad have hit all 23 provinces leaving at least 340 people dead and 1.5 million affected since July. The situation continues to evolve very rapidly with the number of people affected rising from 960,000 to more than 1,495,000 (over 266,000 households) in the last week. Torrential rainfall has caused rivers to overflow, displacing communities and disrupting access to essential services. As of September 10, the government has recorded 164,000 houses destroyed, 5 million hectares inundated, including 400,000 hectares of croplands, out of which 259,000 are completely destroyed, and 66,700 livestock washed away. This number will continue to increase as assessments continue.

The Chad national flood management committee has classified the 23 provinces into three categories, of which 12 are a priority. These are Tandjile, Mayo Kebbi Est, Logone Oriental, Lac, Guera, Salamat, Ennedi Ouest, Batha, Borkou, Mandoul, Ennedi Est and Tibesti.

countries.name: Senegal
dtype.name: Flood
name: SEN: Flood - 09-2024 - Senegal: Flooding
summary:
Heavy rainfall from 16-17 September have caused widespread flooding in Senegal, including Touba, a holy city in the Diourbel region, affecting thousands of people.

 According to local medias, several neighbourhoods were submerged in water and more than one hundred houses were severely damaged forcing inhabitants to flee, while many people are still living in flooded houses, surrounded by stagnant water. Two people have died, as the result of their collapsed houses.

countries.name: Sierra Leone
dtype.name: Flood
name: SLE: Flood - 09-2024 -  Floods
summary:
There has been reported cases of multiple disaster incident in Freetown and several part of the country between late August and September 2024. According to the National Disaster management Agency ( NDMA), the Bumbuna Dam in Tonkolili district, overflowed beyond its capacity due to persistent heavy downpour of rain on 16th September 2024. This incident resulted in severe flooding in communities downstream  and displaced 747 people, loss of household items, food supplies and  livelihoods (livestock, farmlands  and crops). Also, the stagnant floodwaters affected WASH facilities thus posing risk to cholera, typhoid and malaria.

Similarly, NDMA has reported flooding incidents from seven other districts (Kambia,  Port Loko, Moyamba, Bonthe, Kailahun, Pujehun and Bombali districts). Over 1,500 farmers have seen their farmlands submerged, with crops either destroyed or severely damaged, loss of properties, livelihoods and displacement  in over 50 communities. This has threatened not only their current food supply but also their long-term income and ability to recover after the floods.

Sierra Leone has recently recorded frequent infrastructure collapse in the western area. On September 16, whiles the Red Cross, Goverment and other partners are busy planing and evacuating the dam victims a seven storey building in the east- end of Freetown ( Shell, Kissy) collapsed and destroyed nearby buildings. As at today the search and rescure teams have recorded 15 deaths, 8 injuries and it is estimated that people are still trapped under the rubble.

countries.name: Portugal
dtype.name: Fire
name: PRT: Fire - 09-2024 - Wildfires - Heatwave
summary:
As of September 15, 2024, Portugal is grappling with significant wildfires, especially in the central and northern regions. The fires have been exacerbated by unusually high temperatures and dry conditions. Emergency services are actively working to contain the blazes, but the situation remains challenging due to the fires' intensity and rapid spread. The government has issued warnings and evacuation orders in the affected areas, and resources from neighboring countries are being mobilized to assist with firefighting efforts.

So far, there are 6 big wildfires in course. Firefighting efforts in Aveiro Region (Oliveira de Azeméis, Albergaria-a-Velha, and Sever do Vouga) have resulted in three fatalities, according to the National Authority for Emergency and Civil Protection. One person was found carbonized in the Sever do Vouga fire, another suffered a heart attack in the Albergaria-a-Velha fire, and a firefighter died during a lunch break in the field.

There have also been 18 reported injuries, as reported by civil protection authorities, with 6 being civil protection officers. Approximately 70 people have been evacuated, and at least five properties, including homes, have been affected by the flames. Additionally, about 20 houses have been destroyed. The fires, which began between Sunday and today, have impacted various rural areas in the North and Central regions.

The Portuguese Government has requested support from the European Civil Protection Mechanism (UCPM), leading to the deployment of eight aircraft to assist with firefighting.

 

The Portuguese Red Cross has deployed the following resources since September 15:

  • 1 Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) Officer in Crisis
  • 7 Liaison Officers at Command Posts
  • 4 Multiple Transport Vehicles for Supporting Evacuations
  • 46 Emergency Medical Technicians in 23 Basic Life Support Ambulances
  • 1 Mobile Medical Post to upgrade an active Health Center with Advanced Life Support
  • 2 Command and Communication Vehicles
  • Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) National Disaster Response Team activated for wildfire monitoring
  • 1 Temporary Emergency Shelter with 15 beds
  • A total of 80 staff/volunteers
  •  

Data from field interventions is still being collected.

The Disaster Management Department has still pre-positioned 500 hygiene kits and emergency shelter supplies for 500 people.

The situation is expected to worsen during the night due to high-intensity winds and new fire projections.

 

Updated at 9pm 16th September

countries.name: Slovakia
dtype.name: Flood
name: SVK: Flood - 09-2024 - Storm Boris
summary:
16th  September 2024 update

The weather forecast for the week of September 9th provided information on potential heavy rains in Slovakia as storm Boris was proceeding through European countries. Rainfalls were expected from Thursday, September 12th, with the culmination of perturbation on Saturday, September 14th, or Sunday, September 15th. The expected heavy areas were in west and northwest Slovakia, close to the Czech and Polish border and on the lower Danube.

Since Thursday, the Slovak Hydrometeorological Institute has collocated different districts in Slovakia into yellow, orange, or red zones (3rd level of flood alert) during the weekend in the districts of Skalica, Senica, Malacky, Bratislava, Senec, Dunajska Streda, Komarno, and Nove Zamky.

The map from Monday 16th of September. https://www.shmu.sk/sk/?page=1680

 

The level of the Kysuca River has risen dangerously due to persistent rainfall (Cadca and Kysucke Nove mesto) The Slovak Hydrometeorological Institute has issued a warning for the District of Čadca - 3rd level of flood activity, which is valid from Sunday 15 September from 2:00 to Monday 16 September at 10:00.

From Friday onwards, the most affected areas are Zahorie (Skalica, Senica, and Malacky) and Myjava, as heavy precipitation was also complicated by the strong wind.

The regional branches in the affected areas are actively participating in the local crisis management boards led by the district offices. So far, besides the Bratislava branch, which received the order from the district office, noassistance has been requested, as the primary focus is on the heavy machinery and equipment for the firefighters who need to enter the affected areas.

As the rainfall in Austria was heavier than expected the situation on the Danube River became more alarming. The Danube in Bratislava has exceeded the third flood level and is expected to reach 950 centimetres on Tuesday (September 17th). Anti-flood barricades were built on the lower sections of the Danube and in the city centre to prevent the river from entering the city as it was flooding out of the riverbed.

The city of Devin is the most affected area of Bratislava, which is impossible to reach if not by heavy machinery. Approximately 200 households were evacuated from Devinska, Nova Ves, and Kuchyna, villages in the northwestern part of Bratislava, which was heavily affected by the floods. Due to the floods, this area is hard to reach, and people have left their homes individually. This area is at a high risk of landslides.

The Bratislava city branch provides the base camp for the first responders (firefighters, police, and army) who are supporting in this affected area. SRC’s volunteers work on rotations, also during the night. They prepare meals for approximately 60 responders. Blankets were also provided. The branch was also requested to assess the situation of the inhabitants, monitor whether they have the medicines they need, and, if necessary, provide the medication so people will not risk leaving their homes.

In some other affected areas, the population was also requested to evacuate. Still, most people left their houses and moved to friends and family, and the established evacuation centres are mostly empty.

The highest third level (red) of alert persists in the western part of Slovakia, in the city of Bratislava, the Bratislava counties, and the towns on the lower course of the Danube River (Nove Zamky and Komarno).

Since Friday (13 September), more than 100,000 electricity outages have affected more than 100,000 sites in west Slovakia.

The worst situation is in Bratislava, Trencin, and Záhorie, where an emergency operating state has been declared. The main cause of the faults is fallen trees and branches on the lines, which are being continuously eliminated to recover.

So far, the overall number of affected people is unknown and is not being communicated, even in the daily situation report shared by the Ministry of Interior.

 

 

 

Update 18th September 2024

As of September 18, 2024, the situation is improving in most of the affected areas but remains critical in Devinska Nova ves (Bratislava County).

As per information reported by the regional branches in the most affected areas:

1.        Cadca—The river Kysuce and other small rivers are returning to the riverbeds, and the count of the damages is about to start. Several bridges need to be assessed, and approximately 100 households have been affected, mostly in the surrounding villages. The branch is still working on removing the damage and sanitation of the premises.

2.        Senica and Skalica district—The Senica branch has participated in the crisis management board in the Senica region. Water is entering the riverbed. The branch director is in touch with the three villages most affected and will deliver the packed water and cleaning items for the affected families. She is also in touch with the local branches to assess their needs.

3.        The Dunajska Streda branch has participated in the crisis management board; so far, no engagement has been requested, mostly from firefighters and volunteer firefighters. The third level of alert was called off. Local branches provided hot drinks to the affected people and the first responders. The count of the damages is starting, as is the cleaning of the basements of the flooded houses.

4.        Senec (Bratislava okolie)—The branch is delivering packed drinking water and cleaning products. The overall situation is improving, and the branch will engage with the mayors of the most affected villages to learn the needs of the population.

5.        Komarno—so far, it has not been heavily affected, as no river has flooded out of the riverbed. However, the situation is expected to worsen in a few days as the levels of the underground water rise and damage people's properties.

6.        Bratislava – branch is engaged in participating in the regional crisis management board and the municipality-driven response. Since Monday, the 16th of September, the branch has been providing support services for the first responders engaged in alleviating the situation in Devinska Nova Ves. More than 100 households were isolated in this part of Bratislava County. Food, drinks, and a base camp for the first responders were established at the cultural centre house, and the branch staff and volunteers assessed the health needs of the isolated population in terms of the availability of medication. No financial support is needed as the branch is operational under the order from District, and all the expenses are covered.

7.        Coordination with the NGO sector—The NGO sector is engaged in coordination groups that have regular online meetings. Ipcko (MHPSS crisis intervention organization), Adra, Charita, People in Need, and others are participating and informing about their response.

8.        SRC has engaged with several donors for packed drinking water, disinfection items, and some other NFIs that can be distributed to the people. No public appeal was opened. The engagement with the donor continues according to the requests from the field.

countries.name: Romania

name: ROU: Flood - 09-2024 - Cyclone Boris
summary: On September 14, 2024, the counties of Galați and Vaslui were hit by flash floods, with over 150 liters of rainfall per square meter recorded in less than 24 hours across several localities. The most affected area is Galați, specifically the localities of Cudalbi, Cuza-Vodă, Pechea, Slobozia-Conachi, Tudor Vladimirescu and Costache Negri, where floodwaters reached depths of 1.5 to 2 meters in some places. Over 6,000 houses have been either destroyed or partially damaged, 7 people died and thousands of residents have been evacuated from high-risk zones. Severe weather conditions are expected to persist, heightening the risk of further escalation.

countries.name: Poland
dtype.name: Flood
name: POL: Flood - 09-2024 - Flood in Poland 2024
summary:
Heavy rains have continued since Friday, causing flooding in southwestern Poland. The flood affected Dolnośląskie, Opolskie, Śląskie and Małopolskie voivodships.

Water has flooded, towns, villages, destroyed dams and bridges.  It is taking away houses and cutting off many people's escape routes. The  authorities in towns and cities are ordering evacuations.

By 3 p.m. on Sunday (15 September), the fire service had intervened 12 439 times in the following provinces: Śląskie, Dolnośląskie, Opolskie, Małopolskie, Łódzkie, Wielkopolskie and Mazowieckie.

The situation is most difficult in the Opolskie Voivodeship. According to media reports, there are still some towns in the Kłodzko district which cannot be reached even by boat.

So far, five people have lost their lives as a result of the floods.

The head of the Ministry of Defence said that 2,600 people have been evacuated in Poland since yesterday (15 September). These figures could quickly change. It is estimated that a total of 8 000 people (directly and indirectly) have been affected by the disaster at this point.

The Ministry of National Education reported that classes in more than 350 educational institutions have been cancelled.

The situation is dynamic, with data changing from hour to hour. More locations in danger of being flooded. The government is planning to prepare an ordinance to declare a state of natural disaster.

summary: Starting from 8 September 2024, strong winds and heavey rainfall, driven by Typhoon Yagi, impacted Naypyidaw and 11 other states and regions in Myanmar. It is estimated that 100,000 people have been affected and 33 reported death.  It has brough significant damage to road networks, and potential impact on telecommunications and electrity across all 9 S/Rs. Thousands of houses damaged including MRCS branch office in Tachileik (Eastern Shan). It also affected the livelihood to the people of those areas. The affected people are in great need of emergency shelter assistance, basic food, clean water, clothing and hygiene items.

countries.name: Viet Nam
dtype.name: Cyclone
name: Viet Nam: Typhoon YAGI - September 2024
summary: Cyclone Yagi has steadily strengthened all week and became a Super Typhoon on the afternoon of Thursday September 5, with maximum winds of 201 kph (125 mph), as it traversed warm open water between the Philippines and China’s Hainan. That island may endure a direct hit before Yagi moves into the Gulf of Tonkin with reduced (but still very strong) wind speeds and makes landfall in the Quang Ninh/Hai Phong area early morning Saturday. The National Center for Hydro-Meteorological Forecasting has warned that the northern and north-central regions should expect severe weather from Friday's evening through the weekend, with heavy rain and strong wind possible in other regions as well. According to the meteorological agency, the rain, with a common rainfall of 150 - 350 mm, in some places over 500 mm, concentrated in a short time (from 6 to 9 September) due to the influence of Super typhoon Yagi may lead to high risk of flash floods and landslides in 106 districts and towns across the northern midland and mountainous provinces. The Government of provinces by the coastal line banned all vessels from heading to sea, while officials are monitoring storm protection systems and agricultural areas. Small boats are being brought onshore and tied down, while cruises in Hạ Long Bay have been suspended. The officials also announced that Van Don, Cat Bi, Tho Xuan and Noi Bai airports will close for most of Saturday. The National Society at headquarter has ordered its branches in danger zone to review the current resources (cash and relief goods), to activate its local disaster response team while closely coordinate with local authorities in providing assistance at temporary shelters/evacuation sites and reinforcement of houses for the vulnerable communities.

countries.name: Uganda
dtype.name: Flood
name: UGA: Flood - 09-2024 - Uganda Floods (SOND) Western Region - Kasese District September 2024
summary:
Kasese Municipality flood situation. Following yesterday’s heavy downpour in the late evening, today at 10:00 am, the volume of water from River Nyamwaba drastically increased causing it to burst its banks. The overflowing water has diverted to the Municipality into people’s houses affecting 13 villages in Nyamwamba Division, Kasese Municipality, Kasese District, Western Uganda.
 
Close to 1,000 households have been affected, forcing many to vacate their homes and seek shelter with relatives and neighbors. Household property has been severely impacted, leaving many families homeless and in desperate need of assistance.
 
Tragically, four lives have been lost so far:
  1. One woman ventured outside to record a video, unknowingly standing on weak ground and was swept away by the floodwaters.
  2. Another woman attempting to cross a small bridge while carrying a baby fell into the water. Her body has been retrieved, but sadly, the baby is still missing.
  3. A man was observing the water nearby when the soft ground gave way, causing him to fall into the river and lose his life.
     
Our volunteers have been actively disseminating SOND advisories and the rising water levels via community radios, but the urgent needs remain:
  1. 1. Non-food items support.
    2. Setting up an evacuation site at the Nyakasanga playground for temporary shelter.
Below is a list of the affected villages:
  1. Kitoro Cell
  2. Acholiquaters
  3. Mumbuzi
  4. Base Camp Lower
  5. Kizungu
  6. Nyakasanga West
  7. Kisanga A

We continue to carry out assessments of the situation in collaboration with the District Disaster Management Committee. However, some areas remain submerged making them inaccessible for the time being. Despite these challenges, we are working to reach and assist all affected communities as quickly as possible.

countries.name: Algeria
dtype.name: Flood
name: DZA: Flood - 09-2024 - South Algeria Floods
summary: As of September 8, 2024, severe flooding caused by a tropical disturbance has significantly impacted several provinces in southern and western Algeria, displacing approximately 500 families, primarily from nomadic communities. The provinces of Béchar, Elbayadh, Beni Abbes, Tamanrasset, Tiaret, Ghardaia, and Tindouf have experienced the most severe effects. In Béchar, where 280 families have been displaced, roads have been cut off, 5 bridges have been destroyed, and both water and electricity infrastructures have been damaged. Rescue operations have been carried out to save individuals trapped by rising floodwaters. In Elbayadh, 60 families were displaced, and homes were damaged as floods swept through remote areas. In Beni Abbes, 40 families were forced to evacuate due to rising water levels that also cut off major roads. Meanwhile, in Tamanrasset, 20 families have been affected, with search and rescue operations ongoing for missing persons following heavy flooding. Additionally, in Tiaret, 50 families have been displaced, 30 families in Ghardaia, and 20 in Tindouf. Tragically, the floods have claimed four lives, including a father and his two children in Elbayadh and one person in Tamanrasset, with one individual still missing. The affected populations are facing immediate threats to their livelihoods and safety as authorities and humanitarian organizations, including the Algerian Red Crescent, work to manage the crisis and provide emergency relief.

summary: A tropical disturbance expected to impact southern and western Algeria. This disturbance, with the potential for heavy rainfall, flash floods, and strong winds, poses a serious threat to both urban and rural communities, particularly in high-risk provinces: Tamanrasset, Adrar, Béchar, Tindouf, Ghardaïa, Ouargla, Bordj Badji Mokhtar, Ain Salah, Timimoun, and In Guezzam. Additionally, community outreach programs have been initiated to educate residents on flood safety and preparedness, with emphasis on high-risk areas. National response teams and resources have been mobilized to ensure a rapid and effective response if the situation escalates.

countries.name: Pakistan

name: Pakistan: Monsoon Rain/Floods - August 2024
summary:
Pakistan is going through an intense monsoon season currently, leading to significant damages to infrastructure, casualties and injuries. This month of August has witnessed above normal rainfall and increase of 137% has been recorded till date. Geographically the 239% more rain than expected recorded in Baluchistan, Sindh 318%, Punjab 111% and KP 25% above normal.

This year the rain remained continued at different regions with some difference in intensity and intervals however the repeatedly affected the population. The latest spell which was forecasted by Pakistan Metrological department Starting from 26th to 30th August resulted in further damages and human losses.

The national disaster Management Authority data as of 2nd September reveals that since 1st July 2024, 306 people have been died, 584 people have been injured, 40 bridges have been damaged, 20653 houses damaged, 1100 livestock perished, a total of 119 KM roads at different location flooded away. The floods have also displaced approximately 9500 people in Sindh province. The damages caused by heavy rainfall and floods have increased the vulnerability of people and posing ongoing risks.

The latest spell of rain started from 26th of August caused further damages in communities already exposed by the previous floods and rainfall since July 2024, significantly increased their vulnerability. The latest spell resulted in damages, human loses and injuries which intensified on 31st August resulted in 13 deaths, 15 injuries and more than 1000 houses damaged on a single day. In addition, 2700 more house reported damaged in last 24 hours. Government has declared 13 districts as calamity hit district in Baluchistan and earlier emergency declared in Chitral district of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

Weather Forecast:

Met office informed that moist current from Bay of Bengal are likely to penetrate upper parts from 02nd September. A westerly wave is also likely to approach western parts of the country on 02nd September evening.

More rain have been predicted in the coming days with the possible impact of urban flooding, GLOF incidents, pluvial flood/inundation in low lying areas.

countries.name: Malawi
dtype.name: Epidemic
name: MWI: Epidemic - 08-2024 - Measles outbreak in Malawi
summary:
Malawi has reported measles cases in Mangochi District in the Southern Region. On 29thAugust 2024, Mangochi District Heath Office was alerted on a cluster of suspected measles cases in a village under Mkuchinga Jwambone Health Center. Six samples were collected for laboratory investigation at Kamuzu Central Hospital in Lilongwe. Three samples were confirmed positive for Measles on 9th September, 2024. The ages of the confirmed measles cases are seven months, five and seven years old. Measles, is a highly infectious viral disease characterized by a generalized rash, fever, running nose and at least cough or Coryza or red-eye. It spreads through direct contact with mouth or nasal droplets when an infected person breathes, coughs or sneezes. While the disease can affect anyone, unvaccinated or under vaccinated under five children and pregnant mothers are at high risk of contracting and developing severe form of the disease. If untreated, measles can cause serious complications like blindness or death. It is therefore, important to seek urgent medical help. There is no specific treatment for measles. The symptoms are usually mild and self-resolving within a period of about one week. 
Communities are advised to take preventive measures as the disease has the potential to affect more people. Vaccination is the most effective way to prevent measles. Ministry of Health with support from its partners including Malawi Red Cross is encouraging parents to vaccinate their children.

countries.name: Mali
dtype.name: Flood
name: PWM: Flood - 08-2024 - Flood August 2024
summary:
Hydro-climatic forecasts for the period from July to October 2024 indicate above-average rainfall throughout Mali, with increased risks of flooding in the Niger and Senegal river watersheds. Water levels observed in these basins are already showing trends above hydrological averages from 1991 to 2020, signaling conditions conducive to significant flooding.
Heavy rainfall and excess runoff in the Niger and Senegal river basins can lead to significant flooding, particularly in areas downstream of the Sélingué and Manantali dams.
Urban and rural areas along rivers, particularly in Bamako, Koulikoro, Mopti, Gao, and Kayes, are at risk of submersion.

Floods can affect thousands of people, causing displacement, loss of property and livelihoods, and increasing the vulnerability of local communities.
Large cities such as Bamako, Koulikoro, Mopti, Gao, and Kayes are particularly at risk, with potential impacts on critical infrastructure and public services.

countries.name: Liberia
dtype.name: Epidemic
name: LBR: Epidemic - 08-2024 - Liberia Mpox Outbreak
summary: Liberia has confirmed five (5) cases in three counties. According to the National Public Health Institute of Liberia (NPHIL), the cases have been traced and reported since January this year. The pronouncement was made on Friday, 16th of August. Liberia has recently conducted a monkeypox baseline preparedness assessment using the WHO AFRO. Results from this assessment show that the country's overall preparedness capacity for monkeypox is currently at 51%, which indicates a need for improvement. There is a draft preparedness and response plan has been developed. According to the plan, 13 thematic pillars have been identified as requiring strengthening and prioritization. To enhance the country's preparedness capacity to the target level of 85% or higher, resources are needed to address the key gaps in 13 thematic areas.

countries.name: Africa Region
dtype.name: Epidemic
name: Africa -Mpox Epidemic
summary:
A concerning surge in mpox cases and deaths has been observed in Africa throughout 2024, with thousands of cases and hundreds of deaths reported across several countries in Africa.  The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has become the epicenter of this outbreak, accounting for 92% of the total cases in Africa. Alarmingly, mpox cases have now been confirmed in all 26 provinces of the DRC, with multiple Clades of the virus appearing in different regions. Cross-border transmission is escalating from the DRC's eastern provinces, particularly North and South Kivu, into non-endemic countries such as Burundi, Rwanda, Uganda, and Kenya. The situation is further exacerbated by the gradual expansion or re-emergence of outbreaks in endemic countries like Nigeria, the Central African Republic, and Côte d’Ivoire.

In response to these alarming developments, the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (AfCDC) and the World Health Organization (WHO) have declared the ongoing mpox outbreak a public emergency of continental and international concern. The IFRC has echoed this urgent call, issuing a statement on August 13 and activating its internal coordination mechanisms to bolster preparedness and scale up response efforts. Mpox, a viral illness related to smallpox but less severe, is primarily transmitted through close contact with infected individuals or contaminated materials. While the disease is endemic in West and Central Africa, the emergence of new Clades, including Clade 1b in Eastern DRC and Clade 2 globally, underscores the heightened risk of widespread transmission. The IFRC remains committed to supporting public health initiatives and reinforcing measures to control the spread of mpox, particularly in regions where the virus is rapidly advancing.

summary:
On Sunday, 11 August, a wildfire broke out at 3 p.m. and quickly reached the village of Varnavas, 35 km (20 miles) north of Athens, Attica, Greece. Due to the windy weather, the fire spread out very quickly.
 
Evacuation orders were issued for more than a dozen areas near Varnavas, including Marathon and several Athens suburbs, causing residents to flee their homes. In addition, a children's hospital, a military hospital, and two monasteries were evacuated early Monday. At the same time, three Athens hospitals were put on heightened alert to treat any potential injuries.
 
As a result, burned trees, houses, cars, and smoke clouds covered Athens, the Greek capital. 
The number of houses, cars, forest and agricultural land, livestock units, and all kinds of businesses that have been burned remains unknown.

Approximately 700 firefighters, backed by 27 teams specially trained to tackle wildfires and including more than 80 members of the armed forces, were battling the flames. More than 180 vehicles were deployed, while more than 30 water-dropping planes and helicopters provided aerial support.

Even if the situation is currently under control, the area is still on alert.

dtype.name: Flood
name: CMR: Inondation - 08-2024 - inondation Logone et Chari
summary:
The Far North region of Cameroon in general, and the department of Logone and Chari in particular, recorded unprecedented rainfall this year. The recurrence of rains since July to August 2024, combined with a succession of heavy torrential rains (with an average duration of about 7 hours per shower, from 11/08/2024 to 19/08/2024), have plunged the department of Logone and Chari into a series of rainfall floods. The most affected districts are   Blangoua, Makary and Zina with more than a dozen villages completely flooded. Similarly, some localities in the districts of Logone birni, Kousseri and goulfey are affected.

These floods are finding vulnerable communities due to climate change, pockets of drought, locust invasions, seed-eating bird invasions, pachyderm invasions and the very volatile security context since 2014. All of these factors significantly affect the resilience and livelihoods of these communities.

As soon as the floods occurred, assessments of the situation were made from 12 to 20/08/2024 by the district committees of Blangoua, Makary and Zina under the supervision of the Logone and Chari Departmental Committee. These assessments report a provisional assessment of 13140 households directly affected and in an emergency situation in the 03 arrondissements for 91,980 people (i.e. 4095 households in Blangoua, 7309 households in Makary and 1736 households in ZINA) as well as significant human material damage:

-          03 loss of human life, i.e. 01 person in the locality of Maltam in Makary, and 02 people respectively in the villages of Bangalia and Ndoulo in the district of Zina;

-          4543 huts destroyed (i.e. 2667 huts in Makary, 1031 huts in Blangoua and 845 huts in Zina);

-           2985 ha of crops swallowed up by the waters (i.e. 1494 ha in Makary, 316 ha in Blangoua and 1175 ha in Zina);

-           More than 601 small ruminants and poultry including lost (i.e. 236 animals in Makary, 84 animals in Blangoua and 281 animals in Zina);

-           Several flooded water points and latrines;

-          The destruction of material property and civil documents.

- 03 cases of death in the commune of Logone Birni (01 breastfeeding woman, 01 infant, a child of 04 years old).

The victims are currently living under the stars and there are a large number of people with special needs (children, pregnant women, breastfeeding women and the elderly) at the mercy of bad weather and possible health risks. Some affected households have taken shelter in the infrastructure of the fortunes (CMPJ, ECCAS, schools, DAADER, place where travel vehicles are parked) and others have been accommodated in the host communities.

Weather forecasts predict heavy rains until September 2024, which would worsen the situation of the localities already affected and a probable extension to the other localities still spared.  In addition, the national weather forecasts predict flooding of the Logone River during the third dekad of August 2024 (from 21 to 31), flooding of the Logone River is forecast.

The risks are diverse, namely:

  •      The threat of a malaria epidemic with the proliferation of mosquitoes during this period;
  •  The threat of a possibility of a cholera epidemic is a risk, given the unsanitary conditions and the flooding of the latrines caused;
  •   The theft of the effects of the victims can lead to conflicts;
  •  The delay in adequate assistance could contribute to the deterioration of the living conditions of the people affected;
  • The high probability of river flooding due to the overflow of the Logone and EL-BEID rivers, which could aggravate and accentuate the situation at the departmental level.

summary:
According to ARC field reports, on August 9, 2024, wildfires erupted across various regions within the province of Tizi Ouzou, Algeria, causing extensive damage to agricultural fields, trees, and forests. The fires initially broke out around 11:00 AM in the daïra of Beni Douala and quickly spread to the neighboring daïra of Larbaa Nath Irathen (LNI). Despite initial efforts to contain the flames, the fires continued to spread, ultimately ravaging a vast number of hectares, including both agricultural lands and forests.

On the following day, August 10, 2024, the fires reignited in the same daïras around 12:15 PM, resulting in a massive propagation across the region. The material damages were substantial: several hectares of vegetation, including olive groves and various fruit trees, were destroyed. Additionally, three (03) chicken coops, housing approximately 10,000 chicks, were incinerated, and a Toyota Hilux vehicle, along with multiple homes, sustained significant damage.

name: JPN: Earthquake - 08-2024 - Earthquake hit Miyazaki Prefecture
summary:
On 8 August 2024 at 16:43 (Japan Standard Time), a 7.1 magnitude earthquake struck southwestern Japan, with its epicenter in the Hyuganada sea off the coast of Miyazaki Prefecture, at a depth of 30km. Strong tremors were observed in many places in the Kyushu region, and the Meteorological Agency has issued a tsunami warning/advisory for the coastal areas of Miyazaki, Kochi, Oita, Kagoshima and Ehime prefectures. The tsunami reached a height of 50cm in the coastal areas, but no direct damage from the tsunami was reported as of 18:45.

One house has collapsed in Kagoshima Prefecture as a result of the earthquake, and flights to and from Miyazaki Airport and some highways are currently suspended. However, there have been no reports of power or water cuts or abnormalities at nuclear facilities. The number of casualties is still unknown, but three injuries have been reported in Miyazaki and Kumamoto prefectures as of 19:00. The Japan Meteorological Agency is calling for caution in the coming week in the strong level of earthquakes.

JRCS Headquarters have been closely monitoring the situation in contact with local chapters in the affected areas.

Far North Region of Cameroon and more precisely in the District of Yagoua from August 04 , 2024, for nearly 8 hours of non-stop time. These rains continued on August 05 and 06, 2024, causing flooding in several districts of the city of Yagoua. The most affected neighbourhoods are Djibetsou (with 78 households affected), Guidangmoutou (41 households), Danayré (64 households) and Hléké (34 households). 
The provisional assessment shows that 221 households were directly affected, i.e. nearly 1105 people, as well as several fairly significant damages such as the partial or total destruction of houses;   loss of certain material goods, including sleeping materials and clothing; the loss of small rumunants and fowls. 
 No loss of life was reported, but the number of victims continues to rise in view of the continuing rains and the fact that most of  the houses are made of dirt. 
 The victims had to leave their homes to find refuge in the shelters of host families. 

The vulnerability of those affected and their numbers is likely to increase in the coming days and weeks if nothing is done. The affected people include a large number of people with special needs, i.e. nearly 762 people: 114 pregnant women; 119 lactating women; 498 children under 5 years of age; 31 elderly people and 7 people living with a disability. These people are exposed to water-related diseases and cholera. Food pressure at the level of host families is likely to set in.

At the regional level, according to data provided by the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), nearly 10 million cases of dengue have been detected, increasing by 232% percent, compared to 2023, and Panama does not escape the high rates of positive cases.

dtype.name: Flood
name: CMR: Flood - 07-2024 - flood Diamare_Maroua 1st
summary:
Heavy torrential rains fell in the Diamaré Department, Far North Region of Cameroon on July 28, 2024, causing flooding in several neighborhoods, the most affected of which is the Palar 2 district, particularly the Massinika areas; palar galion and Zaika with nearly 951 people directly affected for 122 households. These rains persisted on July 29 and 30, which generated an increase in the water level, and since this rainfall the quarter has been completely flooded.

    These torrential rains caused  quite significant damage such as destroyed houses, the destruction of material property, the loss of small ruminants and poultry, wells were swallowed up by the water and clogged pipeways. Some plots are no longer habitable because of the stagnant water that destroys the foundations of the houses made of earth. No loss of human life was recorded. However, houses are still threatened under the weight of humidity and flowing, stagnant water. Many households can no longer cook or have dignified sleeping spaces due to a lack of dry space. 

Some of the victims  have left the neighbourhood to find refuge with their family members, others under the stars in less humid places, others currently under the stars in less  humid places and there are some who, despite the unsanitary conditions, continue to occupy their homes. For the moment, two temporary resettlement sites have been identified, namely  the CES of Palar and the villa of the district chief. Some toilet structures have been destroyed, forcing the population to create makeshift toilets.  It should be noted that there are a large number of people with special needs, 11 pregnant women; 27 lactating women; 125 children under 5 years old, 34 elderly people and 04 people living with disabilities.  The rainy season is in full swing and the situation could get worse if nothing is done

The Departmental Committee in collaboration with the District Committee and the head of the Palar block mobilized first aid volunteers to help with the evacuation as well as provide first aid.

countries.name: Burundi
dtype.name: Epidemic
name: BDI: Epidemic - 07-2024 - BDI: MPOX epidemic-07-2024
summary:
Burundi faces many threats from diseases with epidemic potential. After a few weeks of suspected cases of monkeypox (MPox), Burundi declared a Mpox epidemic on July 25, 2024. Burundi's border with the Democratic Republic of Congo constitutes an MPox epidemic zone.  
The overall secondary attack rate after contact with a known human source is 3% (study conducted in South Africa in 2023), and attack rates of up to 50% have been reported in people living with persons infected with MPox.
         
As of July 22, 2024, three alerts from the Kamenge University Hospital Center (CHUK), the Kamenge Military Hospital (HMK), and the ISARE Health District reported the existence of suspected cases of MPox. 
The symptoms generally presented by the cases were fever, skin rashes of sudden onset and paroxysmal appearance, lesions of the oral cavity, headaches, physical asthenia, and dysphagia.
The tests from the national reference laboratory confirmed the monkeypox virus for these 3 cases. 
Two positive cases were reported on July 22, one of which was in the Kinama zone of the Bujumbura Nord health district, the other in the SHATANYA 4 district of the city of Gitega and a third case was confirmed in the Tenga district. Local Isare district. These three cases are taken care of at CHUK (2) and HMK (1).
For the 3 cases, a total of 96 contacts including 65 family members and 31 health personnel have been traced and are currently being monitored. Contact tracing continues and will expand to other areas.

countries.name: South Sudan
dtype.name: Flood
name: Sudan : Floods & Cholera
summary:
Heavy rains since May 2024, combined with overflowing Lake Victoria, have caused the Nile River to burst its banks and with severe flooding, submerging villages, and farmland. As of 29 November, the situation remains critical with more than 1.4 million people affected in 44 of the country’s 78 counties (OCHA).

On 28 October 2024, the Government of South Sudan declared a cholera outbreak in Renk, marking the start of a growing health crisis. By 17 November, the outbreak had escalated to “nationwide” status. Cholera cases have since been reported across seven states and one administrative area, including in the capital, Juba.

The outbreak has come at a time when South Sudan is grappling with several emergencies including floods and an influx of people from Sudan where an armed conflict is ongoing.

As of 22 January 2025, over 23 000 suspected cases have been recorded, and 462 deaths in 33 counties across 7 states and 1 administrative area, with cases continuing to climb. The South Sudan Red Cross (SSRC) has activated its cholera response mechanism and has started response activities, including supporting Oral Rehydration Points (ORP) in some affected counties.

The floods have caused extensive damage to homes and have devastated livestock and crops. Critical infrastructure 
has been severely damaged, cutting off supply routes and leaving communities without access to essential services 
such as healthcare and education for displaced people. The risk of disease outbreaks, particularly cholera and malaria, 
has increased significantly. As of 11 February 2025, the number of suspected cases of Cholera has risen to 29,304 
cases with 501deaths, and a case fatality rate (CFR) of 1.5%, justifying the RC/RC Movement mobilization and 
underscoring the urgent need for further action. Mayom County (northwest of Rubkona, Unity State) has in the past 
few days become the top hot spot with cumulative cases at 585 and CFR of 8.4 %, while Rubkona has recorded overall 
the highest number of cases during the outbreak (over 10,000). Cholera cases have now been reported in 30 of the 
80 counties in the country and across seven states and one administration area. Especially in rural areas, poor 
surveillance outside of health facilities and on the other hand poor access to care are contributing to underreporting 
and deaths that could be prevented through community-based interventions. Misconceptions and lack of awareness, 
coupled with poor water and sanitation infrastructure are also contributing to harmful practices, adding to the spread 
of Cholera in vulnerable communities. Children are the most affected population with ages 0 to 4 years at 32.5% of 
cases followed by 5 to 14 years at 22.8% of cases 2
. Oral Cholera vaccination (OCV) campaigns have taken place in 
hotspot areas, with 1,400,000 people vaccinated (out of a total of 3,200,000 doses) as of 22nd of January 2025. While 
the peak of the outbreak has for now been passed (in Mid-January), the outbreak continues to spread to new 
communities

 

Since conflict erupted in Sudan on 15 April 2023, South Sudan has faced an unprecedented influx of over 800,000 people, including South Sudanese returnees, Sudanese refugees, and other nationals crossing the border in search of safety. This humanitarian crisis is now compounded by a cholera outbreak originating in Sudan’s border areas, which has steadily spread across South Sudan. The epidemic has taken hold in key hotspots, including Upper Nile, Northern Bahr el Ghazal, and Unity States, with cases reported in Jonglei and Central Equatoria. Among the returnees, refugees, and host communities, aggravated malnutrition has further heightened vulnerability, creating the perfect storm for rapid disease transmission.

South Sudan faces a complex and worsening humanitarian crisis. The humanitarian consequences of the armed conflict and other situations of violence remain dire. Economic decline, disease, and climate shocks – such as the ongoing floods – are devastating communities across the country. Poor infrastructure and limited access to services mean many cases of illness and disease go unreported, particularly in rural areas. The situation is further exacerbated by the high concentration of people in transit centers and the continuous movement of returnees and refugees to various locations, significantly increasing the risk of disease spread. Overcrowded conditions in camps for internally displaced persons (lDPs), refugee settlements, and places of detention compound these challenges, placing already vulnerable populations at greater risk. This convergence of crises underscores the urgent need for coordinated and comprehensive interventions to save lives and curb the outbreak.

countries.name: Chad
dtype.name: Flood
name: TCD: Flood - 07-2024 - flood
summary: Heavy rains and flooding have occurred earlier than usual in 2024 in Chad and climate forecasts predict this situation to continue throughout August and beyond. According to satellite data provided by the Emergency Team of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), more than 600,000 hectares were already flooded as of 17 July 2024, and more than one million as of 1 August 2024, This is almost double the number observed in the same period in 2022 and 2023, 493,000 and 545,000 ha respectively.   The floods mainly affected the provinces of Salamat, Tandjilé, Lac and Mayo Kebbi East, and in particular the departments of Bahr-Azoum and Haraze-Mangueigne in Salamat; East, Centre and West Tandjilé in Tandjilé; Fouli and Mamdi in the lake; and Mayo-Boneye in Mayo-Kebbi East. More than 57,000 ha of cropland were potentially affected by flooding as of July 17, 2024; This figure tripled to 157,000 ha on 1 August 2024. The most affected crop areas in terms of hectares are in the provinces of Tandjilé Ouest, Salamat, Kabia and Mayo-Boneye, to which are added Logone Occidental and Oriental on August 1, 2024. The departments of Tandjilé East, Centre and West, Bahr-Azoum, Mayo-Boneye, Ngourkosso and La Pendé are the most affected in the overall assessment. These atypical climatic conditions with higher cumulative precipitation (68.13 mm of precipitation in June 2024 while the long-term averages are 27.23 mm) were observed from the beginning of June 2024 compared to the long-term average measured between 1989 and 2015. This phenomenon was also observed in 2022 (with peaks in the second dekad of June measured at 86.13 mm) and in 2023 (115.21 mm in the third dekad of July). Usually, July is essential for agricultural production in Chad, as it corresponds to the planting period for maize, millet, rice and sorghum. Depending on the most affected livelihood areas, including the south-west zone, the floods could have an impact on rice plantings. Indeed, these floods can damage crop development and reduce production. They can also impact the vegetative development of staple crops, including maize, millet, sorghum and groundnuts, due to waterlogging and subsequent crop destruction; and lead to, among other consequences : (i) erosion of agricultural land, (ii) impoverishment of the soil by leaching, (iii) dissemination of weed seeds in healthy agricultural areas, (iv) population displacement due to lack of shelter, (v) degradation of roads and access roads. The consequences of flooding on land used for other purposes (grasslands, shrubs and herbaceous wetlands) have also been significant. According to the results, more than 630,000 ha of grassland, nearly 150,000 ha of shrub-planted areas and 81,000 ha of herbaceous wetlands have already been affected by flooding between 17 July and 1 August 2024. The extent of flooding of grasslands and shrublands could impact the livestock sector due to reduced grazing, which could lead to the displacement of pastoralists. The most affected subsistence areas as of July 17, 2024 were the southeast (flood recession and gum arabic), western (agropastoral and fisheries areas) and southwest (rice-growing areas). The subsistence zone for food and cash crops in the south was also particularly affected on 1 August 2024.

countries.name: Equatorial Guinea
dtype.name: Other
name: GNQ: Other - 07-2024 - Shipwreck in Bata, Equatorial Guinea
summary:
On 20 July 2024, the National President of Equatorial Guinea was alerted by government authorities from Bata on a shipwreck that occurred early morning of 20 July 2024, before dawn. The shipwreck is said to have occurred at the Rio Campo Cribi sea border between Equatorial Guinea and Cameroon. It is difficult currently to indicate the origin of what seems to be a clandestine boat. The rescued passengers indicate that they were travelling to Gabon, and that the boat’s captain immediately escaped upon seeing the coast of Equatorial Guinea, abandoning the passengers to their fate. This resulted into the shipwreck. According to the passengers, the boat had been travelling since 1st July 2024, and the passengers seem to have been promised jobs in Gabon.

The boat was carrying 90 people, including 47 women from different nationalities (30 from Benin and 17 from Togo), as well as 43 men also from different nationalities (10 from Togo, 16 from Benin, 8 Burkina Faso nationals, 2 Niger nationals, and 6 Nigerians. 1 died, and his nationality has not been clarified yet).

One of the passengers died because of the shipwreck, and 89 were rescued. These 89 are wounded, some with fracture. The Equatorial Guinea Red Cross team did not participate in the rescue as the accident occurred very early in the morning (before dawn). However, the host National Society provided first aid services to the wounded as soon as they were alerted by government authorities (the Gendarmerie Nacional).

A rapid assessment conducted by the Equatorial Guinea Red Cros (EGRC) indicate that the 89 rescued passengers are in a small room at the Gendarmerie in Bata, a room that normally can contain up to 4 people. They have nowhere to go as none of them is from Equatorial Guinea. They urgently need water, food, clothes, sleeping matts, mosquito nets, pillows, buckets, jerrycans and cups for drinking water. The National Society also needs first aid kits to replenish their stock and to continue providing first-aid services to the affected people rescued from the shipwreck.

name: PHL: Cyclone - 07-2024 - Southwest Monsoon Enhanced by Typhoon Carina
summary:
The Southwest Monsoon which has been causing widespread flooding in Mindanao since 11 July, continues to affect the western parts of Southern Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao.

 

On Friday afternoon, July 19, PAGASA observe two low-pressure areas within the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR). At 3 PM, one LPA was 365 kilometers west of Tanauan City, Batangas, while the other was 865 kilometers east of the Eastern Visayas.

 

At 8 PM of 19 July 2024, PAGASA reported that the low-pressure areas to the west and east of the archipelago had developed into Tropical Depressions named "BUTCHOY" and "CARINA" by the weather bureau. “BUTCHOY” was located west of Batangas, while “CARINA” was situated east of Eastern Visayas.

 

On Saturday afternoon of July 20, 2024, the Tropical Storm “CARINA” with international name (GAEMI) intensified from a Tropical Depression into a Tropical Storm and further intensified into a Severe Tropical Storm on July 21. On July 22, Carina intensified into Typhoon category.

 

Tropical Depression “BUTCHOY” has exited the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) on July 20, 8 PM.

 

Typhoon “CARINA” further intensifies as it heads towards Taiwan. The center of the eye of Typhoon was estimated based on all available data at 290 km Northeast of Itbayat, Batanes (22.9°N, 123.5°E) maximum sustained winds of 155 km/h near the center, gustiness of up to 190 km/h, and central pressure of 950 hPa.

name: Bangladesh: Floods EAP, 2024
summary:
The Bangladesh Red Crescent Society (BDRCS) has activated its Early Action Protocol (EAP) for Floods. On 9 July, BDRCS convened an EAP Activation
Committee meeting at 10 am in the BDRCS Emergency Operation Centre (EOC). Based on the analysis the forecast from GLoFAS, the Activation
Committee agreed that the conditions for activation were sufficiently met for the first trigger of the EAP. This activation notification aims to communicate the activation of the Floods EAP (under IFRC-DREF anticipatory pillar). 
 
The BDRCS Flood EAP has two preapproved triggers in this EAP:
 
Stage I: Pre-Activation give BDRCS 15 days for preactivation activities. The trigger is: Get ready with the resource and identify the beneficiaries likely to
be impacted based on the forecasted exposed area. Pre-activation Trigger will be reached when flow at Bahadurabad (forecasted by GloFAS with lead time 15 days) likely (50 per cent probability of 51 ensembles discharge forecast or above) to cross the 1 in 5-year return period and flowing over at
least for three days. 
 
Stage II: Activation, this trigger gives BDRCS 5 days for no regrets early actions which aim to reduce or mitigate the impact of the hazard. The trigger is: Activate EAP in the vulnerable households within forecasted exposed area. Trigger will be reached when forecast water level by FFWC at Bahadurabad (5 days lead-time) shows to cross the DL+0.85m and remain above for 3 days. This corresponds to an impact forecast of loss of household assets over 25 per cent or affected population over 40 per cent of the respective exposed unions.
 
Based on the BDRCS decision to activate the EAP, BDRCS HQ has alerted all districts around the Jamuna Basin and requested to initiate all the planned early actions in accordance with the preapproved Flood EAP. BDRCS is targeting 50,000 people and will provide following: (i) support for boat evacuation of people, livestock, moveable assets, (ii) last mile early warning message dissemination, (iii) Unconditional cash grant and (iv) basic first aid
service for injuries and sickness.
 
Noting that the Flood EAP was revised between 2020 to 2021 during COVID-19, there were initially safety measures included particularly the provision of face mask and hand sanitizers. As the COVID-19 situation has evolved since then, this has been removed under the Health sector and will be informed during the EAP final report.

Additionally, considering the current slow evolution of the flood situation, it was decided to increase the operational timeframe of the activation from two to three months.

Belize may start feeling the effects of the storm on Thursday night. As of now, Hurricane Beryl is a Category 5 hurricane in the Caribbean Sea. 

There is a high-pressure system expected to force the hurricane on a more westward track. However, there is significant uncertainty regarding the projected area of landfall, with possible impacts ranging from southern Belize to the northern Yucatán Peninsula. The strongest concentration of projected landfall is estimated in northern Belize.

Northern Belize is already experiencing flooding due to previous rains, which could exacerbate the impact of Hurricane Beryl.

This hurricane marks a historic event as the first major hurricane in June during what is expected to be an above-average active season. 

Today, further evaluations will provide a clearer picture of whether Belize will be directly impacted by the system. 

Ronald Gordon, Chief MET Officer, stated: "There is a high level of uncertainty, so we cannot precisely predict the landfall at this time."

summary:
BERYL is moving quickly and will enter the Southeast and Central Caribbean Sea overnight and is forecast to pass over Jamaica or very close to this island, this Wednesday, July 3. Transverse winds from the west will likely exert shear effects on its conglomerate of convective cells and could weaken it. Another factor that could contribute to its weakening is its interaction with the mainland when it makes contact with Jamaica. However, even though the minimum central pressure of this cyclonic system could increase slightly and its sustained winds could decrease in intensity, BERYL would continue to be a highly destructive hurricane. As for the territory of Panama, although the center of BERYL will be, along its trajectory, at a relatively large distance from Panama, its cloud bands (spiral arms) together with its rotation in a counter-clockwise direction could exert a suction effect of the humidity of the Pacific displacing it towards the Pacific coast of our country. In its path through the Caribbean basin, the maximum approach of BERYL to Panama, taking the city of Colón as a reference, will be approximately 1015 km. As you can see, this cyclonic system will pass quite far from our territory. 

The National Civil Protection System (SINAPROC) reports that a watch warning is maintained for conditions of a storm surge (waves generated by a tropical cyclone) in the Caribbean Sea, from July 03 to 04 , 2024.

Eastern Caribbean: Costa Arriba de Colón and Guna Yala region with waves between 0.9-1.8 meters high and periods 8.0-12.0 seconds.

summary:
The Arrondissement of Vélé, in the department of Mayo-Danay, received on July 03
2024, 148 households or 838 people following clashes between two brotherly peoples
in neighbouring Chad.  These families crossed the border to flee the violence and temporarily found refuge in the premises of the Group 1 and 2 primary schools in Vélé, Guémé, Dobo and others with their acquaintances and host families. The localities in conflict are those of Magaye, Mbouktang, Moulsou against Fara, Tchodira, Hidig and Soumai. The victims who crossed the border into Cameroon are mainly from the localities of Magaye and Mbouktang.

According to the concordant information collected within this displaced community, this pitched fight starts from the fact that two  young initiates who were chasing a dog to its home beat the dog as well as its owner. The neighbors intervened and the exchange turned into a pitched fight.
The toll of the first fight is one (01) dead and more than 20 injured.
Three (03) days after the death, following a purification rite during which the victim's family would have  deposited ashes in the opposing camp, a second clash more violent than the previous one would have broken out causing  one (01) death and many serious injuries currently under intensive care in some health facilities Chad and Cameroon. It was following this second clash that some families fled to Cameroon. It should be noted that these localities are not at their first experience of pitched fights, but on a smaller scale, which  have often led to internal displacement within Chad.  The scale of this fight forced the victims this time to make a cross-border movement. This trip to Cameroon
This is due to the proximity of their village of origin to certain localities in Mayo Danay, as well as the similarity of ethnic and social considerations between the localities.

Arrivals on Cameroonian territory are taking place gradually because it seems that aggressions continue. The first reception sites in the Vele district are full, so the new arrivals have settled in koko school and Balgam in Kai-kai district, with host families and others are under the stars exposed to bad weather of all kinds.

Informed of the situation, the Mayo-Danay Departmental Committee of the Red Cross represented by its President as well as the Disaster Manager and 10 volunteers, carried out a rapid assessment of the situation. This assessment reports the presence of nearly 148 households for 838  people, a large number of people with special needs within these displaced families: 131 pregnant women; 164 nursing women; 318 children under 5 years old and 39 elderly people. These numbers continue to grow. Displaced families also report the loss  of material goods, their homes, small/large ruminants, poultry, clothes, kitchen utensils, blankets, food, food,
mats, jerry cans and provisions, etc. They thus find themselves in a state of extreme precariousness. And if nothing is done, the situation could get worse, exposing the host communities at the same time.

The Sub-Prefect of the district of Vele and his staff as well as the Mayor of the municipality of Vele visited the various sites to inquire about the situation. They called for community solidarity and that of local elites. The district health chief donated a bundle of mosquito nets to the most vulnerable.

To date, no humanitarian organization has been on the ground.
